10 Best Snowshoes for Winter Hiking (2026)

💡 Key Takeaways
  • For winter snowshoeing on hiking trails and in the backcountry, you want a durable snowshoe with aggressive crampons for traction and a secure binding system that locks your boots to the snowshoes.
  • Sources indicate that winter hiking snowshoes serve two key functions: they provide traction on icy trails and when climbing steep terrain, and they provide flotation over snow, so you don’t sink or posthole, which can be quite exhausting.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For winter snowshoeing on hiking trails and in the backcountry, you want a durable snowshoe with aggressive crampons for traction and a secure binding system that locks your boots to the snowshoes. If you want to get off the grid and snowshoe through backcountry terrain, here are our 10 recommended snowshoes. For more information, see our buying advice below.

Sources indicate that winter hiking snowshoes serve two key functions: they provide traction on icy trails and when climbing steep terrain, and they provide flotation over snow, so you don’t sink or posthole, which can be quite exhausting. While all the winter hiking snowshoes listed above meet both requirements, some excel in traction, like the MSR Lightning Ascents, MSR Evo Ascents, and Tubbs Flex VRTs, while others emphasize flotation, like the Tubbs Mountaineers.

According to recent reports, as a rule of thumb, teardrop-shaped snowshoes with synthetic, riveted decks tend to emphasize flotation, while rectangular snowshoes focus more on traction. If you’ll be climbing ice-covered mountains mostly, you’ll probably want a snowshoe that emphasizes traction; snowshoes that focus on flotation are better for areas where deep, powdery snow is the norm.

If you’re trying to choose between different snowshoes, there are four key properties that should guide your decision-making:.

Industry observers note that most winter hikers carry multiple traction devices and switch between them during the day. If you’re hiking a packed trail, you might start in bare boots, relying on your boot treads for traction because less weight on your feet means you’ll fatigue more slowly. If you hit slick or icy terrain, you might switch to microspikes, then snowshoes if you encounter fresh, uncompacted snow or slush.

To have these traction aids when you need them, you need to carry them. Microspikes are pretty easy to pack, but snowshoes aren’t because they’re big and bulky. Their bulk comes from their length, width, and thickness, which depends largely on the binding style they use. Lay-flat bindings, like the simple straps on the MSR Lightning Ascent and the MSR Evo Ascent, make snowshoes easy to attach and carry in a backpack, while snowshoes with Boa binding systems tend to be the bulkiest and hardest to pack.

Weight is also a key factor when choosing a snowshoe. Most snowshoes weigh four to five pounds, and they’re probably going to be the heaviest thing in your backpack, after water. That weight adds up over the course of a day, whether it’s in your backpack or on your feet.

We’ve already considered the packability of snowshoe bindings, but you should also consider comfort, security, ease of use while wearing gloves, whether the binding can freeze and become inoperative, and how easy it is to repair if it breaks. For example, some people worry that Boa closure systems can freeze if they get wet and stop working until they thaw. It’s a valid concern. One advantage, however, is that they are easy to use while wearing gloves and provide a secure grip that’s unlikely to come undone once set. Contrast that to the flat straps used on MSR snowshoes. They’ll never freeze up, they’re easy to replace if torn or lost, but they can be hard to attach when wearing gloves, and they tend to pop open once or twice during a hike.

Snowshoes come in a wide variety of sizes. These are determined by the total weight you want to carry (body weight + pack weight) and the flotation you need. Men’s sizes are usually larger than women’s because men are taller and heavier, while women’s snowshoes tend to be narrower because their gait is narrower.

If you’re buying a more traction-oriented snowshoe, you can sometimes drop a size below the manufacturer’s recommendation, especially if you’re hiking in an area that doesn’t get much snow or on trails that other hikers have already broken out. Sizing is directly correlated to gear weight and this is a tactic you can use to lighten your load. If flotation is a priority, you can buy tails, add-on snowshoe extensions that make them longer and increase their surface area. This is another way to cut down on the weight of a snowshoe because you can bring your tails when you need more flotation, but carry a lighter-weight snowshoe in less challenging conditions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that one summer evening, I was hiking a trail near Marias Pass in Glacier National Park, returning to the car after a few hours of wildlife photography at a lake— nothing but deer and mosquitoes to show for it—when I noticed something blondish-brown moving toward me. It barely registered. I felt relaxed, though, truthfully, I’m never fully relaxed.

And then we were on top of each other.

Industry observers note that A grizzly cub, major as an overgrown Saint Bernard. I was fascinated—until reality hit. The mother wouldn’t be far behind.

According to recent reports, “Hey, bear,” I shouted, my voice cracking. The cub woofed an alarm and took off to my left, a dark blur swallowed by the forest.

In a recent development, I turned toward the trail ahead. And—boom—there she was. Running at me, massive and fast and flat to the ground.

It has been revealed that I grabbed the bear spray strapped to my chest, fumbled the can free, and held it out like a pistol. She closed in. I could see the whites.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo.
  • He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio.
  • According to recent reports, the wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Excerpted from the novel Nearshore (Viking, 2026).

Sources indicate that palmer was midspan on the Tunitas Creek Bridge, southbound, when the boat came into view through the gunsight notch of the arroyo. It was a Whaler circling clockwise fast and tight, maybe a quarter mile beyond the surf.

He’d wanted to ride a few waves at a sandbar that had been assembling itself over the past few days at Pomponio. A quick lunch-break session before the wind came up. But then he got the call about the boat, and now that he saw it spinning he also saw that his day was officially fucked. He crossed the bridge and powered up the Coast Highway to the overlook at the top of the rise. He lifted his Bushnells from the dashboard and got out of the truck and glassed the vessel.

According to recent reports, the wake’s widening spiral told him the wheel had been hard to starboard a good long while. It looked to be stirring up some kind of suicidal whirlpool.

The first thing you notice in an abandoned Spanish village is the swallows.

Outside, they swoop zestfully up and down in wavy crests and troughs, cutting through the air, darting through broken windows and front doors at reckless speed, slipping through holes in the masonry with astonishing precision, and alighting, casually, in their chosen nests. It’s as if they know every corner of the building. It’s as if they own the place.

#44710. We Decoyed Major Bull Moose in the Alaska High Country

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3546 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

We Decoyed Major Bull Moose in the Alaska High Country

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3546 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As we loaded our gear into the bush planes, Bruce Werba offered one last piece of advice.
  • I’d spent enough time in the Alaskan backcountry over the years that he wasn’t going to get an argument from me.
  • Our squadron consisted of three Super Cubs with tundra tires.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As we loaded our gear into the bush planes, Bruce Werba offered one last piece of advice. “Be sure to use all 44 stakes. It’ll get windy up there—I guarantee it.”.

I’d spent enough time in the Alaskan backcountry over the years that he wasn’t going to get an argument from me.

Our squadron consisted of three Super Cubs with tundra tires. I folded myself into the cramped space behind the pilot where the rest of my gear was stored, my shoulders touching both sides of the fuselage. We lifted off the gravel runway that’s the primary connection between the 160 souls who call Holy Cross, Alaska, home and the rest of the world, and banked over the wide and muddy Yukon River before my pilot, Matt, put us on a westerly bearing.

According to recent reports, we were in the air for nearly an hour, heading into the Yukon Delta National Wildlife Refuge, a massive region that borders the Bering Sea and is bigger than the state of Maine. I took mental note of the terrain we flew over, a mix of pine-­covered mountains, tundra, vast patches of willows, and countless bogs, ponds, and rivers. It occurred to me that if, for whatever reason, we had to trek out on foot, we’d probably never make it back.

Industry observers note that over the roar of the engine, Matt shouted that we were approaching our landing zone. He made a large circle over an exposed flat that was surrounded by mountains on three sides to make sure he could put us down safely.

He pointed the nose of the plane into the stiff easterly wind for the final approach, and we bounced to a standstill in a matter of feet. He jumped out of the cockpit and signaled by hand to the other pilots to help them land.

According to recent reports, as soon as the three planes were down, the pilots swiftly pitched our gear onto the tundra and just as quickly took off. “Good luck,” Matt stated before firing up his engine. Time is money for these guys, and they weren’t wasting any of it.

It has been revealed that the three of us looked around at the place that would be home for the next 12 days. I was with my longtime friend Jason Nash, who works at Federal Ammunition, and photographer Tom Fowlks. This was Jason’s first moose hunt, and we had decided to do it on our own terms: getting dropped off in the wilderness during the rut and calling bulls.

Recent findings suggest that we had to manhandle our tent, which was bucking in the strong wind, to get it set up. The forecast noted the prevailing winds for the next 10 days would be out of the south, so we oriented the entrance toward the north and, with Werba’s admonition in mind, pounded all 44 stakes deep into the rocky soil with large stones.

Industry observers note that werba, who runs Alaska Pike Safaris with his wife, Connie, is a bit of a legend in Alaskan outfitting circles. He has the friendly demeanor of everyone’s favorite grandpa (he’s in his 70s), but is almost inhumanly tough. That spring, a few months before our trip, he’d had a heart attack while guiding pike fishermen and wasn’t able to get to a doctor in Anchorage until four days later—yet he was back on the job in a matter of days, doing work that would grind down a man half his age. His reputation for putting both his guided and self-guided hunters on significant bulls is why I sought him out. I’ve been on half a dozen moose hunts over the years and have killed three, but I’d never had a chance on a true monster—one of those gaggers in the mid-60s that just takes your breath away—until now.

Recent findings suggest that while Jason and Tom set up the cots in the tent, I dug a pit and lined it with a tarp that I weighted down with rocks to collect drinking water from the rains that were sure to come. Once the camp was set, we fired up the stove, heated water, and ate freeze-dried spaghetti and beef stroganoff straight from the bag. We had some bourbon to celebrate the start of the adventure, half a bottle disappearing with alarming speed. We’d only purchased two bottles back in Anchorage, a nod to modesty that the three of us instantly regretted. For the rest of the trip, we invoked emergency rationing.

It rained heavily that first night, and the wind beat on our tent, making the rainfly snap and pop like a flag in a gale. The next morning, I fiddled with the guide lines until I got the rigging right, and the tent quieted down.

After downing mugs of instant coffee, we explored our outpost. The broad flat was covered in tundra with patches of gravel and a few small stands of pine and willow. Everywhere I looked I could see bushes laden with ripe blueberries, and dark crowberries carpeted the ground.

In a recent development, both ends of the flat, which was about three-quarters of a mile long, gave commanding vistas of the country. The north end overlooked a long, broad valley rimmed by mountains that descended to a river about a mile away. To the south, we had views of more mountains and the upper reaches of a pine-forested draw that dropped steeply down to god knows where. I hoped that if a good bull were down there, I could coax it out of the timber—because there was no way on Earth I’d chase one into that hellhole.

A large grizzly came through our camp at lunch. We were back at the tent, comparing notes and eating sandwiches, when he appeared. He angled slowly toward our tent, head down, eating berries. He was a massive brute: small ears, broad across his shoulders and rump, sagging belly. I couldn’t tell what his hide would have squared—I’m not particularly good at that—but he was a toad. If I were chasing grizzlies, he’s exactly the kind of bear I’d be looking for.

Recent findings suggest that as it was, the three of us just watched him strut our way. The wind was at his back, and he hadn’t noticed the interlopers on his turf. He dropped down and rolled on his back like an enormous dog, trying to deal with the swarm of bugs around him. We stood there, Jason and I, with rounds chambered in our .30/06s, as he cruised past us at 75 yards. Later that afternoon, while glassing for bulls, I saw him through the spotter about 2 miles away on a mountain, still going.

Our hunting technique wasn’t complicated. We had two cow moose decoys and a makeshift moose paddle that consisted of a white mesh game bag I had stretched over a wire hanger. Because the wind rarely let up, we put one decoy in a small willow-choked gap on the edge of the northern lookout, where any bull to the north or west of us would see it.

Sources indicate that from a spot above and behind the decoy, we’d glass while calling every 10 minutes or so. Cupping my hands over my mouth, I’d wail like a lonely estrous moose, emptying my lungs for all they were worth. Sometimes I’d mix in bull calls, a deep, guttural mwah that to me always sounds like an old man grieving some terrible loss.

The wind picked up, and fog and rain rolled in, which cut our visibility to a couple hundred yards but provided relief from the swarms of tiny black flies that pounced whenever the breeze died. We had Thermacells to help with the mosquitos, but they didn’t dissuade those psychotic little bloodsuckers. Only our full-face bug nets and a liberal dousing with pure DEET kept them at bay.

On the fourth day, I spotted my first moose. I was trudging across the tundra, working toward the south end of the flat to glass, when I saw the cow in a small patch of willows. She’d spotted me too, and even though 700 yards separated us, that was too close for her, so she turned around and loped over the hill and out of view. Watching moose cover ground is an impressive sight. Standing still, they are awkward-looking creatures, but nothing moves through rough terrain the way they can, like skaters on ice. They can run through timber blowdowns that would stop any two-legged hunter in their tracks.

I posted up on an exposed knob that was flanked by several large willows, giving me some cover from which to glass the area. At one point, I watched a nervous-­looking black bear work back and forth across the hillside that dropped into the hellhole. He was eating berries in the same patch I’d walked through a couple of days before. Between mouthfuls, he’d pop up on his hind legs and look around before grabbing some more. After 20 minutes, he saw or smelled something he didn’t like and beelined into the depths of the dark timber.

Recent findings suggest that by the end of the day, I was tired and scanning on autopilot. So when I swung my binocular to the right and got a full-frame view of a grizzly walking toward me, the adrenaline surge felt like a physical blow.

Once my lungs and heart started to work in concert again, I took another look. Like the grizzly that had strolled through our camp, he was a significant bear, walking with the assured saunter of an apex predator.

Recent findings suggest that he was 300 yards away, and while he wasn’t walking fast, his every step was bringing him right to me. It was getting late, and the light was failing. Even though I was well-armed with both my .30/06 and a .44 on my hip, I wanted to give the bear his space. So in the spirit of General O.P. Smith, commander of the 1st Marine Division at the Chosin Reservoir, who remarked, “Retreat, hell! We’re not retreating, we’re just advancing in another direction,” I packed my gear and headed back toward the tent, glancing over my shoulder every few seconds to make sure the griz wasn’t closing the gap.

According to recent reports, before I could make it to camp, I spotted Jason and Tom walking toward me. They were both grinning.

In a recent development, jason told me that earlier that day, he had called in a bull and gotten a good look at him. He judged it at slightly larger than 50 inches. Many places in Alaska impose a 50-inch minimum on nonresidents, but we happened to be in an any-bull area, so his main concern was just making sure it was a mature bull. The most common way to size up a moose’s rack is to wait for it to face you, then compare the width of the antlers to the distance between its eyes.

According to recent reports, measured from the outside corners, a bull moose’s eyes are about 10 inches apart. So, if the antlers extend at least two eye-widths off the side of its head, you’re at 50 inches.

It has been revealed that during that first encounter, Jason let the bull melt back into the willows. We still had many days to hunt, the rut hadn’t hit its peak, and the promise of a mythical 65-incher kept his finger off the trigger.

But later, when the bull reappeared, again drawn by Jason’s calls, that logic flew out the window. Jason couldn’t resist, and his 160-yard shot took the bull through the shoulder, and it piled up in a shallow ravine in the willows. His smile told me he had no regrets.

The grizzly that had been trailing behind me vanished, but we still had bears on our mind as we put on our headlamps to recover the bull. The terrain down in the willow thickets is featureless in daylight; at night, it’s a maze.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, we found the moose and got to work. It was a long, wet night. A pea-soup fog rolled in and gave the kill site an otherworldly feel. We managed to get the hide off, the moose quartered, and the first loads—the rear hinds—strapped to our backs. The fog rendered our headlamps nearly useless, blinding us more than lighting our way.

Industry observers note that the hike to camp was less than half a mile, but it was all uphill and through the boggy tundra with more than 130 pounds of meat and bone on our backs. By the time we crested the final hill, my legs were shaking, and it was 5 a.m.

Jason groaned. “That’s some Navy SEAL shit.”.

We each took a shot of bourbon and tried to dry off as best as possible before crawling into our sleeping bags, but by this point in the hunt, everything was wet, and our tent smelled like a sweatshop. The next day, we hauled the remaining meat, cape, and antlers back to camp. By then it was raining hard, and our first priority was to protect the venison. Tom took the camp ax and cut down a few small pine trees so we could build a lean-to against the side of the tent to keep the meat dry. We chopped off the boughs to make a bed, and tied sections of the trunks together with paracord to form a frame over which we draped tarps.

According to recent reports, after removing the meat from the bags, we dumped a Costco-size container of pepper on it to keep the flies away. We spread the game bags on the branches and put the meat on top of the bags. As the smell of the spiced fresh meat hit my nostrils, I salivated like one of Pavlov’s dogs.

Sources indicate that I called Bruce Werba on the sat phone to let him know we had a batch of meat to fly out. But the clouds and fog were keeping all the planes grounded.

When I asked when the conditions might shift, he remarked, “Be patient.” When I told him about our scant moose sightings, he repeated that mantra. “Be patient. It can change at any moment.”.

Recent findings suggest that of course, we didn’t have a choice in the matter. The weather was going to do what it would do, and the same with the moose. So we went back to glassing as the rain and the temperature fell.

Sources indicate that the very next day, I spotted a good bull high on the mountains behind us to the east. He was feeding up a draw to a saddle. I cow-called and he paused but didn’t turn around or look my way. Eventually, he crested the ridge and vanished.

It rained nonstop for the next three days, a cold downpour that finally managed to defeat my Gore-Tex rainwear, making for some truly miserable glassing. Every few hours I’d return to the tent to heat water and make coffee or hot cider to stop the shivering.

It has been revealed that at night, our tent offered a fragile haven from the elements, rocking back and forth like a ship in the violent winds that Werba had predicted. The lantern above our heads created a small pocket of warm air at the top of the tent, and we hung our wet gloves and socks around it each night in the hopes they would dry. Much of our conversation turned to how best to stay warm. We stuffed the edges of our sleeping bags with extra clothes, and I started wearing my down jacket as I slept, even though it, too, was wet.

Read Next: A DIY Caribou Hunting Adventure in Alaska.

On day 10, I saw two more bulls. The first looked to be in the mid-50s and had three brow tines on each side. He was angling toward the river, and I last saw him at 500 yards as he went into the timber. I figured he’d show again later so I could get a better look at his antlers, but I was wrong—he was gone for good.

At the end of the day, I called in a bull in the low 50s. It had gotten foggy again, so we didn’t have much visibility, but I watched him come my way through the willows as he tipped his rack from one side to the other. He walked right below my perch, almost within bow shot.

That night, another bear came into camp and dragged Jason’s rack away. We found it 50 yards downhill the next morning. A couple of the points on one paddle had been chewed, and we could see where the bear had scraped bits of meat off the skull. Fortunately, the bear hadn’t worked up the courage to raid our stash of meat under the tarp’s lean-to. He had, however, left an impressive pile of brilliant purple scat next to the tent that, in my addled state, looked like the filling for a delicious blueberry cobbler.

The fog that morning was the thickest it had been. We couldn’t see more than a hundred yards in any direction. But this was the last full day of the hunt, so I went to the northern lookout and stared into the mist. Eventually, the clouds lifted, and I glassed a pair of antlers that appeared like the sails on a man-of-war emerging from a fog bank about 800 yards away.

In a recent development, he was with three other moose: a cow, her calf, and a spindly-horned young bull. After a closer look, I realized he was the smaller bull that we’d already called in several times. There was no calling him today, however: His intentions regarding the cow were unmistakable. He separated her from the calf like a cutting horse. She tried to get back to her calf a dozen times, but he was faster and stronger and herded her off into the willows as the younger bull and the calf watched.

And that was the last moose of the trip.

In a recent development, that night we polished off the bourbon and ate the final bags of Mountain House lasagna, which we had saved for the occasion. I got Werba on the sat phone the next morning. The good news was the weather had cleared and the Super Cubs could take off from Holy Cross to collect us. More good news came in that his self-guided hunters who had been on the river had done well. One shot a 68-inch bull, and another had dropped a 74-incher.

Werba noted he was sorry the substantial boys hadn’t worked their way up higher, and that none of the mountain hunters had shot toads. The weather had been too warm to get the huge bulls moving, and that was that. Whenever your heart is set on a trophy animal, leaving with an unpunched tag is always a possibility. Truth is, I didn’t mind. Jason got a terrific bull, we’d had the great adventure we came for, and I knew at some point I’d return to the Lower Yukon to try again.

After I hung up with Werba, the three of us pulled the 44 stakes from the ground, packed up, and looked to the sky, waiting to hear the drone of motors of the airplanes that would take us home.

Moose are big animals, but they aren’t especially difficult to bring down. Even moderate cartridges work well on them. In Sweden and Canada, more moose have been killed with the 6.5×55 Swede and the .303 British than anything else, and neither are punishing to shoot. As always, shot placement and bullet construction are the key factors.

Sources indicate that on this hunt, Jason and I were both carrying .30/06s. My rifle (above) was built for the elements. I used a stainless Shilen DGR action and Shilen barrel with a Manner’s EH-1A stock and topped it with a 2.5–15×44 Maven RS.1. The rig handled the cold and wet without any problems.

Sources indicate that one reason I went with the .30/06 was to try out some of Federal’s upcoming loads. After several years’ hiatus, Federal is working with bullet-makers beyond the Vista Outdoor family of brands. (Vista is Federal’s parent firm.) So, once again, hunters can get Federal Premium cartridges topped with bullets from Barnes, Nosler, Hornady, Berger, and others. I’m glad these companies have decided to kiss and make up.

Read Next: I Spent 12 Days Trapped with a Moose Guide Who Wouldn’t Give Up.

I shot the 165-grain Barnes TSX, which, thanks to its monolithic construction, plows deep into whatever you’re shooting, smashing through hide and bones, and retains nearly all of its weight.

Industry observers note that jason used a 180-grain Nosler Accubond, which I think is about the best all-around big-game bullet made. It is accurate, mushrooms beautifully, penetrates well, and does everything a bullet is supposed to. Another benefit of these projectiles is they would work well on grizzlies. Just in case.

This story was originally published in a 2019 Concern of Outdoor Life.

Backyard Ultras Are Booming. Here’s Why.

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2986 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024.
  • In a recent development, it’s 8:55 P.M.
  • Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024. (Don’t ask him about the race name grammar.) He also spoke with backyard ultra mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell, several other backyard ultra race directors, and key backyard ultra runners, including Harvey Lewis and Maggie Guterl. What he found is that the format of running a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until only one runner remains is about so much more than running in circles. Since this article was originally published on Outside Run in 2024, backyard ultras have further entered the mainstream with the rise of figures like Mark Dowdle, Belgium resetting the world record, and Team USA winning the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship.

In a recent development, it’s 8:55 P.M. on Friday, August 9, and I’m with a small group of runners huddled together in a tent on a farm near Greeley, Colorado, that momentarily shelters us from our bad life decisions.

Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.

Sources indicate that before the starting gun of this backyard ultra goes off in five minutes, Jessy Nelson needs to make an announcement. I’m assuming it will be about safety. Instead, she tells us that she is not a narcissist.

In a recent development, yes, Jess’ Backyard Ultra does carry her name. But she named the race for about a dozen friends, all named Jess. (Seriously!). She met them all in an online chat group during a 1,000-kilometer Great Virtual Race Across The States.

Nelson started the race on her farm for them in 2021 with the hope that one Jess could run far enough to qualify for Major’s Backyard Ultra—the original Bell Buckle, Tennessee, “backyard ultra” event that pioneered a quirky new kind of endurance racing format in which runners must complete a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until they can no longer accomplish the task.

In a recent development, for the record, this event is Jess’ Big Backyard Ultra, not Jessy’s. Understand?

We nod as the rain comes down harder. It would be a fun, goofy, quaint little race that seems to match the aesthetic of many backyard ultras across the world, except it’s been raining for three days, transforming the dirt roads on which we will run into what seems like gooey Jello pudding.

Nelson is worried. The Plank of Doom is seriously dangerous, she tells us. Sure, it’s pink and twinkly, but the four-foot fall that could result with any misstep could mean a broken ankle or, according to Nelson’s narrowed eyes, instant death. Nelson is so serious about the plank that she forces the four of us competing to vote to keep it on the course instead of bypassing it through a paved road 100 yards to the south. We vote to keep it, 3-1.

It’s hard to take anything Nelson says seriously, given that this is a race seemingly held on the set of Little House on the Prairie and that a stuffed toy squirrel named Skittles awaits us in a rocking chair at the turnaround to our 4-ish-mile loop. One of the Jesses befriended a squirrel in her backyard, you see, and that’s a tribute to her. Nelson once befriended an eagle, who would follow her during her daily 10-mile loops around her property. But now, she presumes, the eagle is taking cover. We are about to do the opposite.

Nelson’s odd race is now one of an estimated 500 backyard ultras held around the world that are certified by concept creator Gary Cantrell. You may know him as Lazarus Lake, or simply Laz. He is  probably the sport’s most famous race director and certainly  the quirkiest. Cantrell is known first and foremost for creating the Barkley Marathons, a grueling 100-plus-mile largely off-trail race in Tennessee that’s considered to be the world’s hardest running race to complete. While there’s only one Barkley Marathons, Cantrell’s backyard race format has boomed over the past five years or so.

There is no predefined end length or time in a backyard ultra, as long as multiple runners can complete each 4.167-mile loop within an hour. (Cantrell chose that peculiar distance because running 4.167 miles per hour is exactly what it takes to run 100 miles in 24 hours.) A race ends when only one runner remains to complete a lap and is declared the winner, while all other runners are relegated to did not finish (DNF) status with whatever total number of laps they are able to complete. The runner who completes the second-most laps in a race is often referred to as the “assist,” in the sense that their effort is ultimately what determines how long the race is allowed to continue.

Industry observers note that most backyard races are not like Cantrell’s Big’s Backyard Ultra, which, even though it maintains a grassroots feel, has gained worldwide fame and is filled with elite runners. Most backyard races are more like Nelson’s: small, fun and grueling little get-togethers that last a couple days and bring most runners to tears. Most backyard race directors are like Nelson, too; they have“real” jobs outside of race directing and simply love the format and camaraderie their events foster amid runners of all ability levels pushing  themselves beyond what they ever thought possible.

Sources indicate that when Cantrell started his race and named it after his pit bull, Massive, in 2012, he hoped to have enough interest for just one event. He was pleasantly surprised when people asked if there would be another race the following  year. Now tens of thousands will likely tune in to the livestream to watch this year’s race on October 19. Cantrell guesstimates more than 25,000 people have run in a backyard ultra event this year, and those are just in the races he’s certified: He knows there are probably dozens more who don’t bother with the paperwork.

In a recent development, “The continued growth really has been a surprise for me,” Cantrell mentioned. Indeed, there are backyard races in 83 countries now. Even the renowned Tarahumara tribe of Indigenous people from Chihuahua, Mexico, (aka the Raramuri people, who were profiled in the 2009 Upcoming York Times bestseller Born to Run,) have their own race, Cantrell noted.

It has been revealed that cantrell relishes putting on the world’s hardest events, almost to a sadistic degree. Only 20 individuals have finished the Barkley Marathons since he began it in 1986. It’s a race as ominous as its location, Frozen Head State Park in Tennessee. The race, over 100 miles with a staggering 65,000-feet-plus of elevation gain, is a miserable quest for survival through thorn-infested bramble, often terrible weather, and ridiculously steep hills on a “course” with no real route.

Recent findings suggest that he started Major’s as another way to test people, and at times, it resembles Stephen King’s The Long Walk, a fictional horror story about 100 walkers who are forced to trudge hundreds of miles and are shot when they quit. Big’s format is also horrifyingly simple: Run 4.167 miles, a “yard,” in under an hour, and then line up and do it again, and again, and again, on the hour, until one person is left. No breaks from the on-the-hour start are allowed, not even to use the porta-potty, but if you finish the yard early, you can eat and drink to your heart’s content, sleep a few minutes, and yes, answer nature’s call. Last year’s winner, accomplished Cinncinnati ultrarunner Harvey Lewis, set a world record by running 450 miles over 108 hours—or four and a half days.

Cantrell now finds himself surprised not only by the race format’s popularity but also the allure many runners have found in the design. These backyard races are, like Nelson’s race, more about community and the comradery of people pushing each other to go farther than they ever have than about fighting your competitors to the near death. While the format becomes exponentially more grueling over time as variables like sleep deprivation escalate, for the first 24 hours or so, the backyard ultra format is an approachable way for many to cover a very long distance. And Cantrell admits that he likes what these mom and pop backyard races have become.

“There are a lot of aspects to it that I didn’t really consider,” he mentioned. “I do know we get a lot of people who never thought they could ever run an ultra. It’s a race for everyone.”.

Cantrell thought of the idea for a backyard race close to 50 years ago, when he was in high school struggling to keep up with the fast kids on his track team during interval workouts. He noticed by the end of an interval he was often a little closer to their heels.

Recent findings suggest that “I’d get left in the dust early, but eventually, I’d wear them down,” he said. “So in a 4-mph race, I thought I could beat everybody.”.

According to recent reports, the idea stayed in the recesses of his mind until he could do something about it on his property in central Tennessee. He didn’t have the money to put on a massive race, but with the format, all he needed was a stopwatch.

Industry observers note that “This format doesn’t require very much,” Cantrell noted. “I think that’s why it’s caught on.”.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also caught on because it’s spectator-friendly—both online and in person—perhaps more so than any other race not on a track. It not only made a household name out of Lewis but acted as a coming-out party for Courtney Dauwalter when the two went head-to-head for nearly 20 hours in 2020 and ran a total of 283 miles before Dauwalter outlasted him by a lap and won. Cantrell remarked this was another aspect of the race he didn’t consider, and it’s partly what makes it fun.

“Women are on an equal competitive footing with men,” he said, and indeed, Maggie Guterl also won Substantial’s Backyard Ultra, now considered the format’s national championship, in 2019.

The format, Cantrell remarked, is supposed to measure willpower, not VO2 max or speed or other aspects of physiological talent. There are enough races for that. Instead, Massive’s measures grit—the one thing he had over those speedy, more talented guys on the track in high school.

“The most challenging part,” Cantrell said, “should be the distance between the chair and the starting corral.”.

Sources indicate that tens of thousands were captivated last year by Lewis’s win, his second at Significant’s Backyard, which Cantrell now livestreams and provides real-time written commentary. Lewis was already well known for winning the 135-mile Badwater Ultramarathon in 2014, but he wasn’t taken seriously as a trail runner when he first entered Big’s in 2017, he said.

“I like the trails though,” Lewis remarked. “I’m very strategic. They were doing it wrong. Everyone was running up the first hill, and I was in the back, just walking up. The next day, everyone walked up the hill.”.

Lewis kept going even after making a lap by just a second. He eventually gave in after 200 miles, taking the assist, but it made him wonder just how far he could go. He decided to devote part of his life to it.

It has been revealed that “Massive’s is so great,” Lewis said. “You’re walking into an ultimate game board, with strategy, perseverance, and skill level. The course itself is nothing special, and it’s usually that way with a lot of them. The genius is behind the format.”.

Sources indicate that lewis races at Major’s to win, no doubt, but as a teacher at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati his living does not depend on it. (Good thing, as there’s no prize money anyway.), Despite his competitive drive, he’s learned to relish in the non-competitive moments on the course and treasures his two assists as much as his wins.

Industry observers note that last year, he says his goal was as much to help get runners through the third night as it was to outlast them all. He remembers 2020 mostly for the way he and Dauwalter spent nearly a full day and night taking turns leading the race and pushing each other to approach 300 miles, a number that was, at the time, unheard of to run in this format. Lewis called it a “collaboration” instead of a race. It was a much-needed feel-good story during the pandemic delivered by two nice people.

“We were very encouraging of each other,” Lewis noted.

Recent findings suggest that this is one of the evolutions of the race that took Cantrell by surprise: Backyard races build community among runners with different ability levels because of the unique format. Many other ultras around the world are in intimidating places for beginners, but the accessible four-mile loop obliterates those fears.

Mandy Mullen, the owner of run.Windsor in Windsor, Colorado, changed the format from a 50K to a backyard race for her Weld Your Mettle ultramarathon because it helped foster that community aspect.

Industry observers note that “There’s so much more to running than just running,” Mullen said. “In this the competition goes away, and it’s more teamwork. There’s zero of, ‘I want to beat this person.’”.

It has been revealed that katie Stroud is the president of a running and walking club that’s existed since 1979 in Alice Springs, a small town in the desert of Australia. She hosted the second annual backyard ultra this year as a part of the races the club puts on.

“It’s such a terrific format for people to push their distance in such a wonderful and supportive way,” Stroud said. “It’s so much more than people running in circles.”.

Sources indicate that indeed, Cantrell believes more people ran 100 miles in 24 hours, a benchmark so elite that races usually give out special belt buckles to those who do it, this year in backyard events than all the other ultramarathons around the world combined. The final two left standing this year in Alice Springs, Stroud stated, were running buddies who just wanted to push each other to 100 miles.

Recent findings suggest that “There are all these little moments like that in our event every year,” Stroud remarked. “It’s really cool to be there for that.”.

Carl Worth was another one who caught the backyard bug. Even though he’d never run more than a half marathon, he ran the virtual backyard race during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and astonished himself by covering 54 miles. He liked the camaraderie and community of backyard running so much he began organizing the Banana Slug Backyard Ultra the following year in Oregon’s Champoeg State Park.

At this year’s event, the winner ran for 49 hours and 200 miles for a “Silver Ticket,” which qualifies him for Big’s Backyard, since the Slug was one of the six events where the winner qualified him for the World Team Championships.

According to recent reports, but Worth prefers not to focus only on the winner. During the race, he puts up a spreadsheet on a TV—he’s a software engineer by trade—and posts everyone’s longest distance they’ve run. Whenever they break it, and many do, they can ring a bell, a tradition that Cantrell established at his own race. At this year’s Banana Slug event, 34 runners surpassed their personal bests.

“It’s a really satisfying thing to put on as a race director,” Worth stated. “You get to see some amazing things.”.

This is true for Jess’ Backyard Ultra as well. The sun rises, illuminating the gray sky and shining some welcome light on our muddy trails. Nelson decides to take a small nap at the house. Our fourth competitor rolled her ankle in the wee hours of the morning, making my friend, Bret Naber, the winner after 30 miles, but we decided to run through the night and see how far we could go. At 9 A.M., after 12 hours and 50 miles of running through the mud, we go home for a shower and some sleep.

This year’s Massive’s Backyard Ultra on October 19 is the biannual international team competition, called the World Satellite Backyard Team Competition. Team USA will compete at Cantrell’s event in Tennessee, and the 15-member U.S. roster will have at least two women, Megan Eckert, who won the Saguaro Showdown Backyard Ultra in Mesa, Arizona, and Jennifer Russo, who won Ohio’s Backyard Ultra, as well as Lewis and Scott Martin, the three-time winner of the Banana Slug race put on by Worth.

Cantrell remarked there are 68 national teams, the members of which will compete simultaneously in backyard ultras in their home countries to earn points for their teams. It’s much like the Olympics—with each country enjoying a home field advantage—and it makes you wonder if this event will finally get ultrarunning there.

Industry observers note that “I think you have to reasonably see how it goes,” Cantrell noted. “A lot of things start up, and they are really popular, and then they fade out. Maybe somebody more politically skilled than me could get it there.”.

Recent findings suggest that but Cantrell’s favorite part about the race format isn’t the superstars, even if his own includes some of the most elite ultrarunners in the world. It’s that time isn’t a factor. It’s about the distance you run, and if you run a personal best, you get recognized for it, even if you finish 30 seconds before the bell.

“The age groups in other races are won by the same people over and over,” Cantrell mentioned. “But in this one, everyone has their day.”.

In a recent development, baboons are assholes. After leaving his birth troop at around age seven, a male will find a new one and spend his prime years trying to fang his way up the hierarchy. Once he’s gained a modicum of status, he devotes his days to terrorizing lower-ranking males and females, who only grow to half his size. Gashes, puncture wounds, and missing ears are not uncommon among baboons.

In the mid-1980s, Dr. Robert M. Sapolsky, a primatologist living in Kenya, documented an unprecedented cultural shift when he noticed that the alpha males of a baboon population suddenly vanished. The alphas had come upon a garbage dump near a tourist lodge, and they defended their spoils furiously from low-ranking males and females, who were relegated to leaves, seeds, and insects on the forest floor. One day, in the East African heat, the alphas were exposed to tainted meat at the dump, infecting them with bovine tuberculosis. They died soon after. Left behind were sixty-two baboons. The.

Tech Report: How Two WWII Fighter Pilots Hacked Through the New Guinea Jungle for the Best Duck Hunt of Their Lives

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A duck hunter is always a duck hunter.
  • According to recent reports, you duck hunters know exactly what I mean, but I doubt if any of you ever felt the old longing as much as I did that day in Fresh Guinea in February, 1943.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Ducks Can Improve Any War,” appeared in the December 1944 glitch of Outdoor Life.

A duck hunter is always a duck hunter. No matter how long he’s been away from the sport, he still longs for that song of the wind on the lake reeds. He craves the acrid smell of burning powder and the comfortable feel of his favorite gun. He never forgets the beauty of the cold gray mists of dawn, the hazy silhouettes of decoys, the tense, exciting wait, and finally, the sight of fast gray wings above him.

According to recent reports, you duck hunters know exactly what I mean, but I doubt if any of you ever felt the old longing as much as I did that day in Fresh Guinea in February, 1943. Yes, New Guinea — hot, steaming, sultry. I had been in the Pacific area for eighteen months, flying a fighter. Four of those months were combat flying. I was getting in plenty of hunting — a serious kind of hunting that I enjoyed — when late one afternoon while sitting on alert, a flock of ducks, real live ducks, passed right over our pilot’s hut and lit in a near-by swamp.

In a recent development, when those ducks flew over, two old-time duck hunters jumped to their feet and watched ’em till they’d disappeared. Then they turned and looked at each other. They didn’t say anything; they didn’t have to. One of those duck hunters was Lieut. Fred Sibley from Maine. I was the other one. And right then and there the war we were in had improved 1,000 percent.

Industry observers note that when we opened the boxes of No. 6s we found that half the shells were bloated by the damp atmosphere, and wouldn’t fit into the guns. So we had to take our knives and patiently whittle each shell down until it would slip into the chamber.

We started right in, lining things up for our next day off. We dug up a couple of old double-barrel guns from the squadron supply and, after making the rounds through several camps, found some honest-to-goodness 12 gauge ammunition a pilot had bought in Australia. We finally succeeded in heckling the officer into turning some of it over to us — by promising him a big fat duck for dinner.

Now, this was really an effective offer, since his squadron had been practically living on bully beef for six months. It didn’t hurt our consciences to take advantage of the poor man, as we knew we could feed a lot of hungry soldiers if we could get him to come across.

Anyway, we got back to camp with two boxes of No. 6’s. Later, when we opened them we found that half the shells were bloated by the damp atmosphere, and wouldn’t fit into the guns. So we had to take our knives and patiently whittle each shell down until it would slip into the chamber. Then we gave every shell a coat of grease to protect it from the humidity until the massive day.

Recent findings suggest that we had found previously from wandering around in the jungle that it was absolutely imperative for a man to sprinkle himself with some kind of sulphur as a protection against the chiggers and ticks. These tiny parasites were dangerous not only because their bites caused infections which took weeks to heal in that climate, but because they were known to carry a tropical disease. We also knew it was necessary to use mosquito lotion as millions of these pests swarmed everywhere.

In a recent development, our problem, then, was to concoct something that wouldn’t wash off our bodies when we were wading through swamps and marsh land after those ducks. We hit on the bright idea of mixing the sulphur powder with vaseline, and it worked like a charm. The mosquito lotion was no problem as we could carry plenty of it along in a small bottle. For extra protection we each obtained a mosquito head net and a pair of leggings. Two canteens of water completed our preparations in the way of equipment for the unique duck hunt.

According to recent reports, we still had a couple of days to go before our day off, so we decided to do some aërial scouting. We knew we’d be doing some flying in those remaining days, and that while on our landing patterns we would have an opportunity to study the swamp and determine the best possible way of getting into it from our camp.

To appreciate the importance of this, one must imagine a typical Florida swamp surrounded by the most dense undergrowth in which, every five or six feet, giant trees rear their heads. Undergrowth and trees are connected by a maze of hanging moss and tough vines, the only trails being pig runs and an occasional hidden native trail that no white man can follow. The only way a white man can get through such stuff is to cut and fight his way through. So our problem was to determine the spot where we could cut our way through with the least effort. We studied the jungle carefully during the next two days’ flying, and found that a few miles from our camp a grassy hill cut through the jungle to within about a quarter of a mile of the swamp. We could get to this hill easily from the camp, and figured that with the aid of a compass we should be able to bore through the jungle to the swamp itself in two or three hours. Our aims were now complete.

The big day came at last. It dawned misty and cool — for Newly introduced Guinea — as near a perfect duck-hunting day as that part of the world could have provided. And it found Fred and me hacking our way into the jungle surrounding the swamp. We looked more like a couple of jungle soldiers than we did duck hunters. We had our .45’s on our belts for use on snakes or crocodiles, and also because neither of us was sure there might not be a stray Japanese pilot hiding in the brush. We knew several had recently bailed out or crash-landed in the vicinity.

We looked more like a couple of jungle soldiers than we did duck hunters. We had our .45’s on our belts for use on snakes or crocodiles, and also because neither of us was sure there might not be a stray Japanese pilot hiding in the brush.

Our heads were covered by our mosquito nets, and our canteen and ammunition belts rattled as we whacked at the undergrowth with a big jungle knife, taking turns at hacking and resting.

All through the jungle we encountered many varieties of beautiful birds. Most of them were of the parrot or pigeon families, and were of every color of the rainbow. Some were as small as wrens, others much larger than domestic pigeons. Once we caught a glimpse of an Australian jungle turkey, a magnificent bird almost as large as the American wild turkey, but were unable to get a shot at it in the thick undergrowth. We also saw a couple of dark brown jungle chickens of the grouse variety. Later, in another part of Latest Guinea, I was fortunate enough to kill several of these birds, and they were very delicious, the meat being light and tender. But this story is about duck hunting — and what duck hunting!

In exactly one hour and thirty minutes after the first swing of our jungle knife we broke into the swamp — and, believe me, it was beautiful to behold.

“Look at them, Dave, look at them!” Fred was wild with excitement.

“Gee, it’s been a long time,” I remarked.

Ducks were everywhere — circling the swamps by the hundreds, quacking, whistling, and splashing down into the open spot among the tall reeds.

Sources indicate that we stood there just looking for a long time. Then Fred noted, “Dave, you know what we’ve got to do?”.

Ducks were everywhere — circling the swamps by the hundreds, quacking, whistling, and splashing down into the open spot among the tall reeds.

“Yes, I’m afraid I do,” I replied. “But it’s sure going to be hard to remember all the hungry people at camp when those singles start flying over. Boy! I wish we had plenty of shells.”.

“Yeah,” sighed Fred, “or not such a large family to feed.”.

I had an idea. “I’ll tell you what let’s do,” I stated. “Let’s each of us get fifteen ducks with as few shells as possible, and then use the rest of the shells for singles. That will give us at least thirty ducks to feed the sixty guys back at camp.”.

“O.K., Dave, we’ve got to do it, I guess,” agreed Fred. “It’s going to seem real unsportsmanlike to take pot-shots, but bully beef is sure getting tiresome. Let’s go!”.

Neither of us relished shooting those beautiful birds on the water, but this was one time we had to bring home the bacon.

In a recent development, we decided that since the length of the swamp lay north and south we would separate, Fred going south and I going north, this way keeping the ducks moving back and forth between us. So, out we started. The water in the swamp proved to be from ankle to almost waist deep. The bottom, however, was solid, so walking was not difficult. Most of the swamp was covered with thick dead reeds about six feet high that broke easily as we waded through them. In the midst of these reeds were a great many small open spots where some kind of short green water grass grew which the ducks fed upon. These openings were also the feeding grounds of many different kinds of wading birds which swarmed up with the ducks as we approached. Then there were several flocks of large white herons that seemed almost psychic, as they would take wing long before we reached their resting place, circle, climb high into the sky, and disappear into the distance. They alone seemed to leave the swamp. All other birds, including the ducks, would fly to some other clearing in the swamp and settle there.

According to recent reports, related: We Had a Week Off from Active Combat, So I Went Trout Fishing. I Got Pinned Down by a Sniper.

In a recent development, hundreds of large coots were present too. They were about twice the size of any I had seen before, and looked like American birds, except they had brilliant red bills.

Before I had made my way very far into the swamp I heard Fred fire twice and, looking in his direction, saw hundreds of ducks getting up. A dozen black mallards passed right over my head. How I wanted to shoot! But didn’t, remembering my promise to Fred to get my first fifteen with as few shells as possible.

Most of the ducks lit about 100 yards north of me, so I began creeping in that direction, making as little noise as possible. As I crept closer through very thick reeds I came to a small opening no more than ten yards in diameter, and, lo and behold, there sat about twenty honest-to-goodness greenwing teal. They saw me and shot up like a covey of quail. I caught them just as they rose, and fired once, knocking down three. I had a tough time recovering them in the reeds, but finally found them all. At the sound of the shot the mallards got up about seventy-five yards away and circled for some ten minutes, settling back down in the same place about the time I had recovered my last teal. With the teal in my belt I crept toward the mallards, crawling through the ankle-deep water on my knees and one hand, holding my gun in the other, as the reeds were not tall in this area.

According to recent reports, how I wanted to shoot! But didn’t, remembering my promise to Fred to get my first fifteen with as few shells as possible.

In a recent development, when I reached the edge of the clearing where the mallards were I saw they were all about fifty yards away on the opposite side. About halfway across the clearing was a small clump of tall reeds that I thought I might be able to keep between the mallards and myself until I could get them a little more in range.

It has been revealed that I started crawling toward those reeds, making every effort to keep the ducks from seeing me but, alas, ducks seem to be as wary in one part of the world as another. Just as I got started they spotted me, and off they went in every direction. The largest bunch of them circled over the edge of the swamp and then seemed to disappear into the trees. This I believed to be an illusion — ducks don’t light on trees, especially mallards.

By this time I had decided that it was too hot for crawling and that I would let Fred do the work for awhile. So I took my station in the clump of reeds in the center of the clearing and waited for him to send some ducks my way. I took off my head net, wiped the perspiration from my face, applied some mosquito lotion, and put the net into my pocket, deciding I could shoot better without it.

Industry observers note that after about ten minutes’ waiting I heard Fred open up again, firing three times, and, looking in his direction, I saw them coming. There they were, hundreds of them! And from then on, things went too fast to tell about. All the ducks seemed to want to light in the clearing I commanded — and I did command every inch of it!

There they were, hundreds of them. And from then on, things went too fast to tell about. All the ducks seemed to want to light in the clearing I commanded — and I did command every inch of it.

First, a massive flock of mallards tried to light within ten yards of me, and I opened up with both barrels just as they were settling, getting four of them. A bunch of pintails came in right after them; then teal, and more mallards. I was firing as fast as I could reload. I could hear Fred doing the same thing and knew he was in their favorite clearing at the other end of the swamp. I had never seen so many ducks at one time, and they were flying back and forth between the two of us. The boys at camp were all going to get a real meal.

Sources indicate that after about fifteen minutes of the fastest shooting I have ever done I took inventory. I found I had seventeen ducks — and four shells left! And I actually had four black mallards, a couple of beautiful little ducks that I couldn’t identify, three pintails, and several greenwing, bluewing, and cinnamon teal. The teal were larger than any I had seen in the states, but were exactly like our teal in every other respect.

Since I had more than my quota of fifteen birds I felt I could use the remaining four precious shells for the tough shots that I have always loved so much. So I took my station and waited.

A high flying mallard came in fast and weaving. It was one of those shots you make once in a lifetime and never forget. I led him plenty and just hoped. He came down from way up there like a rock, and I felt a thrill inside I hadn’t come close to feeling for two years.

In a recent development, A minute later two teal came in fast and low. I caught one with the first shot, but missed the second. But the first bird came down so clean I didn’t feel badly about the miss. With my remaining shell I stopped another mallard, not as high as the first, but it was a sweet shot.

I gathered up my birds and started back to meet Fred. We met just in front of our trail that led back into the jungle, and as we waded through the last few yards of swamp Fred said, “Look at ’em, Dave. We’ve got thirty-five of the most beautiful ducks I ever saw!”.

“Heavy, too,” I mentioned, laughing.

A bunch of pintails came in right after them; then teal, and more mallards. I was firing as fast as I could reload. I could hear Fred doing the same thing and knew he was in their favorite clearing at the other end of the swamp.

We reached the edge of the jungle and sat down to rest. As we sat there we beheld a most astonishing sight — about ten black mallards flew right out of the tree we were sitting under and winged their way back into the swamp. Believe it or not! Mallards do light in trees, in New Guinea anyway.

It has been revealed that we started home and Fred noted, “It’s a funny war, isn’t it? Black mallards lighting in trees; our belts loaded with ducks, and a bunch of hungry boys back at camp to appreciate them more than any ducks were ever appreciated before. I think, Dave, today has been the most wonderful day of my life.”.

In a recent development, related: I Hunted Ducks from a U.S. Naval Destroyer During the Korean War.

Sources indicate that I was glad Fred stated that, because it was his last duck hunt. Fred went down fighting — doing his bit to guarantee a free and fearless future full of “wonderful days” for all of us.

‘Pillaging Our Public Lands for AI Data Centers.’ Interior Lays Out Latest Initiative to Sell Public Lands, Shrink Federal Workforce, and Ramp Up Development

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1300 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Department of the Interior released a five-year strategic blueprint Tuesday that outlines the federal government’s intentions to sell public lands, further reduce the workforce at its agencies, and continue to pursue natural resource development for energy dominance.
  • Industry observers note that the 28-page document lists four key goals for fiscal years 2026 through 2030.
  • Industry observers note that “The Department will consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies,” reads the proposal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Department of the Interior released a five-year strategic blueprint Tuesday that outlines the federal government’s intentions to sell public lands, further reduce the workforce at its agencies, and continue to pursue natural resource development for energy dominance.

Industry observers note that the 28-page document lists four key goals for fiscal years 2026 through 2030. One of the most critical sections of the document for the conservation community is nested under the fourth goal of collaborating with states, tribes, and communities:.

Industry observers note that “The Department will consolidate its workforce to advance operational efficiencies,” reads the proposal. “The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands. Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands.”.

According to the Interior, the proceeds from sales of lands that aren’t considered “nationally significant” will go toward “purchasing entities to use for conservation purposes elsewhere” for “improved recreation access for American citizens, while at the same time decreasing the federal taxpayer’s financial responsibility to manage federal lands.”.

According to recent reports, “From a hunting and angling perspective, we love the places that are not of national significance,” Backcountry Hunters and Anglers president and CEO Ryan Callaghan tells Outdoor Life (we interviewed him while he was deer hunting a piece of no-name BLM ground out West). “Because they don’t have a substantial spotlight on them, and that’s where we go to hunt and fish.”.

Selling and transferring federal lands — of any significance — is also wildly unpopular with American outdoorsmen and women.

Sources indicate that “I’d need to see the criteria for disposal, but at first blush this flies in the face of overwhelming positive appreciation and sentiment for America’s public lands,” states Callaghan. “We’ve proved that middle-of-nowhere BLM land in Utah is of national significance during last summer’s budget reconciliation process. From an end-user standpoint, the American people want more public land and a workforce that can manage them responsibly.”.

The staff cuts to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, National Park Service, Bureau of Land Management (as well as the U.S. Forest Service, which is managed by the USDA) have also been a point of contention for hunters and anglers. As we reported in September, key public land agencies have already been chronically understaffed and underfunded for decades, with an accelerated decline under the second Trump administration.

Agency Staff CutsMeasured by direct civilian full-time equivalent.

The only sectors where the DOI’s strategic plan promises to add staff are law enforcement and public safety — not conservation roles. That includes building a larger Park Police presence in Washington, D.C. The plan includes no staffing numbers or targets. These priorities are the heart of the objective: “Interior protects Americans and public lands.”.

Transferring federal lands to states poses both the risk of further sell-off to private entities — and greater regulation for hunters, anglers, and outdoor users in general.

According to recent reports, “People have got to understand [the restrictions of state land],” says Callaghan. “You can’t camp on state land in Colorado or Wyoming unless posted. You can’t drive on state land even on established roads unless they’re signed here in Montana. It’s illegal to shoot clay pigeons on state land in Montana. We just literally got de facto public access to our state lands in Montana about 20 years ago. State lands are private lands first, and the public access components come second to the ability to make money off those state lands. You’re not going to have [default state] public access unless it’s compatible in some way.”.

The strategy also merges wildland fire programs into the new U.S. Wildland Fire Service as part of a massive restructure of how the federal government fights wildfires.

Burgum also emphasizes the role of “super intelligence” throughout the DOI’s strategic plan.

“For the first time in human history, we can turn electricity into intelligence,” he writes, in the only bolded line in his letter that prefaces the plan. (Nowhere in the document does the DOI use the phrase “artificial intelligence.”).

Recent findings suggest that the Trump administration is considering proposals for no fewer than a dozen data center projects on public land, as we reported in September. Together, those data centers could impact at least 17,600 acres of public land in the West.

“At every turn, the initiative prioritizes extraction over conservation, emphasizing the need to pillage our public lands in order to power AI data centers,” Center for Western Priorities communications director Kate Groetzinger noted in a statement Wednesday. “Of course, that’s no surprise given Burgum’s financial ties to the AI industry. But it flies in the face of the American public, who have made their feelings about data centers abundantly clear.”.

Related: The Rush to Build Data Centers on Public Lands Is Worse Than You Thought.

In the strategy Burgum directs DOI employees to “harness technology to power efficiency,” pointing to efforts to replace manpower with artificial intelligence. The directive comes just days after the USFWS revealed it wanted more “boots on the ground” to better manage our national wildlife refuges.

“Our team is actively expanding domestic energy production and securing our critical minerals supply chain — reducing reliance on foreign adversaries, accelerating innovation and protecting the global environment,” writes Burgum in the plan. “…Timber, grazing, geothermal energy, hydropower, outdoor recreation, hunting and fishing, mining, oil and gas and more contribute mightily to every facet of American life. As President Theodore Roosevelt, who helped shape and define our department, explained: ‘Conservation means development as much as it does protection.’”.

Industry observers note that burgum is referencing a speech then-former President Roosevelt gave in 1910, in which he spoke forcefully against private interests. The full quote from Roosevelt reads:.

In a recent development, “Conservation means development as much as it does protection. I recognize the right and duty of this generation to develop and use the natural resources of our land; but I do not recognize the right to waste them, or to rob, by wasteful use, the generations that come after us.”.

Sources indicate that “Releasing this [plan] anytime would not get positive feedback. Releasing this during the middle of hunting season is absolute proof the people administrating our public lands right now are extremely out of touch with the American people and their needs,” says Callaghan. “You’re not going to stop at a diner, a truck stop, a bar in America right now and find someone wearing hunter orange who says, ‘You know what? I want less of this. What would be good for me, and my kids, and my hunting season now and in the future, would be less land.”.

The DOI’s strategic initiative was released on the same day the BLM proposed a rule that would make the goals defined in this plan easier to execute.

The potential rule is rooted in public-land rule making, but it would essentially overhaul the guidelines for writing BLM resource management plans. That includes eliminating the 90-day public comment period for major plans, throw out the right now required draft plan for public comment period, and potentially replace public comment periods with public meetings.

According to recent reports, related: Public Comment Periods Don’t Usually Matter Much to the Feds. Duck Hunters Made a Difference Anyway — for Now.

“Those aims decide where drilling, mining, and grazing can happen on public lands, and which lands can be sold,” according to the Center for Western Priorities. “Under the Federal Land Policy Management Act, BLM can sell land only after a resource management initiative identifies it for disposal.”.

Sources indicate that the proposed BLM rule is open for public comment through Jan. 11, 2027.

Two Hikers Were Killed by a Sow Grizzly with Cubs in ‘Very Rare’ Predatory Attack

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack.
  • In a recent development, “It’s surreal.
  • The remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that two women and four grizzlies are dead near Bella Coola, British Columbia after an unusual and horrific predatory attack. A sow with three cubs killed two hikers, a mother-daughter pair who had been missing since November 1. DNA tests confirm the women were killed by the bears.

In a recent development, “It’s surreal. It doesn’t seem real,” Josh Balcarras, a family member, told CBC News. “The way it starts is a few hours of not hearing from them. That turns into a day, and then a night. Then a second night comes and it becomes a real thing.”.

The remains of Jennifer Balcarras, 48, were found November 2. The remains of her daughter, 20-year-old Selah Reed, were found November 3. The two were not far from a trail  in the steep and heavily-wooded Snooka Trail System. Both were buried in caches, something bears often do to hide their food from other animals. Investigators consider the attack to be motivated by predation.

It has been revealed that “This attack involved predatory behavior, which I can tell you is very rare,” Jeff Tyre, British Columbia Conservation Officer Service (BCCOS) inspector remarked in a recorded statement issued November 10. “That is to say, we don’t know how it started but we know how it ended. Out of respect for the family, I’m going to decline to answer what predatory behavior looks like specifically in this case.”.

The mother grizzly bear was in her late teens. Her three cubs were born this year. BCCOS unveiled November 10 that all four were captured and euthanized for their predatory behavior. A week after finding the remains of the second woman, the case is considered closed and trapping equipment has been removed. Nuxalk Nation cultural leaders will decide how the bear remains will be used.

“They all had to be destroyed because bears that are involved in attacks on people cannot be rehabilitated or relocated,” Tyre remarked. “This type of behavior presents an extreme risk to the public and such bears are dispatched to protect the public and prevent similar attacks in the future.”.

It has been revealed that this most recent attack happened nearly a year after a grizzly attacked a group of tribal school children who were having lunch in the same region last November. In that case covered by OL, three students and one adult were hospitalized after a grizzly raided their picnic.

Despite the two high-profile incidents, investigators say grizzly bear attacks are not increasing near Bella Coola. They also cross-checked DNA from bears involved in both cases. None of the grizzlies euthanized this year were involved in the group attack last year. That bear was never located.

The tribe renewed its safety protocol during this year’s investigation. It has since lifted curfew but continues nightly patrols and offers escorts to take kids to school.

“This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year’s attack,” stated Samuel Schooner, Nuxalk Nation elected chief. “Our focus continues to be on taking care of our community members.”.

In a recent development, bella Coola is in the coastal region of British Columbia. Coastal bears and interior bears are genetically the same grizzly species, but their size and diet are different. Coastal bears have access to salmon, a nutrient-rich food source.

“Individual bears with increased access to salmon tend to be larger, have bigger litters, have lower stress hormone levels, and exist at higher densities at a population level,” reads an October 2025 study by Lauren Henson and Kris Christensen published in the scientific journal G3: Genes, Genomes and Genetics. “Interior grizzlies [have] smaller body mass and skull size than coastal individuals.”.

Read Next: These Alaskans Stopped a Charging Grizzly at 5 Yards with Their 10mm Pistols.

BC’s combined coastal and interior grizzly bear population has increased from 6,600 in the 1970s to 15,000 in 2018. In 2017, BC implemented a controversial grizzly bear hunting ban. Those in favor of the ban believe that a lack of grizzly hunting does not lead to more human fatalities, but organizations opposing the ban refer to recent attacks as reason to re-open the hunt.

According to recent reports, “We have to do something,” Jesse Zeman, B.C. Wildlife Federation executive director told CBC News. “What we’re currently doing is very clearly not working.”.
