  • As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Sources indicate that trail Runner’s travel columnist Andy Cochrane has run all over the world, including five trips to the Lofoten Islands above the Arctic Circle in Norway. He shares his hard-earned recommendations on where to run, stay, and eat, what to pack for the unpredictable weather—and how to get there.

As a travel writer, I fly an embarrassing amount. Over three quarters of a million miles in the last decade, or roughly three laps around the Earth each year. That’s a lot of time in a pressurized tube sitting next to strangers, but perhaps a fair price to pay for the privilege of running trails all over the world, from Patagonia to Morocco to Greenland. Picking a favorite destination is difficult, but often actions speak louder than words. I’ve returned to one more than any other: the Lofoten Islands in Norway.

Hidden a hundred miles above the Arctic Circle, Lofoten is best known for its Viking heritage, red fishing  villages, and dramatic coastline—sandy beaches, turquoise waters, and walls of rock that rise 3,000 feet out of the Norwegian Sea. There are very few places in the world where mountains collide with the ocean in such a cinematic way, giving it the best of both worlds—and incredibly unpredictable weather.

It has been revealed that on my first trip to the Lofoten Islands in 2017, a snow storm shut down trails in the alpine, so I explored the lowlands, dabbled in fishing and kayaking, and enjoyed a nightly sauna. Since then I’ve returned four times to explore different corners of the islands and am planning to go back again next year, because there is still so much to explore, especially if you love empty trails and technical running. Here’s why I think Lofoten could be the next great trail destination and how you can visit before it gets too crowded.

In a recent development, the Lofoten Islands are an archipelago in northern Norway that stretch from the mainland into the North Atlantic. At 68 degrees 54 minutes north latitude, they sit further north than most communities in Greenland and all but a dozen or so towns at the top of Alaska. The chain consists of five main islands and hundreds of smaller ones, connected by bridges and underwater tunnels. (Oh, the joys of Norwegian infrastructure!).

Combined, the islands cover a total of 474 square miles, roughly the size of the city of Los Angeles. However, they are home to just 25,000 full-time residents, most of whom live in Svolvær and Leknes. Suffice to say, the interior is remote and rugged; it’s common to find yourself on a trail without a single human in sight, despite the lack of trees and views in all directions.

Industry observers note that although there are offshore oil reserves nearby, drilling is prohibited in Lofoten (unlike much of Norway), which has allowed cod fishing and tourism to flourish. The landscape is a mix of granite spines and tussocked tundra, with a few birch and mountain ash stands sprinkled in. When storms roll in—which they do often—there is very little protection, which can be a humbling experience.

The trail network in Lofoten is a patchwork of everything from unmaintained user trails to heavily engineered routes like Reinebringen’s 1,978 stone steps. As a whole they skew towards the technical end of the spectrum; most are steep, rocky, and stout. It’s common to gain a thousand feet per mile or more.

In a recent development, the vast majority of trails start near sea level and ascend through bogs and brush, climbing into the alpine via scree fields and off-camber granite slabs. Expect your shoes to get muddy and shirt to be saturated in sweat as you climb to the summit. Some marshes have wooden planks and some ridgelines have cairns, but they aren’t guaranteed. It’s best to always bring a good map and a better attitude.

While there isn’t an official count of trails on the islands, a good estimate is around 150, including everything from short beach hikes to high ridge lines. For ambitious trail runners, the Lofoten Crossing is an unofficial 100-mile thru-route from Delp to Å, and uses a mix of local paths, beaches, and roads. It’s a great way to see the entire chain of islands, even if it skips some of the serene trails. A few of my other favorites are the steep climb up to Himmeltindan (2,700 feet in 2.1 miles), crossing the interior of Vestvågøya from Leknes to the eastern end, and almost any of the remote trails at the end of the archipelago near Å, many of which reside inside Lofotodeen National Park.

In a recent development, lofoten sees over a million tourists each year, heavily focused on the summer months. The crowds get so bad in July and August that iconic trails like Ryten, Fløya, and Mannen are probably not worth visiting. In the spring and fall Lofoten becomes a lot more enjoyable, because it offers more solitude on the trails, open spots at restaurants, and generally friendlier locals. I have a slight preference for the fall, mostly because I reserve most of the spring for skiing, which also is pretty great in Lofoten.

Recent findings suggest that it’s also worth considering the weather and daylight. For about a month from early December to early January, the sun doesn’t rise above the horizon. Days lengthen dramatically in the spring, from 6 hours in February to over 18 by the end of April. The Midnight sun rises in late May and sets in mid-July, offering 24 hours of daylight for a month and a half straight. Almost too much!

Weather is fickle all year but especially in the spring and fall, as temps float in the 40s and 50s Fahrenheit. Snow usually melts in May and the mountains undergo a rapid transition to green. In the fall the foliage turns to a golden and red mix, storms begin to batter the coast, and the Northern Lights illuminate the night sky as early as September. Thankfully saunas are common and help make cold weather running more enjoyable.

Recent findings suggest that getting to Lofoten takes more time than most destinations in Europe. The drive from Oslo is around 20 hours and the combination of train and ferry takes even longer. The fastest way to get to the islands is a flight to Bodø and then a puddle hop prop plane to Svolvær or Leknes. This saves time and helps avoid weather-dependent ferries, but is often more expensive.

It has been revealed that I prefer to fly from Oslo to Narvik, which sits on the mainland adjacent to the islands, and rent a car. The drive takes between 2-4 hours, depending on where I’m staying, but is always worth it for the views. Plus, public transit is limited in Lofoten, so having a car allows me to get to quieter places. For example, the cinnamon rolls at Unstad are to die for—but the only way to get there is to drive (or go on a 80-mile round-trip bike ride).

Traditional fishing lodges, called rorbuer, are built on poles over the water. Many have been converted to cozy places to stay. My favorite is Hattvika Lodge in the town of Ballstad. The restaurant next door, Fangst, is one of the best in the area. For those wanting to stay further off the beaten path, Nusfjord would be a great option. For a wider selection of restaurants, consider a stay in Svolvær or Leknes. Regardless, it’s important to book early, because the best places fill up months in advance.

If someone told me the Offtrail Ultra was designed specifically for Lofoten, I wouldn’t blink an eye. The 5 mm lugs are perfect in mud and scree, the toe grip is great on granite slaps, the integrated gaiter keeps out debris, and the midsole is stable enough for the dynamic movements necessary in this terrain. Hard to imagine a better fit, honestly.

Designed for cold and wet weather, the Run Cold wool socks are designed with high-impact wear zones to help them last longer, but don’t feel overbuilt at all. Instead they are stretchy and comfortable, with a seamless toe to reduce chafing. They work well with tights and running pants, which I use in spring and fall running in cold climates like Lofoten.

Sources indicate that over the last few years I’ve trended towards running belts, but I make an exception for a place like Lofoten, where you want to bring a few extra things. The Triack has a snug fit with almost no bounce thanks to a bungee system that’s easy to adjust on the fly. Plus, with four easy-access pockets, I can carry spare layers, gloves, snacks, water, camera, and first aid easily.

The name is a bit of a misnomer, because it’s actually made of merino wool. The wool helps regulate temperature better than other materials, keeping you warmer at the start and cooler when you heat up, not to mention not smelling after days of use. I love the hood and neck gaiter for colder days, and how the hoodie works great under a raincoat, too.

#44670. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Deer Hunting When the Weather Finally Turns Cold

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures.
  • Wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet.
  • Industry observers note that whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that without doubt, bass fishing and whitetail deer hunting are the two most popular pastimes of sportsmen searching for outdoor adventures. And as strange as it may sound, bass and deer are really very much alike, at least in the ways they respond to bitter cold weather.

Wise anglers know that bass do not experience discomfort when water temperatures plummet. However, bass do begin exhibiting changed behavior. Generally bass will drift away from the shallows and into deeper water as the thermometer falls because temperatures in the depths remain relatively stable on a day-to-day basis. Here, their metabolisms begin to wind down. The bass, therefore, do not require as much food intake to sustain various bodily functions. Consequently, these two alterations in their lifestyle can make them very tough to catch for all but the most experienced fishermen.

Industry observers note that whitetails respond to winter’s periodic onslaughts in much the same way by abandoning their usual haunts until the weather either stabilizes or eventually reverses itself. Yet few people, aside from biologists, are aware that deer also eat less as extremely cold weather approaches. Chemical changes take place in their bodies, causing their digestive processes to switch to s-l-o-w. This, in turn, allows for the maintenance of various body systems at a greatly reduced rate of food intake.

According to recent reports, another important point to emphasize about the anatomies of whitetails is that their brains are comparatively small in relation to their overall body sizes. Therefore, the integrated nervous system coursing throughout their bodies is rudimentary at best. As a result, like most wild creatures that do not possess a sophisticated neural apparatus, their pain thresholds are quite high — making them relatively insensitive to bitter cold temperatures. Many hunters are not aware of this because for generations they’ve been led to believe that when the weather goes sour, deer can be expected to do this or that in order “to seek protection from the elements and be more comfortable.”.

Body comfort actually has little to do with their changed behavior patterns. After all, the northern boundary of the whitetail’s native range extends more than 150 miles beyond the United States/Canadian border to approximately 52° latitude. Anyone who has lived thereabouts can tell you that winter temperatures frequently average -20°. The wind-chill factor often makes it seem as cold as -75°. Therefore, it just doesn’t stand to reason that animal species such as whitetails would be native to such hostile climes were they not virtually immune to such weather.

We’ve even seen evidence of this immunity right on our southern-Ohio farm where it is not uncommon to experience at least several days of -20° temperatures each winter.

Behind my barn there is an old tractor trail that wends its way through a 40-acre oak forest. Numerous times, while hauling out firewood, I’ve seen deer bedded on nearby slopes. Often they reveal a thick dusting of new-fallen snow covering their backs — the hollow hairs of their coats providing such superb insulation that their body heat is unable to escape. If I approach too closely, the deer will predictably rise to their feet, shake themselves like soaking-wet dogs and cause clouds of snowflakes to fly — then saunter off to other parts with an air of nonchalance at having been rousted from their beds.

If deer are able to adapt to such gelid temperatures so easily, why is it then, that legions of otherwise knowledgeable hardworking hunters so often strike out when the freeze is on?

It has been revealed that say, for example, that you’ve been hunting in balmy temperatures for several days, have had the opportunity to look over a number of animals but haven’t seen anything you’d really be satisfied with. So you’ve decided to hold out a while longer, hoping you’ll eventually stumble onto “Mr. Massive.”.

According to recent reports, suddenly, you wake up one morning to the sound of icy sleet pinging against your bedroom window. Bounding from the rack, you are shocked to discover that the wind is whistling a siren song and that overnight the temperature has dropped 35°.

After sitting on a stand for several hours that morning without seeing a thing, you look and feel like a popsicle. So you begin moving around — sneak hunting — but eventually conclude that the deer have vanished. By day’s end the temperature has fallen another 10°, a light skiff of hoarfrost blankets the ground and your expectations have long since dwindled. You’ve forgotten entirely about taking a nice buck this season and have begun thinking that if you can just manage to fill your doe tag you’ll be very very lucky.

Sources indicate that the scenario is the bane of all hunters living north of the Mason-Dixon Line. Because it’s obvious that the deer couldn’t possibly have just disappeared from the face of the earth, the best prospect for success undoubtedly lies in learning more about their behavioral reactions to severe weather.

According to recent reports, one of the most telling clues to unraveling the mystery of their disappearance can be traced to changes in the whitetails’ body chemistry — the changes that cause them to require less food. Biologists say that this is an annual occurrence and that, like the rut, it is triggered by progressively shorter days and diminished periods of sunlight. Sometime around mid-November, the growth hormone thyroxin, which for the past eight months has been flooding the body, begins dissipating and will remain at a very low level until the following spring.

This shoots down another popular myth about bucks not feeding much during the rut because they are so love struck. Actually, their reduced food intake can be attributed to a conservation measure on the part of nature. In other words, with each additional week of cold weather, food becomes less and less available so nature accordingly reduces the animals’ need for food by enacting significant changes in their body metabolisms.

Hunters should realize that, as the season progresses and as increasing numbers of severe polar blasts begin descending upon their regions, deer can be expected to move around less and less in search of food. The movements they do exhibit are no longer going to be concentrated during the traditional early and late hours of the day but during midday when it is likely to be warmer. Again, the deer are not seeking “comfort” but rather are conserving energy to more efficiently make use of the sharply reduced food supplies.

Industry observers note that I’ve seen this happen with such consistency that I now almost consider it axiomatic. At our northern-Minnesota hunting camp, for example, members of our regular group begin bowhunting in October. We’ve learned from more than 80 years of combined experience that the odds of taking a whitetail early in the season are in our favor if we take up early-morning stands, nap during midday when deer are bedded, then resume our vigils late in the afternoon.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant.

Yet during the final days of the gun season in December, those in our party who still have not scored have entirely reversed their strategies. Now the order of the day, paradoxically perhaps, is to sleep late in the morning, wait on stand during midday, then quit early. There’s just not enough likelihood of seeing anything move — particularly at dawn’s first light — to justify the oftentimes agonizing ordeal of sitting as still as a statue in weather so bitter cold that it gnaws at your innermost fiber.

Of course the most serious hunters — diehard veterans who are never willing to give up — may find such tactics repugnant. As far as they’re concerned, they want to be in the field every available minute. That’s fine and dandy but, if they want to maximize their chances for success, they should still be willing to make certain adjustments in the way they hunt.

Late in the season, and particularly when the freeze is on, they should stillhunt or sneak hunt early and late in the day when deer are most likely to be sequestered in their beds. During midday, hunters should play the waiting game on stand when deer are inclined to be traveling to and from feeding sites.

Recent findings suggest that but where, exactly, do the deer go when the bottom falls out of the thermometer and ice storms or sheets of wind-driven sleet are lashing the countryside? The three-pronged answer to this is thick cover on a protected south-facing slope in a low-elevation area of terrain.

It has been revealed that two of the most desirable types of thick cover are dense stands of head-high honeysuckle and nearly impenetrable pine plantations. The pines are most often thickets of immature trees that have their whorls of branches close to the ground.

Sources indicate that in the face of adverse weather, deer retreat deep into such seclusions where they can wait out the ensuing tempest. Again, trying to stay warm or achieve some other comfort level has little to do with their evasive behavior. Windy stormy weather makes whitetails extremely restless and nervous. By their very nature, whitetails are already hypertensive and are extremely paranoid creatures. When they’re no longer able to detect, classify and catalog sounds and scents because of the competition from noisy winds and erratic air currents, they waste no time finding a place where they can maintain a low profile. Therefore, rather than allowing themselves to remain vulnerable by bedding on their customary hillside benches and ridgelines, they retreat into deep thick cover. This not only helps to block the wind but perhaps also gives them the feeling that hiding from ready view somewhat compensates for their impaired senses.

Sources indicate that once, for a period of several days in the dead of winter, I had the opportunity to watch an eight-point whitetail buck in a fenced enclosure. This was a wild deer that had recently been captured by biologists for use in various nutrition studies. Its temporary fenced-in home was five acres of relatively open hardwood forest with scattered swatches of second-growth ground cover here and there.

Whenever the weather was warm, sunny and there was no wind, the buck had a particular place it liked to bed. The deer could see in every direction from the high hammock. Yet whenever a frontal storm system moved through the region and the wind began howling, the deer quickly vacated its usual turf. It always went downhill into a little pocket of thick multiflora rose — the only significant cover in the compound — and buried itself right in the middle.

Recent findings suggest that one day as snow clouds scudded against an ominously gray sky and ice-riddled branches creaked in the wind, I watched in amazement as the buck laid on his belly for long hours, his front legs outstretched and his chin resting on the ground. Yet when the wind occasionally intensified with its typical freight-train drone, or an ice-laden branch suddenly crashed to the ground, the buck’s head would instantly come up, swiveling in all directions. Assured that nothing was on the prowl, the buck would then promptly duck back down again. Moments later his head would be up, down, then back up again. Just observing all that nervous energy and pent-up anxiety exhausted me — under these conditions the buck’s entire personality was like a violin string about to snap.

I’m confident that the penned buck would have liked to have had access to much thicker deeper cover to increase his feeling of security. I’m also certain that unconfined deer in their native habitat behave much the same way when the freeze is on. Moreover, a biologist at the research station told me that during one terrible winter storm, the penned buck stayed put for four consecutive days until the weather finally abated.

Industry observers note that in addition to tangled jungles of honeysuckle and conifer forests, whitetails also like to retreat into swamps when the freeze is on. Because of the continually decaying organic matter, swamps are always warmer than other regions and this, coupled with the fact that they’re always found in low-lying terrain, keeps them somewhat sheltered from the brunt of the weather.

Recent findings suggest that however, without meaning to again kick the proverbial dead horse, deer don’t seek out swamps in order to stay warm. They go there because past experience has taught them that they’re not likely to bump into hunters in such forbidding territory and, similarly, a swamp is one place where they can continue to effectively rely upon their senses to forewarn them of impending danger.

Yet no matter what type of cover deer may elect to use for hiding, hunting them when the freeze is on can be extremely difficult because the animals’ minds and senses are so preoccupied with monitoring their immediate surroundings. But there are several tactics that seem to be far more productive than others.

Industry observers note that first, of course, pay attention to weather forecasts. Deer seem to have built-in barometers that give them advance notice when hostile weather is about to assault their regions. They take due advantage of this insight by stocking up on groceries, instinctively knowing that once the bitter weather strikes it will preclude safe traveling to and from feeding sites for several days. Then, immediately after the frontal system has passed and calmness again prevails, the deer come out of hiding and return to their favorite food plots. Consequently, stand hunting or sneak hunting — just before and immediately after a storm — are two key strategies no enterprising whitetail hunter can afford to pass up.

According to recent reports, cornfields can be prime places to try because, throughout the Midwest and the northern border states, it is becoming an increasingly popular agricultural practice to leave corn standing as long as possible. In the past, it was either chopped or combined sometime in October or November. But with storage costs escalating like never before and future market prices uncertain, many farmers nowadays are leaving the corn in the field until such time as they have a specific need for it or until the price increases. Quite often this means as late as February.

Recent findings suggest that already-picked cornfields are also good bets because a substantial amount of harvest residue may continue to draw deer months after the corn has been combined. On our own cornfields we’re sometimes amazed to see a dozen deer at a time pawing through a foot of snow cover to find spillage.

Recent findings suggest that I emphasize the importance of finding corn when the freeze is on because native wild foods are becoming more and more sparse with each additional week of winter weather. Other popular agricultural foods such as soybeans are rarely allowed to remain in the field beyond their peak harvest times, so corn is a deer magnet beyond compare.

Sources indicate that hunting during a storm can also pay off. The best opportunity occurs when the temperature does not fall dramatically. This usually means that the wind velocity will not be too fierce and any precipitation is likely to be in the form of huge wet snowflakes that begin clinging to cover like giant globs of cotton candy. Under such conditions, whitetails don’t seem to become as jittery and frantic about their safety and may continue to feed during midday periods. The fluffy snow itself may also pacify them just enough during nonfeeding periods so that they will remain tied to their usual haunts rather than diving headlong into thick security cover.

It has been revealed that any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground.

Recent findings suggest that conversely, hunting during the most ravaging freeze-outs offers the least chance of success. Now, patiently waiting on stand is inherently a futile endeavor. The animals simply will not come to you. It is necessary for you to go find them by prowling through swamps, honeysuckle or evergreens.

Never try to approach such cover on level ground. Any deer hiding within a thicket will merely vamoose out the other side, giving you only a fleeting glimpse of their white semaphore flags signaling goodbye. Instead, try to mentally dope out the lay of the land and then approach from high ground. This will allow you to look down and through the cover and will make it far easier to spot bedded or sneaking deer.

Another option is to round up several pals and begin staging drives, particularly in the case of expansive pine plantations. Here is a unique situation, not unlike hunting rabbits, where the drivers themselves are likely to be awarded as many shots as the hunters placed on stand. The reason, as we briefly touched on earlier, is because deer that have retreated into the catacombs of thick cover are extremely reluctant to expose themselves, to travel great distances or to sever their close ties with that chosen cover where they’ve decided to holeup. As a result, a buck pushed out by a driver may chart a bounding weaving escape flight that actually takes him only a very short distance before he swiftly ducks back down to resume hiding.

Read Next: Tips for Patterning and Hunting a Late-Season Buck.

Because the drivers are likely to see a good deal of shooting, those hunters placed on stand should use portable tree stands situated as high as practical so they are not in the direct line of fire of their approaching partners. Also — and this cannot be emphasized too strongly — every hunter participating in such a maneuver should be fully clad in fluorescent orange clothing and should maintain loud voice contact so everyone is well aware of each other’s location.

Industry observers note that when hunting during freezing stormy weather, wise garment selection also requires careful thought. For sneak hunting or stillhunting, wool is always the best bet because it is noiseless when the fabric grates against brambles and brush. But when toughing out long hours on stand, I rely exclusively upon down-filled duds and bundle up like a snowman.

It has been revealed that I’d be the last to say that hunting deer when the freeze is on is purely enjoyable. Human beings just weren’t designed with bitter-cold weather in mind. But when such conditions prevail, any hunter can indeed fill his tag. Just keep in mind the changed behavior the animals are certain to begin exhibiting and proposal your strategy accordingly.

This story was originally published in the November 1987 matter of Outdoor Life.

Tech Report: Deer Hunting Has Never Been Easier Than Right Now

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1099 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like.
  • It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change.
  • The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, I’ve been hunting whitetail deer for about 20 years now, and I can still remember what hunting a low deer density, heavy hunting pressure area was like. When I was a kid, more than 1 million hunters would enter the woods and hunt Pennsylvania’s opening day of rifle season. In my heavily populated area, I always saw a lot more hunters than I did deer.

It wasn’t until about 10 years ago that I started noticing a change. The deer population was skyrocketing and it hasn’t slowed down. Paired with a decline in the hunting population, I’ve experienced the highest deer numbers of my life recently.

But it’s not just in my area. The population has soared across the vast majority of the whitetail’s range, making it easier and easier for us remaining hunters to fill our tags. Tack on the crazy advancements in technology like cellular trail cameras, the latest crossbows, and even technologically-advanced compound bows, and I truly believe deer hunting has never been easier than right now. Here’s why that’s a good thing — sort of.

Recent findings suggest that across the whitetail’s range, populations are at an all time high. That’s not just my opinion — it’s fact.

In a recent development, “There are between 30 to 35 million whitetails in the U.S. right now,” says Kip Adams, chief conservation officer for the National Deer Association. “That’s a crazy number of deer on the landscape. And, the harvest data is backing that up. Nationally, we’ve only surpassed three million bucks harvested annually four times in the last century, all of which occurred within the last five years. We also have the best age structure in the last 100 years. So we’re killing more bucks, and older bucks than ever before.”.

The good news here is that the increasing population has been met with increases in opportunity from the tag allocation side, and the harvest data proves those opportunities are working.

Industry observers note that “We have expanded seasons across the board, higher bag limits than any point in the last century, and more advanced weapons to fill those tags,” notes Adams. “If you can’t shoot a deer today, you just really aren’t trying very hard.”.

Now, before you go grabbing your pitchforks because you’re still sitting on a pile of tags this season, it’s worth mentioning that Adams and I both agreed that it’s never been easier to kill any deer, but we’re certainly not implying it’s easy to kill a specific deer.

It’s also worth noting that certain areas across the whitetail’s range have seen a decrease in opportunities as diseases like CWD and EHD have impacted herd numbers, and habitat loss continues with urban expansion. But, for most of the whitetail’s range, opportunities abound.

I’ll be the first to admit I love my cell cameras. I check them almost too often this time of year, but that immediate satisfaction and data grab is addicting. And, that data has helped me dial in the movement patterns of the deer herd in my area based on weather conditions in ways that standard SD card cameras couldn’t. That information, when applied correctly, makes filling a tag substantially easier than just guessing and trying to get lucky.

Take the buck my father tagged last year for example. We had gotten a few photos of him in velvet, keying us in on the area he was using. After planning to stay out of the area and wait for mid to late October when the buck started hitting scrapes, we sat back and waited. Around Oct. 21, we got our first photo of him in the area. And he stayed consistent for three days, hitting the scrape every evening in daylight. On the fourth night, we went in, set up, and a shot opportunity presented itself.

Sure, the stars had to align and the conditions had to be just right for that pattern to exist, but without the technological advancements to trail cameras, I don’t know if we would have gotten a chance at that buck.

According to recent reports, tack on the advancements in our gear. From compounds to crossbows, inlines to straight-walls, and even modern cartridge design, we’ve never been better equipped to shoot deer with more accuracy and efficacy.

Sources indicate that “Almost all states in the whitetail’s range allow crossbows for everyone now,” Adams claims. “Plus, more and more states that used to be shotgun only are now allowing straight-wall cartridges or inline muzzleloaders. All of those additions make it easier for hunters to fill their tags.”.

While the pros speak for themselves, the cons come down to more of an opinion than anything rooted in fact. I have to wonder what all this ease is doing to the heritage of hunting. Hunting was never about being easy, in fact, I’d argue the opposite. It was about the thrill of the chase, the reward of filling your tag after a long season, putting your woodsmanship to the test and coming out on top, and the conservation of one of America’s most valuable resources.

I grew to love hunting because it was challenging. I was unsuccessful a lot, which put a fire in my belly to learn more, hunt harder, and find a way to be successful through the lessons I learned along the way. I wonder if kids like me are getting the same experience, and what the hook for them might be if not.

It has been revealed that there’s also the ethical dilemma that an easier hunting experience brings. From the ethics and fair-chase argument relating to cellular trail cameras, to the liberal weapon usage and even baiting tactics in certain states, I fear we’re very close to crossing the line into an unfair advantage over our quarry, if we haven’t gotten there already.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back.

It has been revealed that it’s up to us as the hunters, and up to the states to decide how much is too much of a good thing. And as the deer populations continue to expand, I personally don’t see a world where the states are the ones that are going to draw the line. So, this season, as you continue to chase that substantial buck or a nice doe for the freezer, ask yourself where you blueprint to draw the line. And, feel free to join me in wondering how it’s still possible to struggle to fill a tag from time to time.

Industry News: ‘Full Panic Mode.’ Bowhunter Tags the 205-Inch Louisiana Buck His Family Followed for 3 Seasons

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For three years brothers Zack and Daniel Halbert of Bossier Parish, Louisiana, watched a nontypical buck grow into an incredible 200-class deer. They kept tabs on the buck with trail cameras and debated when it was time to shoot the high and wide whitetail.

“We never got a chance to shoot him last year,” Zack tells Outdoor Life. “Over last summer when he was still in velvet we saw on cameras that his rack had completely blown up and got huge, with lots of palmation.”.

Industry observers note that it was clear this was the season to try to kill him. The brothers hunted hard during a 23-day stint in October, with one of them in a stand every day.

Recent findings suggest that “I was just the lucky one sitting that day when the buck slipped up,” says Zack, a business-studies student at Louisiana Tech University. “My brother, dad, and I put in a lot of work hunting that buck. I would not have taken this deer without their help.”.

It has been revealed that the Halberts had multiple setups around their 80-acre hunting property. Zack took the buck from a ground blind on a 48-degree morning in late October.

“The blind faced the woods, and I’m looking one way out a window, then leaned the other way, and there he was at 21 yards,” Zack claims. “It’s crazy how you can go from calm and in two seconds go into full panic mode.”.

According to recent reports, zack watched the buck for three long minutes as he waited for a broadside shot. When the buck finally turned, he drew and held at full draw for about 15 seconds. Then he let fly.

The buck took off, and Zack watched where it disappeared into the woods. Then he called his brother, dad, and girlfriend with the news.

According to recent reports, “When I shot I was so pumped I almost shook the ground blind over. Before I got out of the blind I was trying to stop shaking enough to finish my prayer for what a blessing it was.”.

Zack began trailing the deer into timber, but the blood became faint and he decided it would be best to call in a tracking dog.

“I didn’t want to mess up on this deer,” he indicates.

Tracker Eric Perry and his dog, Blue, arrived that evening.

Sources indicate that “It was getting toward dusk when the dog got there and was put on the buck’s trail,” Zack states. “Blue found it in just 15 minutes. The arrow was a good hit, but there was no exit hole and so not a good blood trail.”.

According to recent reports, the deer had died in a creek, and Zack had to wade into the cold water to get his buck out. The crew dragged the deer out of the timber and loaded it into a truck and headed home. Zack estimates it was 5½ years old, and Buckmasters scorer Chris Bates measured Zack’s buck at 205 3/8 inches.

Although Buckmasters has a different scoring system than the one used by Boone and Crockett and Pope and Young Clubs (and therefore scores aren’t apples-to-apples), it’s worth noting that the largest nontypical killed with a bow in the state scored, according to P&Y records, 206 5/8 inches. That deer was taken in January 2012 by Alton McLead.

Recent findings suggest that read Next: No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck.

“I know my grandpa Dan, who isn’t with us anymore,” says Zack, “wouldn’t have believed his eyes if he got to see this deer.”.

Industry News: We’d Rather Spend the Holidays in These 7 Gorgeous Ski Town Rentals

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Reflect in the Wild @ Lions Lair, a mirrored Catskills hideaway near Hunter Mountain. (Photo: Courtesy of Airbnb).

I’ve planned most of my ski trips around one thing: the skiing. How’s the terrain? What’s the vert? How deep is the base? When’s the next storm?

Where I’m sleeping has generally been a secondary consideration. Give me a comfortable bed, a place to dry my gear, and a clean bathroom, and I’m happy.

But this holiday season, I’m dreaming bigger. What if, instead of the usual marathon of cooking, cleaning, and navigating family drama, we packed up our skis, gathered our favorite people, and disappeared into the mountains for a few days?

Of course, if I’m going to convince everyone to trade their usual holiday traditions for a ski trip, a cramped motel room and a communal boot dryer probably won’t cut it.

A gorgeous cabin with a roaring fireplace, a proper kitchen for holiday dinners, and a hot tub waiting after last chair? Now we’re talking.

Apparently, I’m not the only one who likes the idea.

In a recent development, according to Airbnb’s latest winter travel report, travelers are increasingly looking to smaller mountain towns for their holiday getaways. Searches for holiday stays in Hunter, Newly introduced York, are up 37 percent year over year, while ski destinations like Brian Head, Utah, and Mammoth Lakes, California, also made the company’s list of trending winter escapes.

And with Airbnb’s new checkout rules, which generally prohibit hosts from requiring guests to strip beds, start laundry, or wash and put away dishes for bookings made on or after November 20, what’s not to love? Sorry, family and friends, the same rules do not apply at Chalet de Shafer. Here’s a sponge.

From a sprawling Mammoth chalet that sleeps 12 to a romantic mirrored hideaway in the Catskills, these seven properties offer a compelling alternative to the usual holiday routine: beautiful mountain settings, plenty of character, inspiration to make a few upcoming traditions, and, most importantly, nearby skiing.

Some ski trips are easy; others require a group chat, a shared grocery list, and a spreadsheet. This five-bedroom Mammoth Lakes townhouse was made for the latter.

It has been revealed that located near Canyon Lodge, the spacious retreat sleeps 12 and offers easy access to one of the West’s most impressive ski mountains. The townhouse puts skiers near several lifts, with access to beginner terrain, intermediate cruisers, and connections to Mammoth’s more challenging slopes. There’s also a free gondola connecting Canyon Lodge to the Village, making dinner and après intends a lot easier.

It has been revealed that I’ve been on enough group ski trips to know that getting 12 people out the door at the same time is an unachievable goal. That’s why staying within walking distance of multiple lifts accessing Mammoth’s sprawling terrain is such a gift. Everyone can ski on their own schedule, and nobody has to organize a carpool.

Sources indicate that mammoth ranked No. 7 in the West in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and landed in the Top 10 for snow, grooming, and terrain variety. With more than 3,500 acres of skiable terrain, 3,100 feet of vertical, and a summit elevation above 11,000 feet, it’s the kind of mountain that can keep even the most ambitious skiers occupied for days.

Industry observers note that inside the townhouse, you’ll find a wood-burning fireplace, private steam room, arcade table, and a well-equipped kitchen designed to feed a crowd. There’s ski and gear storage, too, which anyone who has shared a vacation rental with 11 other skiers will appreciate.

And because the Canyon Lodge lifts are within walking distance, you can leave the cars parked and focus on the notable stuff, like who forgot to buy coffee and whose turn it is to make breakfast.

According to recent reports, fresh Yorkers don’t have to travel far to find a proper ski weekend. Hunter Mountain, about 2.5 hours from the city, offers 1,600 feet of vertical and some of the most substantial lift-served skiing in the Catskills. And while Western skiers might turn their noses up at skiing in New York, anyone who’s spent time on the East Coast knows there’s a particular satisfaction in making the most of whatever winter throws at you. Hunter’s extensive snowmaking helps with that.

According to recent reports, and just down the road is an architecturally stunning 225-square-foot mirrored tiny home that practically disappears into the surrounding forest. There’s a private wraparound deck with a hot tub, hammock, and outdoor fireplace, plus access to an all-glass sauna. It’s the kind of place that makes a romantic ski weekend feel considerably more romantic.

And if you’re a true New Yorker without a car, take a tip from my friend Abby and take the $59 round-trip ski bus from Manhattan to Hunter Mountain. You’ll still need to figure out transportation between the mountain and the cabin, but it’s a pretty compelling alternative to renting a car for the weekend. Check the bus schedule before planning an overnight stay.

This ski-town rental has one amenity that immediately caught our attention: a private sauna overlooking a Vermont river.

Located along the Brewster River near Smugglers’ Notch, this two-bedroom cottage is surrounded by 20 acres of mountain scenery. Large windows frame the water, while a wood-burning fire pit and sauna make post-ski recovery a major draw.

The fully equipped kitchen and riverside dining area are ideal for slow mornings, though there’s plenty of reason to head out early. Just a short drive away, Smugglers’ Notch Resort spreads across three mountains, with 78 trails and plenty of tree skiing.

In a recent development, smugglers’ Notch has a reputation as a family resort (it earned the No. 2 spot for family friendliness in our 2027 Resort Guide), which might lead you to imagine an endless procession of pizza wedges and children in matching ski-school vests. But over on Madonna and Sterling, the mountain has some legitimately challenging terrain, including steep trails and tree skiing that demand your full attention.

It has been revealed that smuggs ranked No. 11 in the East in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and earned the No. 3 spot for value and No. 5 for terrain variety. Not bad for a mountain that still feels refreshingly old-school. In other words, you can spend the day skiing some legitimately challenging terrain and the evening recovering in a sauna with a view, with absolutely no obligation to do anything productive.

One thing to know: The hosts require four-wheel or all-wheel drive for winter access, and Route 108 through Smugglers’ Notch Pass closes seasonally.

According to recent reports, some ski trip lodging is designed for little more than getting some sleep between ski days. Others feel like the main event.

The Cabin at Bear River, a 560-square-foot retreat tucked into 3.5 wooded acres near Sunday River, falls firmly into the second category.

The fireplace, radiant-heated floors, and well-equipped kitchen, complete with a fondue pot and KitchenAid mixer, make a compelling case for a particularly civilized après experience.

Sources indicate that when you’re ready to ski off that Gruyère, Sunday River is just down the road. Spanning eight interconnected peaks and 884 skiable acres, the Maine resort offers everything from long groomers to challenging steeps. Expert skiers can test themselves on White Heat, one of the East’s famously steep double-black-diamond runs, while intermediates will find plenty to explore across the mountain.

Sunday River ranked No. 9 in the East in SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide and earned top-10 honors for grooming, lifts, and terrain variety.

Back at the cabin, there’s a private sauna and outdoor hot tub waiting. Call it recovery if you want. Personally, I don’t need a sports scientist to justify cranking those jets all the way up.

In a recent development, utah’s ski reputation has been built largely on the Cottonwood Canyons, and for good reason. But there’s a whole other ski experience waiting four hours south of Salt Lake City, where the mountains look nothing like the Wasatch, the base elevation is a lofty 9,600 feet, and you don’t have to spend your morning sitting in the red snake of traffic wondering whether everyone else in the state also called in sick.

According to recent reports, brian Head Resort is one of Utah’s highest-elevation ski resorts. Its two mountains, Giant Steps and Navajo, offer 72 trails and 1,320 feet of vertical. Navajo is a good place for beginners to get their ski legs, while Giant Steps has more challenging terrain, including intermediate and expert runs and terrain parks.

Industry observers note that the surrounding landscape is a world away from the Wasatch, too. Think high-desert scenery, red-rock country, and the chance to tack on a visit to nearby Cedar Breaks National Monument.

And tucked among the trees, just a short drive from the lifts, is this striking Scandinavian-inspired chalet that I think I might actually take off this list so I can have it all to myself. (Swiftly Googles “squatters’ rights in Utah.”).

Inside, expansive windows let in plenty of natural light, while the clean, modern interiors make an excellent case for doing very little after skiing beyond enjoying the private hot tub and fire pit right outside.

With room for eight guests, it’s a great option for a group trip, especially if your friends appreciate a good at-home après setup as much as fresh snow.

If your ideal winter vacation includes a wood-burning fireplace, a good book, and excellent Fresh England skiing, let us introduce The Conscious Cabin.

This renovated 777-square-foot log cabin sits on three wooded acres in Fresh Hampshire’s White Mountains, less than 10 minutes from downtown North Conway.

It has been revealed that inside, exposed timber and cozy furnishings deliver exactly the kind of atmosphere you’d hope for from a New England cabin. Outside, there’s a spacious backyard with a fire pit, gazebo, and a short trail leading to a brook.

Recent findings suggest that nearby Cranmore Mountain, just outside downtown North Conway, offers 1,200 feet of vertical and 60 trails, and is particularly well suited to families and skiers who appreciate cruising groomers. For more challenging terrain, head to Attitash, where two peaks offer more than 300 skiable acres, including classic Newly introduced England trails, glades, and steeper runs.

Both resorts made SKI’s 2027 Resort Guide, ranking No. 17 and No. 19 in the East, respectively. Cranmore also took the top spot for lodging and ranked No. 4 for dining, making North Conway an especially appealing base for a winter getaway.

After all, this charming cabin is considerably more appealing than spending the holidays sleeping on your aunt’s pullout couch in the basement.

If your ideal ski vacation includes a little European charm without the transatlantic flight, Mont-Tremblant makes a pretty convincing case.

The Québec resort is known for its colorful pedestrian village, lively après scene, and some of the most substantial lift-served skiing in Eastern Canada.

With more than 100 trails spread across four mountain faces, 763 skiable acres, and 2,116 feet of vertical, Tremblant has enough terrain to keep everyone from beginners to expert skiers entertained. Its extensive snowmaking system is another welcome advantage for early-season trips.

Perched on the mountainside, Horizon 115-204 is a modern three-bedroom condo with ski-in/ski-out access, so you can go from breakfast to the slopes without a complicated transportation strategy.

In a recent development, inside, there’s a gas fireplace, a fully equipped kitchen, and enough room for eight guests. A balcony offers mountain air and space for a post-ski drink, while an on-site hot tub gives you another great reason to get out of your ski boots quickly.

And if you’re not quite ready to call it a night, the resort’s pedestrian village is accessible by shuttle, with restaurants, bars, and enough après activity to keep the evening going.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The state of Alaska may soon decide to close more than 400 square miles to hunting and trapping in anticipation of a controversial mining road. The decision would be part of a push by the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority to build a road creating private access to a future mining district focused on copper and zinc deposits.

While the Ambler Road itself has faced continuous opposition from hunting and conservation groups for its potential to fragment one of the largest remaining caribou herds, among other fish and habitat issues, the recent development is creating even more consternation.

“It’s unprecedented,” notes Mary Glaves, Alaska program manager for Backcountry Hunters and Anglers. “We’re supposed to allow for balanced use of all of our resources. This would show preference to one resource over another.”.

The proposal, which the Alaska Board of Game will consider during an online meeting Friday, would close 1 mile on either side of the 211-mile proposed road in northern Alaska to all hunting and trapping. It first became public in February and is part of a memorandum of understanding between several Alaskan native corporations and the state. The proposed closure is part of a “subsistence safeguard,” according to a story in the Alaska Beacon. Subsistence hunters could still cross through the road corridor to access other legal hunting grounds.

In a recent development, the hunting and trapping ban would begin July 1, 2029, and remain in place through at least Jan. 1, 2036, regardless of when or even if the road is built, Glaves states.

The Board of Game considered formalizing the MOU in a July meeting, and opposition was fierce, indicates Glaves. Still, many Alaskan organizations could not prepare comment because the meeting was in the middle of fishing season. As a result, the board tabled the discussion until its formal meeting in January.

Recent findings suggest that A few months later, the Alaska Fish and Game commissioner revealed another special meeting Nov. 20 to discuss the project, allowing only written public comment and no oral testimony.

“That isn’t illegal,” Glaves states, “but it’s not in the best interest of engaging the public.”.

Even more importantly, if the closure passes, it tells Alaskans that state public land can be shut down to access at the request of an anticipated industry and with no stated biological need.

The road has not been built, and there’s some question about whether or not Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the Democratic governor-elect, will support the project. He has not stated a position publicly but has stated he will carefully evaluate money spent by the state. The Industrial Development and Export Authority, an economic development arm of the state, would be responsible for building the road. The Alaska Wilderness League, which opposes the project, estimates it could cost the state more than $2 billion including construction, maintenance, and financing.

The preemptive nature of the closure is particularly troubling to conservation groups.

According to recent reports, “There is no compelling reason to establish these restrictions years before the project is constructed or in the absence of demonstrated need,” she wrote on Nov. 4. “Doing so would also set a troubling precedent of using the Board’s time and public resources to evaluate hypothetical impacts of projects that may never materialize, rather than addressing actual wildlife management and public access concerns as they arise.”.

The Incredible Hunt for the C.W. Shelton Buck, One of the Widest Bucks in the World

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “I Shot Major Red,” appeared in the January 1967 issue of Outdoor Life.
  • Industry observers note that at 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime.
  • It has been revealed that I might as well quit, I thought.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “I Shot Major Red,” appeared in the January 1967 issue of Outdoor Life. Shelton’s buck is now the 20th biggest typical whitetail ever taken in Kentucky, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. At the time, however, it was the biggest ever taken in Kentucky. It also had a wider inside and outside spread than any deer on the books, including the then-world-record deer.

Industry observers note that at 2 o’clock in the afternoon on November 28, 1964, I was ready to give up the dream of a lifetime. The rain, which had been steady since before dawn, suddenly stopped, and the woods of northern Todd County, Kentucky, were still. I was 20 feet up in a huge sycamore, watching a deer runway that meandered through thick brush. I’d been half-wet most of the day, and I felt another case of chills coming on.

It has been revealed that I might as well quit, I thought. I’m not going to see Big Red, and I probably won’t see any other deer.

My thoughts seemed logical, but another line of reasoning wouldn’t be denied. This was Todd County’s first deer season in modern times, and the season was for this day only. So far as Big Red was concerned, I had good reason to believe he was the best trophy whitetail buck in North America. Besides, I’m mighty stubborn when it comes to deer hunting. I decided to stay in that tree till dark.

It has been revealed that in front of me, to the north and 30 yards away, a tiny creek flowed through a heavily wooded east-west valley. The runway crossed the creek and continued into dense thickets. I couldn’t see the thickets’ far edge, but I knew the growth thinned against a hillside that topped out alongside a stubble cornfield 200 yards away. The cornfield was 40 yards wide and bordered a little-used gravel road. Across the road was 40 acres of tangled cedars, the thickest cover in the area. I figured any deer leaving those cedars would use the runway I was watching.

According to recent reports, around 2:30 a twig snapped behind me, to the south. Then I heard branches rubbing together and sounds resembling a squirrel digging in the ground. I knew I was listening to a deer.

The sounds were a few yards off the runway. In another minute they became more distinguishable, and I knew the animal was working toward me. I had two choices: remain motionless in hopes the deer would move past me, or try to inch my way around so I’d face south.

Though the leaves were off the trees, I figured I had an excellent chance of moving without being seen. I was standing on a huge branch, but I was tight against the trunk. Deer don’t normally look up, so I also had that advantage. In addition, I figured the deer was feeding and not alerted to immediate danger. I moved as cautiously as possible.

It took a few minutes to make my move. Now I was facing south. Surprisingly, I could still hear the same sounds, but I couldn’t see any movement.

According to recent reports, the sounds kept coming closer. Then, as if by magic, there he was. I saw antlers and legs at the same instant, about 30 yards away. The buck was pawing at acorns. I couldn’t get a clear view of his antlers, and I didn’t dare risk a shot through that thick brush. There wasn’t much I could do except wait.

After what seemed like hours, he suddenly tossed his head up. He seemed to be looking straight at me. His rack was massive, but I knew instantly it didn’t belong to Substantial Red. I was sure the buck had caught a glimpse of me or winded me.

It has been revealed that I better take him, I thought. Time is running out.

Sources indicate that my .44 Magnum Ruger carbine was braced against the trunk. I started lining the crosswires of my Weaver scope on his chest. Then, through my variable-power scope, I made an amazing discovery. That buck wasn’t looking up at me at all; he was staring on the level along the runway toward the north.

Sources indicate that now the eight-pointer relaxed and dropped his head to feed again. I heard the same sounds that had startled him. To the north, behind me now, I heard another deer. I glanced over my shoulder and got the second biggest shock of my life. Massive Red, in all his glory, was walking toward my tree stand. The monstrous buck was in clear view, 50 yards away and moving down the runway. There was no question about his identity.

It has been revealed that I had seen him two years ago when we had come face to face under the most dramatic conditions. We had startled each other that time. Now I had all the cards. Or did I? I was in no position to shoot. If that buck was alerted to the slightest suspicion, he’d bound into the thickets and disappear.

This dream situation had been in the making for a long time. I guess it really started when I was nine years old, the day I shot my first squirrel. After stalking the gray for hours, I knocked it off a stump with my brother Rudy’s .22. I decided then and there I wanted to become the world’s best hunter. That boyhood ambition has never dimmed, though it’s been realistically tempered by maturity. At that time my family lived in the town of Mayfield, in southwestern Kentucky. There was plenty of small game and birds, but no deer.

By the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

By the time I was in high school, I was addicted to duck hunting. The area around Mayfield is laced with creeks, rivers, and potholes. It was a duck paradise. I taught myself how to call by sneaking up on flocks of waterfowl and listening to their various calls. I’d go hunting before and after school every day during the season. I practically lived outdoors. But by the time I got a chance to go deer hunting, I discovered I wasn’t much of a hunter after all.

I’m 26 now and live in Bowling Green, where I work as a real estate salesman and auctioneer. My wife and I have a daughter, four, and a son, two.

Kentucky’s first modern deer season opened in 1956, when I was still a teenager. I didn’t get a chance to hunt deer until 1959, but nobody ever dreamed about deer hunting more than I did.

Looking back, I realize I started my first season as quite a stupid deer hunter. I had no experience, and I’d never seen a deer in my life. The 1959 season lasted three days, and I hunted every one of them from dawn to dark. After it was all over, my record was unblemished: I still hadn’t seen a deer. I’m not sure I even saw a fresh track.

It has been revealed that three months before the 1960 season opened, I started scouting my hunting territory on weekends. With six weeks to go, I stepped up my scouting trips to every couple of days. I found runways and beds, examined browse conditions, and located the “use” areas of three herds of whitetails. It all paid off. I killed a fat doe from a tree stand just after dawn on the opening day of the season.

Recent findings suggest that I missed the 1961 season because of a session with Uncle Sam, but I didn’t lose contact with shooting. My ability with a rifle was good enough to win me an instructor’s rating, and I had charge of an army rifle range for 10 months.

Recent findings suggest that in 1962 and 1963, I collected my second and third whitetails. I shot both of them while sneaking silently into bedding areas I’d discovered on scouting trips. My 1962 deer bolted from thick brush 80 yards away, and I dropped him with a single bullet. My third deer, a six-pointer, heard me pussyfooting along, but I saw him before he spotted me. He went down in his tracks.

After I killed my first deer, I studied taxidermy and began mounting deer heads for my friends. I mounted the head of my big six-pointer, but every time I looked at it I dreamed of the day when those six points would be dwarfed by a much larger rack. My dream had plenty of substance because by this time I’d seen Big Red.

In a recent development, we met in October, 1962, while I was living in the town of Elkton, Todd County. I’d heard that the county might be opened to deer hunting, so I started scouting likely areas. I’d done some business with H. Sweeney, a local farmer, and he’d told me he frequently saw deer crossing his fields.

Recent findings suggest that on one of my scouting trips, I found a heavily traveled runway through a hilly area of oak, poplar, hickory, and cedar. The runway was pocked with fresh tracks, and I followed it down through the hills and across a valley to where it led into a rye field. Where the field met the woods, a huge oak tree offered a perfect stand. I decided to climb the tree and see what moved along the runway toward evening.

About 5 p.m. I heard some deer coming through the woods. It was a warm, quiet day, and the trees were still in full foliage, so I heard them for a long time before I saw them. Shortly, three deer walked below me and went out into the rye field to feed. I watched them for half an hour. Then I heard another deer. He moved steadily to the last bit of cover, then stopped.

I made out the partial outline of a huge deer. The whitetail stood motionless for a full five minutes; then he stepped into the field and joined the other animals. He had an eight-point rack and was the biggest deer I’d ever seen.

Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Recent findings suggest that then I heard dogs barking. They were chasing something, and the sounds kept coming closer. A six-point buck suddenly burst out of the woods, ran under my tree, and joined the other deer. As if on signal, they all bolted out of sight.

Recent findings suggest that I never did see the dogs or any more deer, though I stayed in the tree till dusk. I’d traveled farther than I thought, and it was dark before I got halfway back to my car. I decided to bypass the woods and stay in the fields. It was this decision that set up the chance meeting with Big Red.

In a recent development, I was crossing a fescue field when I approached a man-made stock pond. Banks, about 10 feet high, had been bulldozed around the pond to collect and hold water. I could have walked around the embankment, but I decided to walk along the top of it. A full moon had just cleared the horizon, and the landscape was bathed with an eerie beauty. I went up to the top of the bank and got the shock of my life. Across the pond, 20 yards away on top of the opposite bank, stood the most magnificent whitetail buck in all the world.

Recent findings suggest that the huge animal was silhouetted against the moon in fantastic beauty. I guess we saw each other in the same instant, and we both froze, each sizing up the other.

I remember my breath going out in a gasp. My first thought was that I was looking at somebody’s tame elk. Then I knew the animal had to be a deer. His size didn’t awe me so much as did the tremendous spread of his antlers.

We must have stared at each other for seconds. Then the monster buck snorted, whirled, and bolted down the bank and across the field. About 75 yards away, he leaped a five-foot fence. Then he stopped and looked back. I took a few steps toward him, and he trotted into some woods.

In a recent development, I was talking to myself when I got back to the farmer’s yard where I’d parked my car. I went up to the house and knocked on the door. He didn’t seem very impressed when I exclaimed, “I’ve just seen the biggest buck in Kentucky!”.

“That’s Big Red,” he mentioned. “I’ve seen him a few times. You can’t mistake him. He’s a lot bigger than an ordinary deer. His face is sort of reddish. That’s why we call him Big Red. The local farmers know about him, and you’re going to have plenty of tech giant if you figure on hunting that buck.”.

As it turned out, Todd County wasn’t open for deer hunting in 1962 or 1963. Kentucky controls its whitetail population by allowing hunting only in counties where the herds have built up to the carrying capacity of available deer range. In 1956 (the first year that deer hunting had been allowed since 1911) only 27 of the state’s 120 counties were open to shooting. In that season 6,000 hunters killed 1,300 whitetails. By comparison, 14,000 hunters bagged 4,100 deer in 1965. The 1966 population was estimated at well over 50,000 deer, and hunting was allowed in 74 counties.

All of this had its beginning in 1950 when the state began its stocking program with deer bought from Pennsylvania. Original stockings were made in Mammoth Cave National Park and Federal Wildlife refuges. With a ban on hunting, these herds multiplied so rapidly that certain areas became overrun with deer. Live-trapping crews thinned out the overpopulated sections and stocked the deer in other areas that had heavy browse conditions. As these herds build to huntable populations, additional counties are opened to hunting.

Industry observers note that in the summer of 1964, the Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources unveiled that Todd County would have its first deer season, a one-day hunt on November 28. I told my brother Rudy about Major Red, and we planned to hunt him together. We didn’t get much sleep the night before the season opened, and we left for our hunting area at 3 a.m.

A few changes had taken place during the two years since I’d met Substantial Red. The monster buck had moved from the Sweeney farm to adjoining woodlands owned by farmer Ross Laster. The deer’s travel routes had also changed, but I knew all about this because I knew Ross well and hadn’t relaxed my scouting trips. I hadn’t seen the buck a second time, but I’d found his tracks many times, and some of the local farmers had seen him just a month earlier.

In a recent development, dawn was breaking when Rudy and I drove down a gravel road toward Ross’s farm. A mile from our destination, a four-point buck jumped across the road ahead of us, ran to the far edge of a small stubble cornfield and stopped.

“Get your rifle and nail him,” Rudy remarked as he braked the car.

Sources indicate that “No, you take him,” I answered. Neither of us made a move, and the buck walked slowly out of sight. While we wouldn’t admit it, both Rudy and I weren’t the least bit interested in shooting that buck.

We drove to the farmhouse, and Ross had news.

“That bunch of deer are traveling new runways,” he noted. “The best one is about a mile down the road by a cornfield where. . . .”.

Sources indicate that “That’s where we just saw a buck,” I interrupted. “There’s a bunch of cedars across the road.”.

“That’s the place,” Ross noted. “I’d forget your other plans and pick a couple of stands along that runway.”.

Industry observers note that that’s exactly what we did. Half an hour later, I found the significant sycamore I mentioned in the beginning. Rudy decided to follow the runway toward some heavily wooded ridges half a mile away.

In a recent development, the air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

Industry observers note that about 8 o’clock, it started raining hard. By 8:30 I was so wet I went back to the car, changed clothes, and put on a yellow rainsuit. I was almost back to the sycamore when I heard shots from Rudy’s area. I walked up on a ridge and found Rudy all excited.

It has been revealed that “I shot at a buck with a brushpile rack,” he said. “I was curled up under a tree trying to stay dry when I heard a deer coming down the runway behind me. I turned around and we spotted each other at the same time. The buck bolted, and I cut loose with three shots. I lost his tracks right here. He sure was a significant one!”.

In a recent development, rudy was a mighty disappointed deer hunter. He’s 35 and one of the best outdoorsmen I know. He’s been a hunting nut all his life, and he taught me how to hunt and fish when I was a boy. He lives in Mayfield where he works as a heavy-equipment operator. He’s married and has two teenage sons.

Industry observers note that rudy went back to his stand, and I stillhunted till noon. We met at the car for lunch, stillhunted another hour, then returned to our stands. It wasn’t long after that when I glanced over my shoulder and saw Massive Red.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t remember any trace of buck fever, but I do recall coldly analyzing the situation. I studied every bit of cover between myself and the deer. About 40 yards from my tree stand, a clump of cedars edged the runway. Massive Red would have to pass behind that clump. When he did, I’d turn around.

Industry observers note that my change in position came off like clockwork. When the animal appeared again he was unsuspicious, and I was in perfect shooting position with my scope lined up on his chest. I decided against squeezing the trigger. I wanted him to come as close as possible.

Recent findings suggest that at the creek 30 yards away, the trophy buck stopped for a drink. The suspense was terrible. I used this moment of his relaxed alertness to suck in a deep breath. The air rasped into my throat with such suddenness that I momentarily feared he’d heard me. But he gave no sign of caution. He raised his head, walked through the shallow creek, and came directly toward my tree.

It has been revealed that suddenly he stopped, turned his head toward his backtrack, tilted his nose, and tested the air. Then he swung his massive antlers forward and walked behind a couple of cedars where he stopped dead still. I had a feeling he was getting nervous.

Sources indicate that he might bolt at any second, I thought. As soon as he steps from behind those cedars, I’m going to shoot.

The range was now 25 yards, and there was no question about his increased caution. His face peeked from behind the cedars. Then that unbelievable rack. Again he stood motionless. Suddenly he broke into a fast trot.

The crosswires settled at the base of his neck, and my rifle roared.

According to recent reports, substantial Red staggered sideways, regained control of his feet, and lunged straight ahead. I aimed my second shot for his shoulder, and the 240-grain bullet spun him around. He dived into thickets alongside the runway and was gone. I heard him crash through brush; then all was silent. I knew he had fallen.

It has been revealed that I went down that tree as fast as I could. I got within 30 yards of him, and then he staggered away. I snapped two shots through the thickets, but the bullets never got to him. I heard him fall again about 60 yards to my right. I got within 40 feet of him before he tried getting up. He couldn’t make it. Another bullet finished him instantly.

I started field-dressing the buck immediately. It wasn’t easy. His bulk was so great I couldn’t move him. I tied his legs to saplings to spread-eagle his hindquarters. Throughout the job, I whistled for Rudy every few minutes. It’s a whistle note we’ve used for woods communication since we were kids. I was nearly done with the chore when Rudy found me. He stayed with the buck while I went to Ross Laster’s farm for help.

In a recent development, four of the Laster brothers and I got a tractor to within 300 yards of Big Red. Then we had to chop down saplings, clear brush, and cut a fence to get the tractor within 100 yards of the buck. After that it was pure bull work — dragging, hauling, and lifting Big Red till we finally had him balanced on the tractor.

In a recent development, A few hours later, he weighed 260 pounds on a coal scale. I was surprised because I’d figured he would scale over 300 pounds. I guess the massive antlers fooled me. I was familiar with the Boone and Crockett Club method of scoring trophy deer, and I was certain my buck would score near the top of the record list.

Two months later, the antlers scored 185 4/8 points. My trophy won third place for typical whitetails in the Boone and Crockett Club two-year competition period ending December 31, 1965. Though I didn’t kill a newly introduced world record, I did score some impressive ratings. Big Red is the best trophy whitetail ever killed in Kentucky.

The inside spread of his rack measures 30 2/8 inches, more than 10 inches wider than the current world record. While checking the last listing of all-time Boone and Crockett records, I discovered that this inside measurement is the greatest among all typical whitetail deer recorded there. Though I realize that total score is all that counts, I doubt whether anyone will ever kill a whitetail buck with a wider antler spread than Big Red’s.

There’s one thing I can guarantee — nobody will ever know a greater hunting thrill than I experienced when I looked over my shoulder in that sycamore and saw the dream of a lifetime coming true.

Lessons I Learned from Deer Hunting with My Kids
