Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1477 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights).
  • Ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest.
  • According to recent reports, mostafavi never fulfilled his promise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights).

Ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest. In 2019, he trekked to its Base Camp. Under a photo of him pointing to the summit, he wrote on Instagram in English: “Top of the world. I promise to come back to you.”.

According to recent reports, mostafavi never fulfilled his promise. On October 14, he was executed by the Iranian authorities in Kerman Central Prison.

The 38-year-old is one of at least 39 people to have been executed in connection with Iran’s anti-government protests last winter, and one of six athletes among them.

According to recent reports, dr. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, an ice climber and co-founder of the Norway-based Human Rights for Sport, told Climbing, “From a human rights perspective, every single aspect of this case is an absolute violation. The state has not made any credible, independently verifiable evidence public.”.

Recent findings suggest that born in 1987 in Bam County, southeastern Iran, Mostafavi was a professional mountaineer and a member of the Speeco mountaineering club in his home city of Kerman. He called mountains ‘the love of his life,’ according to Abdollahkhani.

It has been revealed that mostafavi climbed two of Iran’s highest peaks, Damavand (5,610m/18,410ft) and Alam-Kuh (4,850m/15,910ft). In 2016, he ascended Mount Kazbek (5,054m/16,581ft) in Georgia.

Recent findings suggest that in 2019, Mostafavi traveled to Nepal and summited Island Peak (6,189m/20,305ft) and trekked to Everest Base Camp. In 2022, he attempted Ama Dablam (6,812m/22,349ft), reaching 6,600m/21,654ft.

It has been revealed that mostafavi was married and had a 13-year-old daughter, Respina. Alongside his climbing career, he was an accomplished musician who played the tar, a traditional Persian lute. Friends spoke of his sensitive, artistic spirit, and his deep love for mountains, music, and animals—notably, his beloved cat and dog.

In a recent development, on his Instagram account, @everest_coldhell, his bio reads: ‘Mount Explorer. Love the nature. Musician.’.

In December 2025, Iran’s economic crisis sparked street protests that developed into nationwide demonstrations against the Islamic Republic’s repressive regime, which enforces compulsory hijab laws restricting women’s autonomy, conducts violent crackdowns on protests, challenges arbitrary arrests, and employs the use of torture.

Industry observers note that in an attempt to suppress dissent, authorities used lethal force, killing thousands and arresting tens of thousands of protesters. The human rights organization Amnesty International called this “the deadliest period of repression by the Iranian authorities” in its decades of monitoring the country.

Following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, Iran’s government intensified repressive crackdowns on dissent under the pretext of “wartime conditions.”.

By October, at least 106 people arrested during the January protests had received death sentences, according to documentation by human rights organization Hengaw.

Industry observers note that iran carries out the world’s second-highest number of executions after China. In 2025, its government executed at least 2,159 people, the highest figure recorded by Amnesty International since 1981.

On Instagram, Mostafavi expressed support for Iran’s former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, an exiled dissident who calls for a secular, democratic, and liberal Iran, describing him as “the only saviour of the homeland.” Two sources claim that Mostafavi’s family were set to move abroad before the 2022 ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests began, but he ultimately chose to remain to fight for Iran’s future.

One obituary claims that he had been arrested twice in recent years for political activism and had spent time in Kerman Prison. This January, the mountaineer joined protests alongside millions of Iranians.

IranWire, an independent pro-democracy outlet, reported that Mostafavi was arrested three months later on April 25 alongside his wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé, while his mother’s home was also raided.

Mostafavi was reportedly beaten during his arrest and was forced to sign confession papers to release his family members. It is not known whether he had access to an independent lawyer, a right frequently denied to defendants in political and national security cases in Iran.

The Iranian judiciary’s account of the case was published by state-aligned media outlets including Mizan News Agency, Tasnim News Agency, the IRIB, and Tabnak. The allegations have not been independently verified.

The Judiciary of Iran claimed that Mostafavi had participated in the widespread anti-government protests in January, and that he was a member of the “Immortal Guards,” an armed wing of exiled dissident Reza Pahlavi’s group.

The judiciary also alleged that Mostafavi had shot and injured two civilians, fired at security forces, and possessed firearms, ammunition, and Molotov cocktails. It further accused him of communicating with foreign media and sharing footage of missile strike locations during the US-Iran war.

According to recent reports, mostafavi was convicted of the capital offense of moharebeh, or “enmity against God,” alongside several charges relating to alleged violence, weapons possession, and communication with hostile media. The evidence against him has not been made public.

The judiciary reported that the fiancé of Mostafavi’s sister received a prison sentence of 12 years and seven months for alleged cooperation, while he, his wife, and his sister were also sentenced to seven months in prison for posting content deemed as propaganda against the regime.

An appeal against Mostafavi’s death sentence was rejected. IranWire reported that he was transferred to solitary confinement the night before his execution and that family members were summoned. The judiciary announced that he was hanged at dawn in Kerman Central Prison on October 14. According to IranWire, Mostafavi asked the prison guards to pass along a message to the judge: “I did not wage war against God, nor did I commit moharebeh that you should charge me with it; my fight was with you.”.

That evening, state-aligned outlet Tabnak published footage purporting to show Mostafavi’s arrest, weapons allegedly found in his possession, and a confession to a planned attack on Kerman Airport. IranWire reported that the confession appeared to have been made under duress and spliced together with unverified footage. Amnesty International has also identified signs of forced confessions in 18 videos of Iranian prisoners arrested between February and May 2026, during the same period as Mostafavi’s arrest.

Shortly after his death, a video of Mostafavi’s young daughter crying on her father’s grave, accompanied by their cat, circulated on social media.

Human rights groups have voiced concerns about Mostafavi’s case in the context of widespread forced confessions and sham trials lacking due process in Iran.

“The complete absence of forensic evidence or transparent court records confirms that his conviction rested entirely on forced confessions extracted under coercion rather than any objective proof,” Abdollahkhani said.

She explained that the arrest of Mostafavi’s wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé fits an established pattern of authorities using family members as leverage.

“The Islamic Republic routinely arrests close relatives and uses threats of torture or sexual violence to force athletes into making false confessions in a desperate bid to save their loved ones,” she stated.

According to Human Rights for Sport, at least eight other mountaineers’ lives are at risk.

Maryam Hadavand Siri, a 42-year-old mother of two, led the Mountaineering Board of Pakdasht County in Tehran Province. She was arrested during the January protests, transferred to Evin Prison, and sentenced to death in April, without access to an independent lawyer. Following an appeal, her case was referred to the Supreme Court for review.

Social media activist and mountaineer Fatemeh Jami was arrested at her home on June 30 by Cyber Police officers. She was transferred to Gorgan Prison, where she remains detained without access to a lawyer or medical assistance.

Sources indicate that tara (Shirin) Masoudi, a member of the Razhan Mountaineering Group in Mahabad, was arrested on August 19. She was transferred to a detention centre and later released on bail. She is awaiting a final verdict.

It has been revealed that mohammad Hakimpour, Mostafa Ghaderi, Mohammad Saleh Hosseini, Hossein Abdollahi, and Khaled Rahimi—all members of climbing clubs in Saqqez—were arrested on October 8. According to Human Rights for Sport, they were subjected to physical abuse in detention and have been denied access to legal counsel, family visits, and telephone calls.

Abdollahkhani urges climbers to raise awareness of Mostafavi’s execution and the status of the eight other mountaineers, and to contact national federations, sports governing bodies, the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

“How is it possible that a member of the climbing community is at risk of execution on alleged political charges, while the global climbing world stays silent?” she asked.

It has been revealed that on October 30, Human Rights for Sport published an open letter to the UIAA executive board and athlete commission. In the letter, Abdollahkhani asks the UIAA to appeal directly to Iran’s national mountaineering federation, along with its Ministry of Sport and National Olympic Committee, to stop further executions and advocate for the release of imprisoned climbers.

This Latest Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing).
  • We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them.
  • Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing).

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

It has been revealed that there is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”.

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

Recent findings suggest that as the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” states Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the newly introduced book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”.

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

It has been revealed that robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”.

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

According to recent reports, robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”.

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”.

It has been revealed that another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

In a recent development, “Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

It has been revealed that vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (421 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers.
  • “His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said.
  • Industry observers note that daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came promptly.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Shah Daulat on Facebook).

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”.

Industry observers note that daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came promptly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

According to recent reports, but his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

Industry observers note that on February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

According to recent reports, after his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”.

In September, the artist Iowna Chichowich installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

Two Hikers Rescued from Wet Snow and Freezing Temperatures Deep in the White Mountains

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (366 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A view west from Mount Bond in Upcoming Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness.
  • Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.
  • Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A view west from Mount Bond in Upcoming Hampshire's Pemigewasset Wilderness. (Photo: MikeCherim / Getty Images).

Two hikers were rescued on Saturday near the summit of 4,698-foot Mount Bond in New Hampshire’s Pemigewasset Wilderness after they encountered deep, wet snow and freezing temperatures along their hike.

Hikers typically climb Mount Bond via one of two routes. The first involves taking the Lincoln Woods Trail, which is generally a 19.9 mile round-trip hike with 3,959 feet of elevation gain and at the moment partially closed. The second route takes hikers up the Zealand Trail, covering 19 miles and up to 4,947 feet of elevation gain.

While it isn’t clear which route the duo took to Mount Bond, 23-year-old Ethan Fena and 21-year-old Matthew Nakota were more than 10 miles into their hike near the summit when they encountered winter trail conditions.

Although they’d packed lights, food, and water, New Hampshire Fish and Game (NHFG) noted the pair had hiked the route without overnight and winter equipment, leaving them struggling to warm themselves. By the time the duo called for help, they’d assembled a makeshift shelter in an attempt to warm up and allow their gear to dry.

NHFG remarked that conservation officers initiated a rescue operation, using ATVs to transport volunteers with the Pemi Valley Search and Rescue Team to the area. Rescuers reached the pair at about 11:45 p.m., and helped them begin the descent back to the trailhead. The whole party arrived safely at the parking lot at about 2 a.m. on Sunday, November 15th.

In the wake of the incident, Upcoming Hampshire Fish and Game officials reminded hikers to consider factors like shortened daylight hours and failing temperatures before heading into the mountains.

According to recent reports, this incident comes just 11 days after two 18-year-olds became stranded on Mount Washington after getting caught on the peak without headlamps. The two hikers reached the Lakes of the Clouds AMC Hut and discovered that it had been closed for the season when they realized they needed help. The group used an emergency shelter located at the hut until rescuers reached the hikers and helped them descend the mountain.

#44597. The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (619 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (619 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels.
  • Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect.
  • According to recent reports, in Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson).

Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

According to recent reports, in Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

Sources indicate that as someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

According to recent reports, I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

According to recent reports, if you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, New Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

Recent findings suggest that the “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

In a recent development, norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.

Industry News: Giant November Waves Threaten Surfers, Swimmers, and Spectators Along California’s Coast

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that powerful waves crash against Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California, on November 14, 2026, as large Pacific swells batter the state's coastline.
  • Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.
  • In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that powerful waves crash against Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California, on November 14, 2026, as large Pacific swells batter the state's coastline. (Photo: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images).

Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.

In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI.

“I’ve seen seasons start off with a bang like this, but we’ve never had this type of impact so immediate,” Ernst Bauen, operations division chief for the Central Fire District of Santa Cruz County, told Outside on November 17.

It has been revealed that the enormous swells were generated by powerful low-pressure systems over the northeastern Pacific, where hurricane-force winds pushed waves toward the California coast, according to the National Weather Service. On November 14, forecasters predicted breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet, with occasional sets reaching 40 to 50 feet at big-wave surfing spot Mavericks, near Half Moon Bay.

Bauen, who spent about 20 years as a rescue swimmer, stated waves are reaching roads, cliffs, and beach access points earlier in the season than usual.

“The ocean is extremely dynamic, and where there used to be a safe amount of space to recreate even on the beach, those spaces are becoming fewer and further between because of the erosion along our coastline,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that on November 14, rescue crews pulled three surfers from the water near Pleasure Point in Santa Cruz County. A fire department rescuer had picked up two surfers on a jet ski when a large wave overturned the watercraft, throwing all three into the ocean.

The rescuer, a part of Bauen’s team, managed to right the jet ski and continue the operation, returning about ten minutes later to help a third surfer.

Hundreds of miles south that same day, a San Diego lifeguard swam through powerful breaking waves to reach a struggling swimmer at La Jolla Cove. Another lifeguard eventually arrived on a jet ski and brought both men to safety.

Recent findings suggest that also in San Diego on November 14, at nearby Windansea Beach, a teenager photographing the waves from nearby rocks was swept into the ocean. A surfer jumped into the water and briefly helped keep the teenager’s head above the surface before waves carried him toward the rocky shoreline, where several bystanders helped pull him out.

The close call underscored warnings from San Diego Lifeguard Chief Daniel Orloff that even spectators watching from dry land were at risk. “If you are close, at any moment, a wave could take you out. It can breach a bluff, a berm, even the boardwalk,” he told ABC 10News.

In Orange County, a surfer helped rescue three people struggling in strong currents at Crystal Cove State Beach on November 15, according to a witness who shared video of the aftermath with TV station 10 News San Diego.

Not every incident ended in a rescue. On November 14, a man disappeared while swimming near Zuma Beach in Malibu. Lifeguards responded to the scene around 1:40 p.m., and Coast Guard helicopters and boat crews searched for the missing swimmer into the following day. The Coast Guard suspended its search on November 15 without locating him. The man has not publicly been identified.

Bauen said the ocean can also lull people into a false sense of security. During these swells, waves can stay relatively small for 15 or 20 minutes at a time, making conditions look calm before a surge of much larger waves suddenly arrives and catches surfers off guard.

Rising tides can also leave surfers stranded when the beach access points they used to enter the water become submerged.

Sources indicate that while the largest waves have eased, forecasters say hazardous surf will linger through November 19. In its November 17 forecast, the National Weather Service predicted breaking waves of 13 to 17 feet along portions of the Bay Area and Central Coast through November 18, with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.

Bauen urged surfers and beachgoers to check the forecast, pay attention to changing conditions, and identify a safe route back to shore before entering the water.

Industry observers note that “Ultimately, it comes down to the individual,” Bauen said. “You really need to know before you go. You need to tune into the ocean conditions, look up forecasts, and do a little bit of research before you explore a secluded beach, decide to go for a swim, or paddle out.”.

#44594. Breaking: I’ve Been a Night Owl All My Life. Here Are 7 Things I Did to Become a Morning Exerciser.

Breaking: I’ve Been a Night Owl All My Life. Here Are 7 Things I Did to Become a Morning Exerciser.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (835 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I am a consummate night owl.
  • Waking up in the morning has never been my strong suit.
  • It has been revealed that for weeks at a time, exercise just wouldn’t happen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I am a consummate night owl. When I was a teenager, my mother used to begin waking me up by knocking on my door, then taking my pillow away, then my bed sheets. When she’d find me still asleep on the bare mattress, she’d push me onto the floor. That’s where my little brother would find me, still asleep, and begin wailing that I needed to drive him to school because he didn’t want to be late (again).

Waking up in the morning has never been my strong suit. But when I graduated from college and no longer had a coach holding me to a daily afternoon cross-country practice, I found that exercise stopped being a priority. By the time I got off work at 5 p.m., I was too tired to go to the gym, or I had dinner aims, or had eaten something weird and decided it was impossible to run.

It has been revealed that for weeks at a time, exercise just wouldn’t happen. Certain that turning myself into a morning exerciser would solve all my problems, I told my mom I was on a mission to become an early bird. She shook her head. “I’ve been trying my whole life,” she noted. “If you figure it out, you let me know.”.

According to recent reports, most folks consider the night-owl versus early-bird categorization a matter of intrinsic wiring—you’re born one or the other, and you cannot change. While there is a strong genetic basis for your natural circadian rhythm, it is possible to switch. In fact, after about a year of working to adjust my sleep cycle, I now wake up at or before 6 a.m. almost every morning (even when I don’t necessarily want to). That means I now get to the gym or trail four or five days a week instead of one or two. Here are all the things I did to help me make the change.

Industry observers note that telling myself that “I will wake up and exercise” was too vague. “I will wake up, drive to the park, walk three miles, and then get a latte at my favorite coffee shop” is much easier to visualize (and get excited for). In the early morning, I only ever plan on doing fun exercise, whether that’s going to the climbing gym, doing pull-ups at the park, or running my favorite loop. If it’s a workout I’m likely to skip at 11 a.m., I definitely will at 6.

Industry observers note that I’m a very guilt-motivated person. If I only have to meet myself at the gym, I’ll stand me up every time. But if there’s another human being waiting, I’ll be there. I am fortunate to know several very motivated and punctual lady friends who also like to lift weights at 7 a.m. Making intends with them two or three times per week keeps me honest.

In a recent development, if I’ve paid for something, I feel a compulsive need to get my money’s worth out of it—even if that means waking up at dawn to do so. One of the best things I did for my sleep schedule was register for a recreational adult climbing team with 6 a.m. practices. I’ve also tried classes like CrossFit or F45, many of which charge $15 to $30 if you no-show.

Caveat: I find the class strategy is only effective if it’s recurring; I’m much more motivated to show up for a group of people I see every day than for a batch of strangers I’ll never see again.

When I’m warm in bed, tired, and dreading exercise, I make the smallest possible promise: I tell myself that I will go to the gym and only do one set of squats. Or only 15 minutes of stretching. Or only a single mile on the treadmill. If I feel good, I’ll do more (and usually, I do). But if only the minimum gets done, that’s still a win.

In a recent development, the less you have to think about it in the morning, the easier it is to roll out of bed. Do every possible chore the night before. Pack your gym bag ahead of time. Grind your coffee, put water in the kettle, and set your car keys by the door.

Industry observers note that this is my winter hack. When it’s cold in the morning, the last thing I want to do is take off my PJs and put on a frigid sports bra. So, I sleep in my running clothes. When my alarm goes off, all I have to do is put on shoes and hit the road.

It can be tempting to hit snooze on the weekends. Resist. If you need to take a short nap here or there to catch up on hours, do it. But sleeping in too long or too often can mess with your body’s natural circadian rhythm—and send you back to square one.

  • The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world.
  • In a recent development, while there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the new skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to massive wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

In a recent development, while there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more upcoming climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

Sources indicate that in 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in major wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” states Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Industry observers note that given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

Sources indicate that take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Major Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”.

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

In a recent development, “We always have a big, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he claims. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”.

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

“Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”.

#44589. Finally, Data on Super-High Carbohydrate Doses

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1360 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Finally, Data on Super-High Carbohydrate Doses

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1360 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that science often moves very slowly.
  • According to recent reports, over the last half-dozen years, top cyclists, runners, triathletes, and others have been pushing back the limits of what was thought possible.
  • Whether these carb megadoses actually improve performance is a different question.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Jordan Siemens / Getty).

Recent findings suggest that science often moves very slowly. But sometimes, when the real-world stakes are high enough, it zips along at an impressive pace. That’s what’s right now happening with carbohydrate fueling for endurance sports. It’s a hot topic with lots of open questions, and a big upcoming study offers some useful—though not entirely final—answers.

According to recent reports, over the last half-dozen years, top cyclists, runners, triathletes, and others have been pushing back the limits of what was thought possible. The existing science mentioned you couldn’t make use of more than 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, but elite athletes are now routinely using 120 grams per hour and, in some cases, far beyond that. At last year’s New York Marathon, Joe Klecker reportedly downed 175 grams per hour—the sports gel equivalent of eating nine servings of cooked pasta during the race.

Whether these carb megadoses actually improve performance is a different question. So far, the research has been equivocal. And critics like the South African sports scientist Tim Noakes have claimed that big carb doses don’t help at all, at least as a source of fuel for your muscles. Noakes argues that a mere 10 grams an hour is enough to keep your blood sugar from crashing, which in his view is all that matters.

Industry observers note that when I wrote about this debate last year, I thought it would be straightforward to dig up “dose-response” data showing what dose of carbs led to the best endurance performances. To my surprise, though, the existing evidence was sparser than I expected. What we needed, I concluded, was fresh dose-response data spanning the whole range from 10 to 120 grams and beyond, featuring well-trained athletes in a realistic test of endurance performance. That’s what a fresh study, from an international team of scientists led by James Morton of Liverpool John Moores University in Britain and published in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise, provides.

Recent findings suggest that morton and his colleagues recruited eight serious cyclists, and (somehow) convinced them to do a challenging cycling test on four different occasions. They rode for three hours at a pace just below lactate threshold, including three five-minute surges in the final hour. Then they introduced immediately into a ride to exhaustion at a faster pace, simulating the all-out finish of a race, lasting on average about five minutes.

Sources indicate that they did these rides while consuming drinks containing a total of 10, 90, 120, or 150 grams of carbohydrate per hour. The drinks, based on a formulation from Science in Sport, contained a ratio of 1 part maltodextrin to 0.8 parts fructose; the mix of carbohydrates helped maximize absorption from the gut into the bloodstream.

Throughout the rides, the scientists took regular blood tests and monitored respiratory gases in order to calculate exactly how much carbohydrate and fat the cyclists were burning.

Sources indicate that the first key finding is how much carbohydrate the cyclists burned. Here’s the data, in grams of carbohydrate per minute, for the four groups (with 10 g in white, 90 g in light gray, 120 g in dark grey, and 150 g in black):.

It has been revealed that the more carbs the cyclists drank, the more they were able to burn—but only up to 120 grams per hour. You can’t really see the data points for 150 grams per hour because they’re virtually identical to 120 grams per hour.

The hope, then, is that the high-carb drinks would leave the cyclists with more fuel available for the time-to-exhaustion ride at the end. Here’s how long each group lasted (in seconds) in that ride:.

According to recent reports, here it’s quite clear that consuming 90 or 120 grams per hour produced better results than just 10 grams per hour. In fact, you’ll notice that there are only four data points above zero in the 10 grams per hour group: four of the subjects gave up in exhaustion before they even got to the end of the three-hour ride.

This is obviously not a good look for the “you only need 10 grams of carbs per hour to keep your blood sugar up” theory. There’s a caveat to this: the ride with 10 grams was framed as a “familiarization ride” to get the riders used to the protocol rather than as a control group—so unlike the other three rides, it was neither blinded nor randomized. The subjects knew they were only getting 10 grams of carbs per hour, so it’s reasonable to assume that they expected to perform poorly.

That said, the blood sugar (i.e. glucose) data tells a clear (and placebo-proof) story:.

Sources indicate that the average blood sugar levels in the three high-carb rides were 4.6, 4.6, and 4.8 mmol/L; in the lower-carb ride, it was 3.8 mmol/L (68 mg/dL), which is considered mild hypoglycemia. Notably, these low levels are already apparent just 30 minutes into the ride. There’s still a big gap between 10 and 90 grams per hour, but it seems clear that 10 grams isn’t enough to maintain blood sugar levels, at least for trained athletes like those in the study.

In a recent development, interestingly, performance on 150 grams per hour was also poorer, despite the fact that it produced identical carb burning compared to 120 grams per hour. There are a few possible reasons for this, which we’ll get into below. But if you take the data at face value, the researchers calculate that for these particular riders, doing this particular endurance test, the optimal dose is 107 grams per hour.

There’s a mystery here. Consuming 120 or 150 grams per hour produced identical levels of carb burning. So where did the other 30 go? It’s possible it was converted to glucose or glycogen (a form of carbohydrate storage in the body) or even fat.

Or it’s possible it was left sloshing around in the stomach, undigested. If that was the case, it might cause digestive problems that would explain why performance was worse with 150 grams. The data didn’t show any significant differences in reported GI symptoms between rides, but with just eight subjects it’s possible such subtleties would be missed.

It has been revealed that there’s another intriguing clue. Check out the data below, which demonstrates the individual data on how much “exogenous” carbohydrate each subject burned during the third hour of each ride. (“Exogenous” means carbohydrate from the sports drink, rather than from the body’s internal stores. The sports drink carbs were labeled with a special isotope tracer so the scientists could tell the different carb sources apart.).

Sources indicate that look at the rider at the bottom. In the three rides (90, 120, and 150 grams per hour), he burned 1.41, 1.45, and 1.46 grams of carbs per minute. In other words, drinking more carbs made no difference to how many carbs he was able to burn. This suggests he wasn’t able to digest them. Tellingly, he was also the subject who reported the highest level of GI symptoms in the 150 g trial, and had the biggest drop in performance in that trial.

According to recent reports, in comparison, some of the other subjects were able to take advantage of more carbs. One subject went from 1.56 grams per minute in the 90 g trial to 2.08 and then 2.30 grams per minute in the 150 g trial. That might—speculatively!—translate into a big metabolic advantage at the higher consumption rates for this individual.

Industry observers note that so the simple final answer to the great carb debate is: maybe 107 grams per hour is the latest magic number. But the real not-so-final answer is that the best dose is highly individual. Ever since the carb revolution kicked off, sports nutritionists have been warning us that we shouldn’t automatically expect to benefit from the super-high intakes of athletes like Tadej Pogačar or Joe Klecker. This data tells us we might not even get the same benefits as our own training partners—and for now, the only way to find your sweet spot is to experiment.

#44588. This 30-Mile-Long Canyonlands Art Gallery Might Be Utah’s Best Backpacking Trip

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1311 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

This 30-Mile-Long Canyonlands Art Gallery Might Be Utah’s Best Backpacking Trip

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1311 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when you think of ancient rock art, what comes to mind?
  • But there’s one canyon in Utah that blows those expectations out of the water.
  • Hidden deep inside Canyonlands National Park, Salt Creek Canyon holds some of the most impressive pictographs I’ve ever seen.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when you think of ancient rock art, what comes to mind? Handprints? Stick figures? Maybe a long-limbed man holding something? For the most part, you’d be right. The petroglyphs and pictographs of the southwest are beautiful, but they aren’t known for their intricate details.

But there’s one canyon in Utah that blows those expectations out of the water.

Hidden deep inside Canyonlands National Park, Salt Creek Canyon holds some of the most impressive pictographs I’ve ever seen. Enormous human figures, elaborate patterns, and colorful paintings that have survived for hundreds of years. It’s an open-air art museum, and one that’s slowly weathering away.

Industry observers note that and the museum doesn’t stop at rock art. There are Ancestral Puebloan granaries, settlers’ abandoned ranch buildings, and reminders of the conservationists who helped protect this landscape.

According to recent reports, A walk through Salt Creek Canyon is a walk through history. Over two days and more than 30 miles, it became one of my biggest backpacking surprises of the year.

Trail: Salt Creek Trail + Angel Arch Detour Start: Cathedral Butte / Salt Creek Canyon Trailhead Finish: Cave Spring / Salt Creek Gate Distance: 30.78 miles (my GPS; mapped distance may differ) Elevation gain: 1,054 feet (my GPS) Type: Point-to-point, vehicle shuttle required Permits: Required for overnight trips Highlight: The All American Man pictograph.

Sources indicate that the trail begins high in the contested Bears Ears National Monument, in the shadow of Cathedral Butte. Typically, this is the sort of view you’d have to earn after hours of climbing. Instead, you start at the highest point, looking down into a canyon that stretches toward the horizon.

It’s mostly downhill from here, but don’t mistake that for easy. Thirty miles with a loaded backpack is still 30 miles, especially when much of it is through deep sand.

About two miles in, we crossed into Canyonlands National Park. My Gaia GPS map was littered with waypoints and “Don’t miss!” markers, the first of which were Kirk Spring and Kirk’s Cabin.

According to recent reports, in an otherwise dusty landscape of sagebrush and juniper, a little oasis appeared. Reeds, cottonwoods, and bright green vegetation surrounded a small spring. We filtered some water and continued toward the cabin, an 1890s-era log home with a fieldstone chimney.

Outside the weathered log structure sat the wheels and axles of an old wagon. Inside, bear traps and antlers hung on the walls. It looked like something out of a history museum, only sandier, dustier, and considerably more authentic.

This was our first introduction to one of Salt Creek’s defining qualities: Layers of human history occupy nearly every corner of the canyon.

Long before ranchers arrived, Indigenous people—Ancestral Puebloans and Fremont, then Ute, Paiute, and Diné—lived, hunted, and farmed here. Later came European explorers, conservationists, and eventually backpackers like us. Different people, different centuries, but all drawn to the same remarkable place.

According to recent reports, one of the biggest reasons was water. Unlike much of Canyonlands, Salt Creek supports a surprisingly lush corridor of vegetation, even in a dry year. We encountered several places to filter water, although sources became scarcer farther down the canyon. (Water here is seasonal and never guaranteed, so come prepared to carry plenty.).

In a recent development, around mile six, a small spur trail led us beneath a sandstone overhang. Tucked into the alcove were several stone structures, likely granaries used by Ancestral Puebloan people to store their harvests. Just below them, dark-green vines spilled across the sand. They looked like squash plants, still thriving in the shadow of structures built centuries ago.

I’d come to Salt Creek expecting incredible rock art, but nothing prepared me for what we found around mile eight: The All American Man.

High inside a sandstone alcove stands a human-like figure, nearly life-size, painted in striking blue, white, and red. He appears to wear white boots, an elaborate headdress, and something resembling an American flag across his body.

Industry observers note that for decades, the figure’s unusual appearance led some to question whether it was even ancient. Radiocarbon testing eventually confirmed its authenticity, suggesting it dates to around the 14th century. Standing below it, I found the whole thing almost impossible to believe. (Do yourself a favor: If you strategy on hiking Salt Creek, don’t look up pictures of the All American Man beforehand. Let it surprise you.).

It has been revealed that not far beyond, we encountered another extraordinary panel near Four Faces Spring. Four enormous, intricately patterned faces stared out from beneath a sandstone alcove. Remnants of stone structures sat beneath them.

Who were these figures? Were they people, spirits, or something else entirely?

Their exact meaning remains uncertain, but the artwork survives, part of a cultural history that remains key to Indigenous communities today.

The farther we walked, the more the canyon changed.

Sources indicate that towering sandstone walls closed in around us. Willows, reeds, and cottonwoods transformed the dusty trail into something resembling a jungle. Small streams appeared beneath the vegetation.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, so did the mosquitoes. I’ve spent a lot of time hiking through the desert, but I’ve never encountered so many of the little suckers.

After miles of hiking, a soft rain finally brought some relief. A rainbow appeared against the red canyon walls just as we approached SC4, our reserved campsite for the evening.

Recent findings suggest that at roughly mile 12, SC4 is the last of the four designated Salt Creek campsites when traveling north. It wasn’t quite halfway through our route, which meant we had an even longer second day ahead.

In a recent development, the next morning, we packed up and headed toward another of the canyon’s great attractions. Several miles off the main trail, at the end of a remote side canyon, stood Angel Arch.

Arches National Park may be famous for its sandstone formations, but Angel Arch can hold its own against just about anything you’ll find there.

According to recent reports, its massive sandstone opening rises roughly 135 feet high, with an unusual formation beside it resembling an angel leaning forward with folded wings. It’s an incredible sight, made even more impressive by the effort required to reach it. We were the only people there. In fact, we were the only hikers on the entire trail: We hadn’t seen a single other person or group. The detour added several miles to an already long day, but I’d do it again without hesitation.

In a recent development, back on the main route, one more archaeological treasure awaited us: the Flying Carpet Panel. Like the All American Man and Four Faces, the artwork was enormous, with figures and intricate designs spread across the sandstone.

Then came the final miles. The beautiful canyon trail eventually gave way to a sandy four-wheel-drive road, where every step seemed to require twice the effort. After nearly 30 miles, walking through deep sand was just about the last thing my legs wanted to do.

Eventually, we reached a gate, a paved road, and the end of our journey.

Recent findings suggest that as spectacular as the scenery was, what I’ll remember most about Salt Creek isn’t the canyon itself. It’s the people who called it home.

For centuries, Ancestral Puebloan communities farmed along the creek, stored food in cliffside granaries, and created artwork that still watches over the canyon today. Walking past these places, I couldn’t help thinking about how many people had traveled this same canyon before us. How many had looked up at those same cliffs, collected water from those same springs, or sheltered beneath those sandstone overhangs?

According to recent reports, we spent two days here, carrying everything we needed on our backs. For others, this canyon was home. For a brief moment, we got to be part of its story too.

One tester, who has a relatively narrow, low-volume foot, loved the fit of the TX1, saying its toebox felt roomy and allowed her toes “to spread and relax naturally.” My wider foot, meanwhile, had me eager to take the TX1 off after an hour-long approach. I wish this shoe came in a slightly wider last.

#44586. 6 Forgotten Backpacking Skills Every Hiker Should Master

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1267 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

6 Forgotten Backpacking Skills Every Hiker Should Master

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1267 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool.
  • According to recent reports, calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times.
  • According to recent reports, whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Westend61/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool. It’s not that we’re Luddites or avoid latest ways of doing things—from lightweight internal-frame backpacks to gourmet freeze-dried meals, there’s no denying that most modern backpacking developments have made our experiences better. But there’s something about seeing a hiking buddy solve a problem with a retro skill that we admire. It reveals knowledge, competence, and the kind of self-reliance that every backpacker secretly aspires to.

According to recent reports, calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times. But they aren’t part of the average beginner hiker’s repertoire anymore, and many hikers go their whole careers without using them. Start practicing them now to level up your skills for next season.

According to recent reports, whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance? While you don’t need a Boy Scout’s skill at knotcraft to go backpacking, learning to use the right knot for each job will help you finish camp setup promptly and break it down without spending ten minutes coaxing apart the granny knot you’ve welded into your cord. Here are a couple to get you started (check out our guide to the 5 Essential Backpacking Knots for videos and in-depth descriptions):.

Slippery Backpacker’s Hitch: Good for hanging bear bags or rigging ridgelines for tarps, and comes undone with a pull. Wrap the rope at least three times around a tree or post, then tuck a bight of the loose end under the last loop.

It has been revealed that bowline Knot: A bombproof method for creating a strong loop. Make a loop in the rope; take the loose end and bring it up through the loop, around the rope, and back down through the loop. (You may or may not catch those of us who learned in school muttering “rabbit comes out of the hole, goes around the tree, and goes back in the hole” while we tie it.) Finish with an overhand and a half-hitch.

It has been revealed that sheet Bend: Need to attach two lengths of cord of different diameters? Create a bight with the bigger cord; bring the end of the thinner cord up through, wrap it around the back of the bight, and run it through the loop it creates.

Lightweight, direct-from-manufacturer shelters and quilts mean that there’s little practical reason to sew your own kit nowadays. However, for those who do like to get handy, the proliferation of patterns for sale and online tutorials on places like YouTube means that it’s never been easier to join the MYOG community. Plus, much like growing your own vegetables, sewing a few pieces yourself will give you a fresh appreciation for the ingenuity and labor that goes into making your gear.

Instead of jumping straight into the deep end with a high-investment piece like a tent or quilt, start small: A “ditty bag” is perfect for holding small items or replacing a torn or lost stuff sack. See our step-by-step instructions from our Spring 1973 issue, which is easy to sew without a machine. All you’ll need is ¾-yard of ripstop nylon, 30 inches of cord, needles, and thread.

Sources indicate that camp baking is everything modern backpacking meals aren’t: messy, ingredient-heavy, and slow. But there’s a kind of magic in coaxing a loaf of bread or a pizza into existence in the middle of the woods. It may not be an efficient way to eat, but it’s a rewarding skill, and as a party trick, guaranteed to impress your backcountry partners.

The most traditional method is to bake in a Dutch oven using campfire. One easier and lighter way to start: Make a cupcake on your camp stove, which is satisfying and near-foolproof. You’ll need a single-wall steel or titanium mug, a pot significant enough to fit it inside, and a lid, plate, or aluminum foil to cover it. Empty a packet of microwaveable cake mix into the mug, add three tablespoons of water, and stir. Drop three small rocks into the bottom of your pot, balance the mug on top of them, and add enough water to the pot that it reaches the level of the cake mix. (If the mug starts to float, you’ve added too much.) Cover and simmer for 20 minutes, then enjoy straight out of the mug. Bonus: also works with pancake mix.

It has been revealed that even if most hikers have moved on to screened-in lightweight tents, flat tarps still have dedicated fans. Besides the unbeatably low weight, there’s a simplicity to making a shelter from a rectangle of fabric that we can still appreciate. (Looking for your first? Borah’s Silpoly Solo Tarps are solid, and at less than $90, eminently affordable.).

There are innumerable ways to pitch a tarp, but the simple plow point shelter is a good place to start. Stake out three corners of your tarp, then use one of your trekking poles to raise the fourth, tensioning it with a guyline. (Pro tip: The first time you do this will take some trial and error to get a good pitch, so give yourself extra time in camp.) For extra dirtbag points, use a 9 x 10 scrap of Tyvek instead; create the guy-out points by pinching a bit of the material around a smooth pebble and tying off the base with a cord.

Recent findings suggest that whittling is one of those camp pastimes that’s largely fallen by the wayside—but to be fair, today’s backpackers are less likely than their predecessors to spend a lot of time kicking around camp. Still, basic knife skills are good to have in your pocket—you never know when you may need to carve a replacement for a snapped stake or shave tinder to build a fire—and whittling is a good, low-stakes way to practice those skills.

Carving a spoon is an easy project (and a useful one, if you forget your own utensil). Split a piece of deadfall, preferably still green. Carve your spoon’s outline, then hollow out the bowl. (You may have an easier time carving a shovel-shaped bowl than a traditional round one with a typical straight pocketknife.).

According to recent reports, once upon a time, planning a route for our magazine meant taking a walk down to the small library of guidebooks and topo maps we kept in the office and poring through them until we found the trail we were looking for. The world has changed since then—today’s mapping tools are quick and reliable for assembling a plan—but sketching out a trip the old-school way is still a good exercise for your brain. Plus, it can help prevent the kind of careless line-following that regularly gets hikers into trouble.

Recent findings suggest that picking up an expert-written guidebook for an area you initiative on visiting regularly is always a good investment. Otherwise, the public library is your friend: Your local branch likely stocks an array of up-to-date guides, or can obtain them for you via interlibrary loan. Instead of carrying the whole thing, xerox the pages you need and jot points of interest and notes right on the copies. Pair with a compass and a current topo map (your library may stock those, too), and don’t forget to check with rangers or local hikers for the latest beta before you set out.

Our testers loved the contoured hip support and the durability of this harness. “I took hundreds of falls and [the Black Diamond Solution Guide] gets the highest praise I can give a harness, which is that I never even thought about my harness after a fall,” one of our testers said.

Our top all-around men’s climbing pant of 2025, Black Diamond’s Alpine Light Pants feature a mobility-friendly design. While the Alpine Light pants are out of stock or low inventory right now, the Black Diamond Alpine Pants (which are, as you might expect, a bit less lightweight) are currently on sale. We found that this pant model struck an ideal balance between breathability while moving promptly, and moderately protective in light winds and rain showers with its DWR coating.

One of our top mountaineering boots of the year, the G-Summit climbing boot accomplishes a small but significant miracle: It’s a double boot that climbs like a single boot. The insulated foam liner—combined with the wrap-around inner shell and external gaiter—creates an envelope that’s warm enough for high-altitude mountaineering, and yet low-profile and precise enough for hard technical climbing up to WI6 and M7. The rubber rand was sticky enough to provide purchase in foot jams on B.C.’s Stanley Headwall, and the Vibram sole gave testers enough grip to cross boulder fields and icy scruff in Norway, Patagonia, and beyond.

The trek over Auden’s Col in India’s Garhwal Himalayas is no stroll: Crossing the pass means working hard at elevations of up to 18,000 feet, crossing a glacier, and, occasionally, dealing with some of the world’s worst weather.

It was that last hazard that an expedition faced earlier this fall, when a freak snowstorm dropped more than six feet of powder on them with little notice. The 29-member team from Indian outfitter Aquaterra Adventures had reached base camp at 16,400 feet when the weather took a turn for the worse, battering them with heavy snowfall, temperatures down to -4 Fahrenheit, and 62-mile-per-hour winds.

It has been revealed that while Jetendra Singh Rana, their lead guide, quickly called off their ascent and sent a message asking for rescue, the storm had flattened many of the group’s tents, leaving them all to squeeze into one remaining cook tent while they waited for help to come. Backpacker contributor Karthika Gupta spoke to expedition members to hear their story; read her full article and see footage from the  group’s ordeal here. –Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief.

Under-the-Radar Overlanding Spots in the West, According to a Full-Timer

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1399 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

💡 Key Takeaways
