  • There is a specific moment, usually about ten or twenty miles after the asphalt dissolves into dirt, when the noise of the modern world begins to cut out completely.
  • Even as a full-time overlander, I’d love to say I gave up on the asphalt lottery long ago, but sadly, for some places, it’s the only way left to experience them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jay Clue has clocked more than 50,000 miles exploring the rugged beauty of North America while chasing stars, stories, and dark skies in his custom-built Jeep Rubicon overland rig. (Photo: Jay Clue).

There is a specific moment, usually about ten or twenty miles after the asphalt dissolves into dirt, when the noise of the modern world begins to cut out completely. The cell bars drop to zero, the tourist traffic vanishes in your rearview mirror, and the real adventure begins. But planning a camping trip these days feels almost like buying concert tickets. You wait months for a release date, log onto a park website, fight for a reservation, and ultimately end up with your tent pitched a few feet from an RV, falling asleep to the soul-soothing sound of their generator howling through the night.

Even as a full-time overlander, I’d love to say I gave up on the asphalt lottery long ago, but sadly, for some places, it’s the only way left to experience them. True wilderness is still out there, though. Finding it just means trading the pavement for dirt tracks and exploration.

While social media loves to showcase six-figure custom trucks wrapped in tactical gear, crawling through hood-deep mud or hanging off thousand-foot cliffs, the real secret to overlanding isn’t in the extremes. It’s about finding your own beautiful piece of serenity in the backcountry. At its heart, overlanding is simply vehicle-based travel. In other words, using your rig as a mobile backpack to carry your kitchen, bed, and gear deeper into the wild than any paved road could ever take you. You don’t need a custom-built rock crawler or axle-breaking trails. All you need is a dirt track, a map, and your sense of adventure.

When you want to trade packed-out front-country campgrounds for untouched wilderness, finding that solitude usually just means looking where others aren’t—whether that’s adventuring down unnamed forest trails or taking that random side road just to see where it goes.

It has been revealed that I can’t give away all my secret spots. But here are three of my favorite under-the-radar areas to get you started on your overlanding exploration list.

A few hours southeast of Salt Lake City’s hustle and bustle lies a massive geologic upheaval, sculpted over millions of years by wind and water into one of Utah’s best-kept secrets. Spanning roughly 2,000 square miles—an expanse nearly the size of Delaware—the Swell makes “massive” feel like an understatement.

The San Rafael Swell is a true overlander’s playground, crisscrossed by hundreds of miles of dirt tracks winding past towering red-rock formations, sweeping desert vistas, hidden canyons, and jagged sandstone ribs. Unlike Utah’s famed Mighty 5 national parks, reaching the heart of the Swell demands some serious off-pavement miles, naturally filtering out the crowds and leaving its wildest treasures to those willing to earn them.

Industry observers note that beyond the driving, the Swell is an open-air museum packed with history. You can spend days searching for dinosaur tracks, hundreds of Native American rock art panels, weathered pioneer homesteads, and abandoned Cold War uranium mines. When night falls, the region has some of the darkest skies in the Beehive State, making it one of my favorite places to stay up until dawn photographing the Milky Way. And once the sun crests the horizon, the adventure shifts into high gear—whether you’re squeezing through narrow slot canyons, tackling desert climbs, hiking rim overlooks, or cooling off from the high-desert heat with a lazy river float.

Industry observers note that every time I head into the Swell, the web of backcountry trails feels virtually endless. The 27–mile Behind the Reef OHV route stands out as a personal favorite, though you can easily link dirt corridors to push even farther—connecting straight into Capitol Reef’s iconic Cathedral Valley or the surreal, lunar badlands of Mancos Shale. Best of all, with the vast majority of this rugged landscape open to free dispersed camping, you don’t just pass through the San Rafael Swell—you get to wake up right in the middle of it.

While mainstream travelers crowd the beautiful Pacific coast, southeastern Oregon remains one of the quietest stretches of public land in the country. Spanning nearly 30,000 square miles and home to the world’s largest International Dark Sky Sanctuary, the Oregon Outback isn’t a single destination—it is a sweeping, multi-day dirt journey through a forgotten corner of the American West.

Rolling east along lonely gravel ribbons, the landscape unfolds in dramatic waves. On the western edge, sheer 3,000-foot basalt cliffs rise abruptly above sun-bleached alkali lake beds at the Hart Mountain National Antelope Refuge. Camping on the high plateau puts you steps away from Hart Mountain Hot Springs, where you can soak in a stone-lined thermal pool under an endless canopy of stars while pronghorn antelope graze quietly in the surrounding sagebrush.

It has been revealed that farther east, the desert floor gives way to the towering fault-block wall of Steens Mountain. The unpaved Steens Mountain Loop Road climbs past 9,000 feet through shimmering aspen groves, opening up to breathtaking, glacier-carved valleys like Kiger Gorge that feel lifted straight out of the Swiss Alps.

To cap off the traverse, drop down to the Alvord Desert playa, more than a mile below Steens’ summit, then head toward the Idaho border, where the horizon fractures into the Owyhee Canyonlands. Winding dirt tracks drop you between towering, honeycombed volcanic spires and deep river canyons that glow fiery orange at sunset. With cell service, fuel, and pavement fading far into your rearview mirror, this vast corridor rewards prepared travelers with the rarest luxury on the road: total, uninterrupted silence.

If I hadn’t driven this route earlier this summer, I probably wouldn’t have included it here. Because it sits just east of the famed North Cascades National Park, I assumed the area would be choked with tourists and far from an under-the-radar overlanding destination. One cloudy afternoon, on a whim, I decided to explore it anyway. To my surprise, I passed only two vehicles on the entire climb and spotted just one more at the summit. This area delivers some of the most dramatic views in the entire Cascade Range, yet I had the ridge completely to myself at sunset—watching the day sink behind endless jagged, snowcapped peaks before the sky ignited in fluorescent pinks and oranges.

Sources indicate that the highest drivable road in Washington, this single-lane dirt route clings to a thousand-foot-high cliff wall along Deadhorse Point with zero guardrails. That immense drop-off not only demands steady nerves around the blind corners, but also acts as a natural filter, keeping standard RVs and casual weekenders away.

Once you clear the shelf, quiet, primitive campsites sit tucked near the timberline at over 6,100 feet. From camp, you can step right onto the Pacific Crest Trail, or push your rig farther onto two distinct offshoots. The rocky Slate Peak spur climbs steeply toward the 7,400-foot summit area for views stretching to Mount Baker. For a tougher, high-clearance run, Chancellor Road drops down the western slope through rugged, rocky terrain toward the 1890s mining ruins of Barron and the trailhead for the Chancellor ghost town.

In a recent development, at the end of the day, the best campsites don’t come with reservation numbers, and they rarely show up on a top-ten list. Use these routes as a launch pad, then keep going—pick a dusty turnoff you’ve never heard of, respect the land you cross, and discover the magic that happens when you leave the crowds behind.

Jay Clue is a professional photographer and Outside contributor who made the switch to overlanding full-time in 2024. Since then, he has clocked more than 50,000 miles exploring the rugged beauty of North America while chasing stars, stories, and dark skies in his custom-built Jeep Rubicon overland rig. After hundreds of nights photographing the backcountry, he can happily report there’s only been one rare occasion when he thought that he was about to be abducted by aliens.

Boost the Performance of Your Canister Stove Without Blowing it Up

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (771 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

Sources indicate that I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed. My fingers were chilled from fiddling with guylines, and I craved the feeling of a steaming cup cradled in my hands. I screwed my ultralight stove onto a fuel canister, squeezed some water from my filter bag into a pot, and lit up. And then I proceeded to wait for what felt like ages. The flame was low and weak. Had I packed a nearly empty canister? No. The feeble flame was a harbinger, much like the leaves littering the trail: Winter was coming.

Recent findings suggest that canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops. Cold temperatures lower the internal pressure of the canister, causing it to falter, sputter, or produce a smaller flame. Regular winter campers often solve this problem by packing liquid fuel stoves like the MSR Whisperlite, which perform well in below freezing temperatures. Some canister stoves have a built-in pressure regulator that helps them stay efficient in the cold. But not every backpacker wants to shell out for an entire quiver of camp stoves. That’s where a little innovation comes in: Keeping a canister warm, even when the ambient temperature is frigid, helps maintain pressure so you can boil water on a regular canister stove all year round. Do it the wrong way, however and you might end up scorching more than your food.

According to recent reports, when it comes to boosting the efficiency of your canister stove in winter, the key is gentle warming. A fuel canister’s contents are pressurized; when it is cold out, your goal is to increase that pressure ever so slightly. But overheating—and thus overpressurizing—can cause the canister to explode.

Sources indicate that warnings printed on the side of a canister tell this tale. Most manufacturers caution people to keep a canister below 120°F. Heating a canister by rapid means, like placing it in boiling water is a very bad idea—just ask the guy who punched a hole in his ceiling trying to heat a canister for a fuel transfer.

In a recent development, how else can one warm a canister? One hiker on Reddit suggested sticking a chemical hand warmer next to the canister and enclosing it in an insulated pouch. But experts Backpacker spoke to did not recommend that method.

“You’re adding a continuous heat source while also insulating the canister, and there’s no particularly good way to monitor or control its temperature,” says Adam Wilcox, senior mechanical design engineer at Jetboil.

Hothands, manufacturer of popular chemical warmers, claims that their products reach an average of 135°F, and warns that the maximum temperature can surpass 158°F. Granted, this doesn’t mean that placing a hand warmer beside your fuel canister will immediately warm the fuel contents to that same temperature, but it does heighten your risk of dangerously increasing  the pressure. Gentle warming is a safer bet.

Recent findings suggest that “Body heat before use or a controlled warm-water bath are much more predictable ways of warming a cold canister,” says Wilcox. “The key with water is warm, not hot, and avoiding excessive heating of the canister.”.

For a quick boil, keeping the fuel canister inside your jacket for a few minutes prior to use may do the trick to increase internal pressure. Of course, the effects of this will diminish rather rapidly as you run your stove and expose the canister to cold air. If you need to run your stove a little longer to cook a meal or melt snow, a warm water bath can provide safe, continuous warming. Place your fuel canister inside a dish or spare pot. (I like to carry a collapsible silicone bowl for this purpose.) Light your stove. As soon as the water begins to warm but before it boils, pour some into the dish surrounding your canister. You should immediately notice improved performance.

According to recent reports, shopping for a upcoming stove? Springing for one with a pressure regulator can help it perform more consistently across seasons. MSR claims that its Pocket Rocket Deluxe can run at full power at a fuel canister pressure of as little as 16.5 PSI. (A full canister would typically be at 45 PSI at room temperature.).

Whether you’re crimping sharp Smith Rock incuts, jamming perfect Indian Creek splitters, or bearing down on your gym’s fresh latest set, you are, at some point, going to tear up your skin. Fear not! Rhino Skin Solutions makes a purpose-built skin balm to restore your digits as efficiently as possible. Split+ is a roll-on cream that comes in two sizes (5oz and 3.4oz) and uses beeswax, vitamin E, arnica, dragon’s blood, and tea tree oil, offering a blend of occlusive (sealing) and antibacterial properties.

Ocun’s fresh Jett S climbing shoes are as comfortable as they are affordable, and best suited for the gym. They excel at precision placements and perform well on steep terrain, hooking, and scumming, on everything from 5.13 tech to the Tension Board 2 at 40° overhanging.

Last year, Petzl updated the Connect Adjust to make a good item great: they slimmed down the dynamic tether from 9.5mm to 9.0mm, making it noticeable lighter and easier to extend/contract. The belay-loop attachment point is now a sewn Dyneema webbing, rather than the thick rope itself, and as a result feels lower profile on the harness. The Connect Adjust also now features a pinhole to attach accessory cord to; if weighting the Connect, clip a carabiner into the accessory-cord loop and it will easily disengage.

It has been revealed that edelrid’s Ohmega brake assistant is a crucial belay tool for partnerships where the climber weighs significantly more than the belayer. By adding friction, the device makes the belayer “heavier,” reducing the size of whips and keeping the belayer on the ground during a fall. We recommend any climbing duo with a notable weight difference to invest in one.

The Friend Camming Device is one of the most legendary and trusted pieces of climbing equipment. Newly updated for 2026, the Friends are a tiny bit lighter than the previous model, but, most importantly, they come with a fresh, seamless “Magic Cord” sling. The bartack-free sling enables smooth extension so you can enjoy your leads without rope drag.

The Free Wall is the ultimate quiver-of-one backpack for rock climbers, made from a super-tough recycled nylon that our testers hauled for thousands of feet this summer. Unlike a traditional big-wall haulbag, with its simple, monolithic compartment, the Free Wall Pack is designed with on-the-wall access in mind: two internal pockets, two gear loops, and a large external pocket on top of the lid.

It has been revealed that apparently Scarpa’s Veloce is designed for beginner and intermediate climbers who spend all of their time at the gym—but our experienced field tester didn’t get the memo. After a quick break-in period, they became his go-to shoes inside and out, where he clipped the chains on the two hardest sport routes he’s sent in the last decade.

Industry observers note that black Diamond’s Magnetron has the smoothest operation of any triple-action carabiner we’ve ever encountered; a true one-handed operation that provides immediate security upon letting go of the gate. Its pear shape is ideal for belaying and rappelling, and it has a surprisingly narrow nose, making it easy to clip into chain anchors and busy masterpoints.

Sources indicate that these insulated rubber gloves were originally designed for fishers, but nowadays you’re equally likely to see them on ice climbers, especially on steep water ice in the Pacific Northwest. The Temres 282-02 is the only fully waterproof glove we’ve ever worn, and they climb decently well thanks to a supple, dexterous rubber, and a wool liner that doesn’t migrate much within.

Climbing tape isn’t just for hardcore climbers nursing a busted pulley or gobie—it’s a needed part of any decent first aid kit, repair kit, and can help you fashion a makeshift stickclip in a pinch. (BYOStick). Tension’s climbing tape is some of the stickiest we’ve used, performing well in both sweaty and freezing environments. The Tri-Pack includes a one-inch roll ideal for larger body parts like wrists and ankles and for making tape gloves should you forget yours at home, the half-inch roll works well for large blisters and flappers, and the 0.3-inch roll is preordained to fit individual digits.

What gift could be better than continued access to America’s best rock climbing? Gift your climbing partner a membership to Access Fund, the largest climbing advocacy movement in the country, which tirelessly protects and conserves historic areas—and opens newly introduced ones. They’ll even get a free t-shirt.

The daughter of Climbing’s editor in chief, Maya Silver, has worn the Black Diamond Momentum kids’ climbing shoe for the past four years. Once she finally outgrew it this last summer, the decision was easy to order her another pair. Like the adult Momentum shoe, the Momentum kids is super comfortable thanks to its neutral last, easy to get on/off with a simple Velcro closure, and offers sufficient performance for most little crushers.

It has been revealed that the daily workhorse of the Adidas trail-running lineup, the Terrex Agravic 2 GTX delivers a reliable, connected ride no matter the surface, distance, or weather conditions. The EVA-based Lightstrike+ midsole provides sure-footed cushioning that protects and absorbs impact but doesn’t bounce you around. A Continental rubber outsole bites into the dirt and doesn’t let go, and the Gore-Tex membrane goes unnoticed until you’re splashing through puddles or post-holing in a fresh snowfall.

The Cyklon Cross GTX is the shoe you want for charging through deep snow and slop, with its stretchy, breathable softshell gaiter that extends past the ankle bone and its waterproof Gore-Tex membrane lining the upper. The shoe’s external BOA dial allows quick, precise adjustments without making you dig around under the gaiter to find and tighten the laces. Underneath, the proven Cyklon trail-running shoe excels on speedy mountain scrambles, off-camber terrain, and slippery trails, with a moderate 28-20mm midsole stack height for a cushioned and flexible ride. Combined with the luggy sole (made of La Sportiva’s proprietary sticky rubber), this shoe made us feel agile and fully protected in burly winter running conditions.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy of Michael Hall).

In a recent development, audrie Pelosi found climbing after moving to Baraboo, Wisconsin. It wasn’t long before the quartzite cliffs of Devil’s Lake became a cornerstone of her life. She climbed there, worked there, and eventually became its steward as a guide with Apex Adventure Alliance (AAA), bringing latest climbers to the same arena in which she’d begun.

Sources indicate that “She was an exceptional climbing guide and human being,” Apex Adventure Alliance wrote in a statement to Outside. “She was a force in our community and at our guide service. We all will miss her dearly.”.

According to recent reports, originally from Duluth, Minnesota, Pelosi had long structured her life around her various passions: snowboarding, cycling, and, eventually, an all-encompassing love of climbing and the community around it. Her passion radiated outwards: she volunteered locally and, in 2026, ran for a Wisconsin Climbers Association board seat, hoping to become more involved in stewardship and community building. “I believe in showing up, doing the work, and listening to the community,” Pelosi wrote in her candidate statement.

Industry observers note that “With her friends and community, Audrie was so generous,” remarked Garrett Hopkins, AAA’s owner. “That generosity flowed into her climbing, biking, and snowboarding too. When I was living on the road, I knew her couch was always open for a spot to crash if my van was being repaired. She spent countless hours with young climbers in an effort to elevate the safety of the next generation coming up.”.

Pelosi met her husband, Jimmy “The Fox” Robinson, at a snowboard event at Welch Village, Minnesota, and in 2023 the two married atop Mount Bohemia (1,465ft) on Lake Superior. From then on, Pelosi had the nickname “Mrs. The Fox.” One of her friends, Anastasia Exterovich, set up a GoFundMe to raise money for Pelosi’s family in the wake of her passing. She called the pair the “raddest couple.”.

According to recent reports, “In my last conversation with Audrie, she joked about selling her handmade bike chain link earrings to anyone who wanted them for ‘free.99,’” Exterovich wrote. “It was such a simple statement made in passing, but it perfectly encapsulated who she was as a person. Even when she didn’t have much, she would give things away freely without hesitation, whether that was earrings, a smile, a laugh, a quick bike tune-up, or a belay.”.

It has been revealed that pelosi passed on May 30, 2026 working as a guide at  Devil’s Lake State Park, teaching a climbing course near the park’s East Bluff. During the course, Pelosi fell from the bluff and suffered fatal injuries. She is survived by her husband, her family, and the broader climbing community in Wisconsin.

#44574. Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (863 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m.
  • In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns.
  • “Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 enhancement on the floods.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 enhancement on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”.

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram shows the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

In a recent development, “Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”.

Sources indicate that according to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video shows the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

In an interview with The Gazette, Talley stated, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”.

According to recent reports, authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”.

The CTF noted that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate intends to avoid the area.”.

Industry observers note that on November 2, the CDTC posted another revision for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it stated. While the interactive map on its website demonstrates no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”.

Recent findings suggest that outside of Colorado, Latest Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”.

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

Sources indicate that “While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”.

#44573. Hannah Otto Broke Her Leg Descending Kilimanjaro—and Kept Riding

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1042 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Hannah Otto Broke Her Leg Descending Kilimanjaro—and Kept Riding

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1042 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hannah Otto celebrates at Uhuru Peak, the 19,341-foot summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, with her mountain bike.
  • By the time professional mountain biker Hannah Otto, 30, reached the final miles of her descent from Mount Kilimanjaro, 19,341 feet, she had already navigated the mountain’s most punishing terrain.
  • Sources indicate that on November 3, Otto became the first known woman to ascend and descend Africa’s tallest mountain with a bicycle in a single day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hannah Otto celebrates at Uhuru Peak, the 19,341-foot summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, with her mountain bike. (Photo: Rachael Galipo).

By the time professional mountain biker Hannah Otto, 30, reached the final miles of her descent from Mount Kilimanjaro, 19,341 feet, she had already navigated the mountain’s most punishing terrain. She’d hauled her bike up snowy slopes, scrambled over boulders at 18,000 feet, and ridden steep, rocky trails where softball-sized stones shifted beneath her tires. Now she was on a rainforest dirt road easy enough to ride on a gravel bike.

Sources indicate that on November 3, Otto became the first known woman to ascend and descend Africa’s tallest mountain with a bicycle in a single day. She completed the effort in 10 hours, 18 minutes, and 51 seconds, despite breaking her leg just two miles from the finish.

According to recent reports, “I came around a gentle bend in the trail, and the trail went from dry dirt to mud, and it was like I hit ice,” Otto told Outside. “The bike just came out from underneath me, and I was on the ground in a second.”.

The fall had broken her leg. But two miles from the finish, she got back on her bike and rode out.

Industry observers note that the attempt was also part of a fundraising campaign for World Bicycle Relief, a nonprofit that provides bicycles to improve access to education, healthcare, and employment. Otto hopes to raise $165,000 to provide 1,000 bicycles to rural African communities.

Sources indicate that otto’s ride established the first known women’s time for a single-day bicycle ascent and descent of Kilimanjaro. Canadian mountain biker Cory Wallace completed an ascent and descent in 8 hours, 55 minutes in 2022, but no verified women’s time had been recorded before Otto’s attempt.

According to recent reports, otto, who has raced mountain bikes for 21 years, spent months preparing for the altitude and dramatic changes in terrain. Kilimanjaro rises through rainforest, heath and moorland, and alpine desert before reaching its snow-covered summit. Otto said temperatures ranged from about 70 degrees Fahrenheit near the base to 10 degrees near the top.

Recent findings suggest that she trained as often as possible above 10,000 feet in Utah’s mountains, scheduled races at higher elevations, and added heat and sauna sessions to her routine. She also hiked on a steep treadmill with a sandbag on her back to train for carrying her bike.

It has been revealed that after seven days acclimatizing on Kilimanjaro, Otto returned to the base, rested a day, and started her single-day attempt at 3 a.m. with a support team that included her husband, a film crew, and local Tanzanian guides, aiming to beat the afternoon storm.

At about 15,500 feet, the terrain became too steep to pedal. Otto strapped her bike to her back and spent three and a half hours hiking three miles up snow-covered slopes approaching a 40 percent grade. Near 18,000 feet, she scrambled over large boulders with her hands, the bike still strapped to her back.

“With every 1,000 feet up the mountain, it felt like the bike gained five pounds,” she said.

In a recent development, otto had planned three different ways to carry the bike, rotating between them for relief. Meanwhile, the altitude shortened her steps, raised her heart rate, and made every stumble harder to recover from.

Snow began falling just as she reached the summit. After hiking down the first steep section, she got back on her bike, thinking she’d beaten the worst of the weather. But rain had soaked the rainforest trails below.

After the crash, Otto tried twice to stand.

In a recent development, “I watched my leg go in two completely different directions, and it was the most painful thing I’ve ever felt in my life,” Otto told Outside. “Both times, I fell to the ground screaming.”.

Sources indicate that her nearest guide was about 15 minutes behind her and could radio for a one-wheeled stretcher to carry her out. At first, she waited for help.

Industry observers note that but as she lay there, supine on the muddy floor of the Tanzanian rainforest, Otto told Outside that she imagined herself at 60, explaining that she’d been physically capable of finishing but had fallen short because of an accident. At the time, the thought made her sick. Living with that disappointment, she decided, would hurt worse than whatever her injured leg might put her through on the way down.

She army-crawled through the mud to retrieve her bike, used it as a crutch to stand, lowered the dropper seatpost, and draped her chest over the saddle to shimmy into a seated position.

Industry observers note that most of the remaining trail was downhill, allowing her to coast. Still, every bump sent pain through her broken leg. She used one hand to lift the injured leg onto the pedal for support, then moved it out of the way to pedal uphill with her good leg.

“There was also a piece of me that was riding out of fear and survival, even though it was excruciating,” Otto mentioned.

When Otto finally reached the finish, about 20 Tanzanian team members sang, danced, and clapped as she approached. They knew she’d summited, but nobody had told them about the crash. As soon as they saw her condition, the celebration stopped.

Within minutes, the team had loaded her into a vehicle for the 45-minute drive over rough roads to the nearest hospital, where X-rays confirmed the break.

Rather than undergo surgery in Tanzania, Otto made the roughly 30-hour journey home with her broken leg. Back in Salt Lake City, she underwent surgery for two tibial plateau fractures and an associated ACL injury. She expects eight to ten weeks without putting weight on her leg, but hopes to return to racing in April 2027.

Despite the injury, Otto stated the experience has changed how she thinks about her own abilities.

Sources indicate that “Now I feel like I have this story and this moment that I can always lean back on and be like, ‘You are so tough, Hannah,'” she noted. “For me, that is the most reassuring thing that I could gift myself.”.

(Photo: L to R: Anthony Walsh, Etsy Glass Carabiner Shop, Metolius, Yosemite Climbing Association, Kong).

If you’ve already taken a lap through our gift guide and still need more ideas, we’ve got you. All three of us editors here at Climbing have selected our top picks for gifts this year, from gear we’ve got our eyes on, to accessories in the climbing zeitgeist right now.

In a recent development, some of these editor gifts picks make perfect mini gifts for stocking stuffers or for that climber partner who you want to thank for giving you the perfect soft catch this past year. Other picks make a bigger impact, from a super lightweight harness to a great gym bag. Most of our picks are great for a variety of climbers, whether it’s your latest boyfriend who you hope to convert into a climber, or your mentor who’s been at it for eons.

We hope these gift ideas make your holiday shopping as painless as a splitter hand crack so you can spend more time training or climbing, and less time scrolling through endless product pages and catalogs.

Originally designed and hand-sewn by Nate Barton—the Missoula-based climber who ran the meme account @beta.sprayer until 2024—the Lolo Hoodie V1 ($169.99) is a functional midlayer for cold-weather climbing and the flagship product of the fledgling brand Lolo Hardware. Its large, zippered chest pocket was originally intended to help ice climbers warm up their hands between pitches.

Industry observers note that having pretty much lived in this hoodie for the past three winters, I’ve found the chest pocket far superior to any sort of pant pocket for storing my phone, gloves, and snacks. Plus, with my items against my chest, I never have to worry about my phone freezing or my car keys accidentally slipping out during a chimney. From Joshua Tree in January to Canyonlands in November, this is a comfy and durable hoodie for the coldest days and nights of climbing.

According to recent reports, it’s 2026, folks: If you’re still using mined chalk instead of seawater-sourced chalk, this is your call to finally make the switch. Climbing’s feature on the hidden environmental impact of chalk revealed how the vast majority of magnesium carbonate comes from mines in China, where magnesite factories poison the water and soil of nearby residents.

According to recent reports, luckily, there are plenty of sustainable brands that produce seawater-sourced chalk by using solar power to evaporate ocean brine from seawater. Here are some of our favorites:.

Shop Midnight Lightning Sea Grip Liquid Chalk.

In a recent development, for climbers with pierced ears, a pair of carabiner earrings is a customizable accessory that never gets old. Recently, I’ve been getting tons of compliments on my pair of silver, locker draw earrings (yes, they actually screw and unscrew!) that I bought at the Yosemite Climbing Museum in July. You can buy them here, but stock is limited. In case they sell out, here are a few other great places to buy carabiner earrings online:.

After breaking a cross-loaded carabiner in a scary trad fall, I now always add some sort of tape or rubber band to keep cam carabiners in place. I wrote about my DIY solution a couple of years ago, but now I simply slide on Avant Climbing’s Flip-Stop Cam Carabiner Stabilizers ($22.50 for a 10-pack). The Flip-Stop makes for easy cam clipping when mega pumped. But unlike my rubber band hack, it also keeps the cam sling open for clipping a long draw into. Crucially, like a quickdraw’s dogbone, the Flip-Stop prevents carabiners from rotating onto the dangerously weak X-axis. Nothing ruins the holidays like a pair of broken ankles.

Sources indicate that the upcoming Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness ($180) may weigh less than the gift wrap paper you’ll hide it in. At an absurdly light 78 grams (2.7oz), the Alpha SL is for those going ultralight in the mountains, whether that’s an alpine rock romp or a big ski traverse. This harness is also surprisingly comfortable to rappel in, thanks to its uber-stiff Aluula-composite construction. And it fits a range of body types thanks to its adjustable leg loops and five waistbelt sizes. Just don’t set it down unattended on a glacier—it’ll blow away in the slightest gust of wind.

Shop Arc’teryx Alpha SL Harness.

The Patagonia Airshed Pro Pullover ($169) might have been built for mountain running, but I wear mine year-round on all sorts of objectives, from sunny rock climbs to cold north faces. The Airshed Pro is a pseudo-windlayer: decently breathable for high-output activities, yet stills blocks the wind and has a water-repellent coating. The result is a shirt equally at home skiing on a glacier or rambling up a gusty rock ridge.

A note on sizing: Since the Airshed Pro was originally designed for runners, the cut is quite slim. I size up to facilitate a wider range of motion.

I have been loving the Black Diamond Solution Hoody ($299) as a light fall belay jacket and even for cold rock climbing when I’m too chilly to shed my jacket. The Solution manages to be super lightweight, movement-friendly, and breathable, yet warm. This is largely because the specific PrimaLoft insulation used in this jacket is made with technology developed by NASA for astronauts. Here on earth, it also works great. It honestly does feel like being wrapped in warm air.

The pocket real estate is also generous, and it’s nice that the whole thing packs into the left hand pocket so you can easily stash it in your pack without a cam or crampon tearing into the insulation. I’m also looking forward to using this as a mid-layer below a shell for ice climbing this winter.

In a recent development, unless you’ve been living under a rock (which many of our readers hopefully have), you’ve heard about the new film about the weed plane that crashed into a Yosemite lake in 1976. What followed was a tragicomic climber gold rush. Now, to mark the 50th anniversary of the incident, you can sport one of several new t-shirts or hats ($29.95-$44.95) memorializing this infamous moment in Yosemite climbing history. All proceeds support the Yosemite Climbing Association and the Yosemite Climbing Museum.

Have I used one? No. Do I desperately want one? Yes. As a 5’2” climber, I’m often just a few inches short of being able to make the clip from a good stance. I’ve heard wonderful things about the stiffy Kong Panic Draw ($54.95-$59.95) that lets you clip bolts otherwise out of reach. Maybe 2027 will be the year I finally gift myself one! If there’s a short or easily panicked sport climber in your life, I bet they would be stoked to get this as a present. Or you could make one for them DIY-style yourself.

According to recent reports, the oversized, durable Metolius Climbers Tote ($64.95) has become my go-to gym bag. It easily fits my personal gear plus a 60m rope, or four sets of personal gear (shoes, harness, and chalkbag for me, my husband, and my two kids). Despite having stored weathered climbing shoes zippered inside for too long, this bag miraculously doesn’t stink yet either. It stows away nicely in gym cubbies (whereas my previous Cotopaxi tote would sort of spill out) and is easy to carry by hand or shoulder. This is a great mid-sized gift for the climber in your life, or you could fill it with other gear you’re gifting for a bigger impact.

Note on price: While this tote isn’t on sale at REI, co-op members get 20% off one full-price item through Nov. 30, so this is a good one to save on.

It has been revealed that I receive a lot of climbing books and galleys to review and consider for coverage. Only some of them are so good that I can’t put them down. That’s how I felt about Erratica, a upcoming collection of true stories from Moab-based, life-long climber Brian Laidlaw. Rare is the read that both keeps you attentive and entertained, yet also evokes deeper reflection. With Erratica, Brian manages to do just that. Pick up a copy ($20) at Moab’s Back of Beyond bookstore, or find one online anywhere books are sold.

Bean Pathfinder Snowshoe Package (Best Snowshoe Package) and Atlas Montane ($250) (Best for Deep Snow.).

Snowshoes are some of the oldest winter gear known to humankind—the tech literally has prehistoric origins, with rudimentary versions dating back nearly 6,000 years ago. Today, the top ‘shoes boost flotation, grip, and ease of use, all while shaving weight. Over the years, our testers have tried hundreds of models in waist-deep drifts, through wet, cement-like snow, and on steep, icy slopes, all in the name of narrowing down the top of the class. Here are the best snowshoes of 2027.

The Revo Explore snowshoes from MSR have been a tester favorite for over a decade: They’re lighter, more flexible, and grippier than most snowshoes on the market today. Credit a hybrid construction, which combines a tough, injection-molded plastic decking with a jagged-edged steel frame and pivoting toe crampon. The 2026 model keeps last year’s upcoming binding—the TPU rubber stretch mesh Paradigm—which continues to impress testers with its security and comfort. The ridged, steel frame boosts side traction, while the two front toe crampons and a small, tooth-lined crossbar provide enough bite to stick to icy hills and steep ravines. Our Oregon tester reached for them in everything from deep powder to spring crust in Eastern Oregon’s Wallowa and Blue Mountains—when other people weren’t using them. “My husband makes fun of snowshoeing (he’s a skier) and claims to hate it, but I caught him happily using this pair,” she mentioned.

The Highlander Instinct takes the snowshoe crampon and dials it up to 11. Most snowshoes have a basic underfoot crampon for some traction on slopes, and a few brands add teeth around the edges. The Highlander Instinct uses a stainless steel crampon under the toe that’s as long and sharp as some mountaineering crampons we’ve used, plus lateral grips around the edge of the chassis and mini serrated grip bars at strategic grip points across the platform. Over three days of steep, icy hills in Rocky Mountain National Park, our tester didn’t slip once, aided, in part, by the easy-to-use heel lifts. The rockered profile and wasp-waist shape allow a natural stride and help the crampons bite, no matter the incline. That narrow waist and tapered tail kept these easy to walk in, too, without the waddling common in most wider snowshoes. They floated well in a few inches of new snow, but drifts of more than a foot proved challenging. The BOA bindings were easy to adjust even with bulky gloves, and once dialed in proved extremely comfortable and secure.

Sources indicate that L.L. Bean’s Pathfinder snowshoe package impressed beginners and experts alike among this year’s Rocky Mountain test team. The BOA bindings—not often found in beginner-friendly packages—were a fan favorite, snugging promptly over mountaineering boots and casual snowboots and never needing another adjustment. The bindings were easy to use while wearing gloves and mittens, a big plus on a trip to Rocky Mountain National Park’s Emerald Lake where the windchill dropped to -20 degrees.

On a windy, late-season day in the Indian Peaks, the crampons easily bit into steep ice crust in the morning, and the decks—made of high-density polyethylene—floated over thick corn snow in the afternoon. The poles are sturdy aluminum and adjust with an external lever lock that never failed or stuck. The only con was the width of the frame, which occasionally snagged on willow tips and low-hanging branches. But once in the open powder above treeline, the wider area underfoot became a plus. If you want a sturdy set of snowshoes and poles that holds up in most winter conditions, the Pathfinder Package delivers.

Many snowshoes are unisex, which means they tend to be too big for lighter folks who don’t need the oversized frame. The women’s-specific Lightning Ascents are nearly an inch narrower and five ounces lighter than the men’s version, making them perfect for smaller people with narrow gaits. The Ascent’s binding, a comfortable rubber mesh toe cup that secures via two rubber side straps that buckle into place, is simple to use with just a quick two-handed pull. The tooth-lined stainless steel frame and pivoting, two-pronged toe crampons impressed on outings in Rocky Mountain National Park’s Glacier Gorge, where our 5’4”, 115-pound tester tackled icy sidehills and slippery windcrust. But the Lightning Ascent isn’t just ideal for smaller snowshoers: Our 5’10”, 155-pound tester also found the precise, narrow ‘shoe design useful while climbing the gullied slopes of northern Vermont.

For those who loathe fiddly snowshoe bindings, the Symbioz Hyperflex Instinct is a godsend. While several snowshoes incorporate BOA closures into their design, few are quite as simple as the Instinct’s. The design: a single knob that tightens the toe, sides, and heel using interlinked cables that run through the perimeter of the binding, eliminating any and all trailhead exasperation. It takes fewer than 10 seconds to step into and secure the snowshoe, but the Instinct stayed glued to our boots all day long, even while walking on bumpy, uneven terrain in Colorado’s Indian Peaks Wilderness. Another characteristic we loved: flexible decking made of injection-molded polypropylene. The pliable material gave us just enough torsional flexibility to enhance comfort and reduce ankle-twisting on uneven surfaces. While sidehilling through a labyrinth of postholes in Rocky Mountain National Park, eight lateral stainless steel teeth kept our Colorado tester upright and stable.

Size: 25 in Weight: 2.2 lbs (Tru Trak bindings), 2.4 lbs (Spin Bindings) Maximum Load: 215 lbs.

Industry observers note that over a pound lighter than the next-lightest snowshoes in our test, the Elite Race Ultralights, designed for endurance and adventure races, delivered on their name. Even with ultralight bindings and minimalist crampons, these snowshoes impressed testers with their durability. The PU-coated nylon mesh decking and aluminum alloy frame stood up to rock-studded snow slopes and scraped across ice with barely any sign of wear. Our testers loved them for their comfort and ease of use; thick foam padding around the binding straps eliminated hot spots, and once set, they stayed on without further adjustment. The narrow tails let you walk—or run—with your normal stride. One tester taught several Avalanche Terrain Avoidance classes for the Colorado Mountain Club in these snowshoes, where their ease of use and float in five inches of upcoming snow was the envy of all her students. There is a cost to mild crampons and the simple plastic ridges on the perimeter frame: The Ultralights gripped well on moderate slopes, but skidded a bit on steep ice.

Pros and Cons + Very affordable + Convenient, effective heel lift + Glove-friendly bindings – Heavy.

The updated version of our perennial budget pick, the Retrospec Drifter, impressed with good flotation, comfortable heel lifts for hills, and glove-friendly bindings.

According to recent reports, the double ratchet strap bindings proved secure, intuitive, and easy to adjust, with buckles that were large enough to be manipulated without removing our gloves. The heel lift was ideal for 30-degree slopes in Rocky Mountain National Park, and was much easier to flip up or down—even with gloves on—than last year’s model. For a shoe that costs less than a quarter of some of our other winners, that’s an impressive feature set.

Plus, the Drifter is just about as bulletproof as a snowshoe gets: The one-piece polypropylene deck and aluminum alloy frame didn’t show a scratch from early-season rocks, surprise tree roots, and a long rattly drive in a roof box full of pointy gear.

Sources indicate that our Colorado testers found the underfoot crampons perfect for hard snow in the Indian Peaks, but with only six main crampons beneath the toes and no teeth around the perimeter, anything steeper than a 20-degree slope felt pretty sketchy when iced over. The Drifters also aren’t particularly strong in the flotation department: Our five-foot-four tester, who used the shorter 21-inch version, struggled to stay afloat the most.

But for $50, these snowshoes pack plenty of great features into an adventure-ready, accessible package.

Size: 22 in Weight: 3.6 lbs Maximum Load: 180 lbs.

Described by testers as “aggressively sturdy,” these near-unbreakable injection-molded snowshoes will get you where you want to go with minimal fuss and fear of equipment failure. The stiff plastic body doesn’t have a lot of flex to match a hiker’s gait, but was ideal for packing down the trail for our Oregon-based tester’s three adventuring huskies.

According to recent reports, the Evo Trail’s serrated steel traction rails, four-toothed toe crampons, and plastic, anti-slide ridges kept our testers upright, even on crusty sidehills. Flotation is great, too, for such a small snowshoe. One of our Pacific Northwest-based testers took the Evo Trails through 20 miles of deep, unconsolidated snow in Oregon’s Blue Mountains and stayed on top of the powder the entire time—no easy feat in the chilly, snowbound region.

This year’s model uses the brand’s Paraglide binding, which combines a wide piece of stretch mesh over the toe with a simple heel strap. They climb decently well without a heel lift, though we think it should be a standard feature, even on this entry-level ‘shoe.

Sizes: 23, 27 in (women’s), 25, 30, 35 in (men’s) Weight: 4.3 lbs (25 in), 4.7 lbs (30 in), 5 lbs (35 in) Maximum Load: 160 lbs (23 in), 200 lbs (27 in), 200 lbs (25 in), 250 lbs (30 in), 300+ lbs (35 in).

Pros and Cons + Great float + Heel lift + Good traction on hills – Bindings can be fiddly.

The Atlas Montane’s lightweight PVC decking and an aluminum tube frame combine for a classic deep-powder snowshoe. Our six-foot-two, 200-pound Colorado tester took the 30-inch version for a winter ascent of Longs Peak and floated easily over two to three feet of latest snow, even with a pack full of heavy climbing gear. Even the smaller decks (down to 23 inches) wowed our testers with easy traverses of powdery alpine meadows and serious forest drifts. Underfoot crampons and carbon steel lateral grips at the snowshoe’s midpoint kept footing sure and steady even on icy sidehills.

In a recent development, the Montane is wider than most of the other snowshoes we tested in both the men’s and women’s models, which gives this ‘shoe its superior flotation, but it does take a moment to adapt your gait and stop banging the snowshoes together. Our testers found the strap bindings fiddly with thick ski gloves on, but once the two straps were latched in place, they stayed there for the whole trip. On powder days, the flotation more than makes up for the simple, slightly inconvenient binding. If you’re planning off-trail travel in deep snow, especially if you’ll be carrying heavy overnight packs, these are the snowshoes for you.

Flat, uncomplicated terrain doesn’t require too much from a pair of snowshoes. Simple, comfortable bindings and a deck that provides adequate flotation are all you need. If icy slopes or deep snow aren’t in your future, save money with a budget pair made from heavier molded plastic and less aggressive traction.

It has been revealed that on the other end of the spectrum are snowshoes built for challenging terrain—slushy hills, narrow singletrack, or mixed rock and ice. A secure wrap around the heel and/or multiple straps along the foot are important for stability. Quick binding systems, like those that utilize a BOA twist lock, are helpful when taking snowshoes on and off in precarious terrain and a huge time-saver compared with fiddly three-strap setups. Snowshoes geared towards mountainous ascents will have a wider variety of spikes and crampons underfoot—and in more abundance—to offer grip both horizontally and laterally, and to bite through different types of ice. A heel lift that provides about 2 inches of lift (that’s easy to flick open and closed with either gloved hands or a trekking pole) is a must for giving your feet and calves an assist on the steeps.

In deep, fresh powder, you’ll want wider, longer snowshoes (or those that come with extensions) for superior flotation. On the flipside, if you’re headed out on a weight-conscious backpacking trip and/or proposal to strap the snowshoes to your pack for much of the trip, prioritize lightweight construction, like a pair made from aluminum and TPU-coated nylon, for reducing fatigue on-foot and outside your pack.

Over the past several years, our veteran testers braved blizzards, sub-zero temps, and icy alpine climbs to find out which snowshoes are really the best. Only nine models stood up to the rigors of our testing to earn a spot on this list.

We looked at design, features, ease of use, comfort, traction, cost, weight, and flotation in deep snow to narrow down the best of the best from the current market. This year, some tried-and-tested snowshoe models received updates, like latest bindings and decking materials, which we then reevaluated. Others haven’t changed through the years: their simple designs and technologies have withstood the test of time.

Latest Update: Latest Research Indicates Why Running Takes More Energy as We Get Older

💡 Key Takeaways

  • A upcoming study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology in November 2026, found that some muscles in older runners were weaker than those in younger runners.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Running can get harder as you age. Normal wear and tear takes a toll, and your body needs more energy to cover the same distance.

A upcoming study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology in November 2026, found that some muscles in older runners were weaker than those in younger runners. Other muscles overcompensated for those weaknesses.

“The aging process leads to decreased strength and volume of muscles, including the calf muscles involved in plantarflexion,” Changal T. Nguyen, MD, a sports medicine physiatrist, told Outside.

Dr. Nguyen is also a clinical assistant professor of orthopedic surgery at Stanford and was not involved in the study. “The calf muscles and Achilles tendon also become less stiff with age, so they work less effectively as a spring, she stated.

Sources indicate that the good news, Dr. Nguyen said, is that adding a few simple exercises to your routine can help keep your calves strong and your Achilles tendon functioning well as you age.

The authors of the latest study recruited 18 runners with an average age of 26.1 years and 18 runners with an average age of 63.4 years. The study referred to each group as “young athletes” and “master athletes,” respectively.

The researchers measured the athletes’ Achilles tendon stiffness and plantar flexor movements. (The plantar flexor muscles—located in the feet, ankles, and calves—propel you forward and upward as you run.) Then, both groups completed two six-minute treadmill sessions at two different speeds—roughly 5.6 miles per hour (mph) and 6.7 mph.

They found that master athletes’ hips worked harder than those of younger athletes. Their ankles, on the other hand, did less work compared to those of younger athletes. Master athletes also exhibited weaker plantar flexors.

Sources indicate that some of these findings could be explained by decreased calf and Achilles stiffness, Dr. Nguyen remarked: “When the calf can no longer generate as much power at push-off, the body compensates by relying more on other muscles, such as those around the hip.”.

The researchers found that master athletes also spent more energy running, and their energy cost increased with speed.

In a recent development, “One notable finding is that the gap in energy cost widened at the faster speed, from about five percent to about 13 percent,” Dr. Nguyen said. “This hints that the age-related deficit may grow as running demands increase, although the study tested only two moderate speeds, so whether the gap keeps widening at tempo or race pace is unknown.”.

According to recent reports, there are a couple of limitations worth noting. The study had a small sample size, and the runners were tested at only two speeds on a treadmill, Dr. Nguyen said. Because of these limitations, it’s uncertain whether the findings would hold in different settings—for instance, on a trail—or at different speeds.

According to recent reports, strengthening your calf muscles and improving Achilles tendon function promotes gait efficiency (the amount of energy needed to walk or run; a high gait efficiency means less energy is needed to complete the motions involved in walking or running), which can help you keep running as you age, Dr. Nguyen noted. She recommended three exercises that can help with this.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: Courtesy Gisely Ferraz).

On August 21, 2026, Jun Kyu Kim was scrambling on the approach to a climb in Eldorado Canyon, when he fell. Even though he was wearing a helmet, he suffered a fatal head injury. The tragedy shook the Denver climbing community he had been a part of. Jun touched so many lives, whether through Cruxing in Color, of which he was an early supporter, or at the crag, where he was known to offer kind advice and encouraging words. He leaves behind his loving family, his girlfriend, and so many friends whose lives were made better by his generosity and kindness.

Born on April 3, 1981, Jun was raised by his loving parents Hyoun Sook Kim and Ho Young Kim, and grew up in Chicago with his two sisters. Throughout his life, Jun was known for his adventurous spirit and zest for exploration. He discovered his love for the outdoors—where he found peace and joy—at an early age during a National Outdoor Leadership School trip to Alaska. It was during high school that he was introduced to rock climbing, which quickly became his true passion.

Industry observers note that jun once remarked that climbing was the thing he lived for. In the climbing community, he was known for his trademark red hat, dirtbag clothes, love for donuts, and his patented naps. He could sleep anytime and anywhere, then upon waking, send his project. After completing a route, he’d often be out like a light. Ever a favorite climbing partner, he exuded confidence, patience, and calm under pressure. And he settled people’s nerves, allowing them to achieve ever harder things. When friends would get down on themselves about their climbing, he was always the first to remind them to not take climbing so seriously, to have fun, and to give themselves grace on high gravity days.

Industry observers note that I spoke with Jun’s girlfriend, Sz-min Harley, and his best friend, Shawnee, to learn more about what Jun meant to the people he climbed with. Many people saw him as a mentor. He would frequently take less experienced climbers under his wing. But he also was famous for sandbagging. If you accepted his suggestion, you knew you could be in for a far more difficult adventure than you had counted on. But Jun’s encouraging words, infectious laughter, and love for fun would make it all worth the story in the end. Shawnee says that the first time they climbed together was in El Salto, where he had Shawnee try his warm-up. She could barely get halfway up before she had to come down. Jun refused to tell Shawnee the grade, but she later found out it was a 5.12b.

Sources indicate that jun was also known for his love of cooking, something that he learned from his mom at a young age. He continued to cook with her until the end. For Jun, food was a love language. He liked few things better than bringing people together around a meal, whether in the kitchen or around a campfire. The first time he came to visit Shawnee, he drove six hours and showed up with a cooler full of homemade Korean dishes for her to try. Once, he cooked dinner for the 20 people who had signed up for his friends’ newly released Beyond Jamming crack climbing clinic in Indian Creek. The entire crew came back from a full day of climbing, tired and hungry, to a grinning Jun. He had made homemade tacos for everyone, complete with vegetarian, gluten-free, and lactose-free options.

That was Jun—a man with an unbelievably big heart who was always looking for a way to help and who showed up every day for his friends. He was the kind of friend who would always be there for you, whether you needed a belay on a project or a partner willing to head out to that route tucked away in a far corner of the desert. Never letting the friendship fade, Jun was known for checking in on the people he loved, making sure you knew that he was thinking of you. He would help fix your van, make you chicken soup when you were sick, and send you a card just to say he was glad you existed. Not only did Jun give love from the bottom of his heart, but he did it without expecting anything in return.

Jun’s friend Adien shared something that has stuck with me: “Jun was a rare, selfless climber. He would go to the crag for himself, but he would go for you.”.

According to recent reports, climbing took Jun all over the world—Thailand, Greece, Columbia, Cuba, Chile, Mexico. But until the end, his favorite place was always Indian Creek. The first time he went, he and a friend only had four cams that they bumped up the routes, bearing miserably cold weather. Yet, the Creek still managed to claim his heart. Over the years, that love became even stronger and more special. Season after season, he made memories of hard sends, campfires, and laughter with his friends. For those who loved him, the Creek will never be the same.

Forty five years around the sun would never be enough, but Jun managed to fill those years with more life than most people do in twice as much time.

We miss you, Jun, and we will always carry you with us, keeping your spirit alive by choosing generosity, connection, and care.

#44565. How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1493 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm.
  • According to recent reports, but as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more key.
  • But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

According to recent reports, but as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more key. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

But, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin says.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

Industry observers note that perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

Scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s key to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

Industry observers note that before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

Loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin states. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

“When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney indicates. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

It has been revealed that when descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

With your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

Keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

Recent findings suggest that you might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”.

“It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin notes. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”.

Sources indicate that it comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

Rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

And before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

It has been revealed that “The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney claims. “You can just sort of ride it.”.

It has been revealed that on a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

When surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

On particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

Sources indicate that “I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin indicates. “I never feel like I have that much control.”.

Martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

According to recent reports, if you’re shouldering a particularly big pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

But if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.
