#44564. How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4439 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How to Clean Overhanging Routes Without Taking the Biggest Swing of Your Life

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission.
  • In a recent development, permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area.
  • So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy.

In a recent development, permadraws are incredibly convenient, but sometimes they are not appropriate for an area. There are a few reasons for this. One is that permadraws are highly visible, turning a natural setting into an outdoor climbing gym. Permadraws also corrode rapidly in marine and coastal environments. Lastly, they are expensive.

So if there are no permadraws, how do you safely clean a steep sport route? Leaving a carabiner is the next easiest solution. But what if you don’t want to do that?

It has been revealed that these nagging questions—as well as recent accidents—have compelled me to put together this long list of options for cleaning your next steep line. I’ve organized these methods into three categories:.

Each method has pros and cons in regards to simplicity, speed, and safety.

Ultimately, no single “best method” exists. Though there is a singular worst method: rappelling. Cleaning steep routes on rappel is a huge hassle for the climber, and bystanders on the ground who inevitably have to assist. Your method of choice will come down to the circumstances of each route and your personal preferences on simplicity, speed, and risk tolerance. Many of these methods are best saved for niche scenarios, or rare “if-then” situations. Still, it is best to be prepared with knowledge and equipment for those odd cleaning scenarios.

Below, I will discuss several methods for cleaning on the way up. I choose this approach if a route has a roof or dangerous swing potential or if, for whatever reason, I’m not ready to clean the route on the way down. Cleaning on the way up can take more time, but it brings safety gains. Methods range from simple to complex. If cleaning on the way down looks like a nuisance, just lower down to the ground and deal with it later (i.e., on the way back up).

Recent findings suggest that if the route is well within the abilities of someone in your party, toproping to clean is always a good go-to. Never turn down a free toprope, right?

Complications with this method arise when the climbing gets hard enough where the climber might fall on toprope, thus becoming stuck in space. If the climber is unable to get back to the wall and decides to lower, then you may end up needing to re-lead the climb to re-clip the draws/directionals, so someone can attempt cleaning on toprope again. This is a huge pain, but I see it very often. Thankfully, there are many methods that can help you avoid this scenario.

Firstly, when someone is toproping to clean, we always say they must promise to get to the top. That way, they won’t leave the rope unclipped from lifesaving directionals. This reminder helps incentivize the climber to “proposal falls.” The worst time to fall is immediately after unclipping a bolt, when the swing will be the farthest, potentially leaving the climber stranded. If you think you might fall, it’s best to adequately rest hanging at a bolt before unclipping. Only unclip the bolt once you’re ready to charge to the next one.

What if you get unlucky and fall into space? You can try pulling on the belayer’s end of the rope if it’s within reach. However, this method is usually much less productive on steep topropes than on steep lead climbs. Oftentimes, pulling on the rope will get you nowhere.

Recent findings suggest that if pulling on the rope is getting you nowhere, the next method is boinking. Usually performed on lead, boinking is a strategy a leader can employ after falling into space and becoming unable to reach the rock or a rope. But it does work (albeit sometimes less effectively) on toprope. It’s also tiring and best for short stretches.

The boinking method is simple, but often executed inefficiently. The belayer takes tight on the rope, ideally, and hovers above the ground, or over an edge where they can hang their full body weight. Then, the climber does a pull-up on the climber side of the rope to create a loop of slack. When the climber rapidly releases the slack, the belayer drops. If the belayer is too low to the ground, they will hit the ground, and usually blame the climber.

For maximum efficiency, the belayer can easily ascend the rope (using an ascender and their Grigri) the same distance that the climber needs to ascend. This obviates the need for timing the boinking/drops and is far more relaxing for both parties. It’s also far more efficient than the belayer jumping to take at the right time.

Recent findings suggest that an alternative to boinking is climbing the leash, as it’s called by highliners. This is the main method highliners use to climb the leash after falling, but also works identically in climbing scenarios when you’re not too far below your clip. If you’re flexible, place your heel above your tie-in knot, then pull on the rope, until you can straighten your leg and reach high for the wall. Once you pull on the wall or a draw, the belayer must rapidly take in all the extra slack.

Recent findings suggest that have the aforementioned methods become too tiring or inefficient? Or is there too much rope drag or rope stretch in the system for them to be effective? The next method is for the stuck climber to ascend the rope. If I don’t want to do the climbing again, I’ll usually jump straight to this method since I always have an ascender with me at the crag. If it’s just a short section to ascend, a prusik or other autoblock will work fine. But for cleaning a full route, you’ll thank yourself for bringing a proper ascender or at least nano-trax, to the crag (they weigh nothing).

If it is too difficult to pull in and release a draw, you can relocate your ascender above the draw, then clip a PAS/draw into the top carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. Slack the rope from your Grigri to unclip the rope from the draw. If you forgot to move the ascender above the clip, it will get stuck here. Begin ascending again until there is a 90-degree angle between your PAS and tensioned rope. The closer this angle is to 90 degrees, the less muscle required to pull in and unclip the draw. When you unclip the draw from the bolt, it stays attached to your PAS as you go swinging.

It has been revealed that sometimes rope shenanigans can get a bit clunky, especially in roofs. If the bolts are close enough together, you can implement some aid climbing techniques as needed. Sometimes it’s easier to ascend via yarding on bolts, and top-stepping in slings than jugging when it’s really steep. Just do whatever it takes to get up there and reclaim those draws! This can be done in a toprope scenario or a jugging scenario, with a slacked rope, or tensioned.

The biggest error when cleaning steep routes is cleaning on the way down, then taking a dangerous swing low on the route. There are many ways to clean on the way down. We’ll start with the standard scenario, then dive into niche techniques for oddball scenarios.

Recent findings suggest that many routes have an anchor just below the steep climbing. If this is the case, once you finish cleaning the steep terrain, the first step is to go off belay at that anchor and untie. Then pull the rope from above, re-tie in, and re-lower. When bolting routes, I love adding this type of anchor, not only to provide an easier, shorter version of the route, but also to greatly simplify the process of cleaning lower down the route.

The most common method for cleaning a steep sport route while lowering is to employ a trolley draw (it goes by many names). This draw connects the belay loop to the belayer’s side of the rope. As you lower, you can pull in on the belayer’s line to clean the draws. Higher up on the route, call for your belayer to hold (stop lowering) when the rope below your trolley draw is nearly level. Lower down on the route, you’ll want to stop sooner, just above the bolt.

There are a few methods for retrieving the draws, but whatever you do, be sure to stop and think before unclipping anything.

It has been revealed that the quickest method is to simply grab the wall, pull in (not up) to slack the draw and remove the draw from the bolt. If you can’t grab holds, often you can draw dyno: grab the draw with two hands and thrust in (not up) to momentarily slack the draw to remove it. In either of these cases, it is far more strenuous to remove the rope from the draw since your trolley draw will be yanking you away from the wall when you still have to clean the draw from the bolt. TLDR: If you’re tensioning the trolley, unclip the draw from the bolt.

If those methods aren’t working, go in direct to the draw you are hoping to retrieve. You can clip your PAS directly to the top carabiner of the draw. If using a draw to go direct, clip an additional draw from the belay loop to the lower carabiner of the draw you wish to clean. It’s best to resist the temptation to relocate the trolley draw into a tether draw. Note that if you remove your trolley draw and do not replace it, you could later unexpectedly fall into space or take a dangerous swing.

Once you’ve clipped direct to the draw, you can unclip the rope from the draw you wish to clean, calling slack if needed. Now, unlike other methods, the primary tension is no longer on the trolley, but instead directly on the bolt. Now pull down on the belayer’s rope to assist them in taking. That 90-degree rule applies here, too. Double check that your trolley is in place, assess the swing potential, then remove the draw from the bolt, and take the swing.

Industry observers note that the lower you go on the route, the more potential energy—and extra rope—builds up in the system. If the trolley accidentally comes unclipped for any reason, it can be catastrophic. You could swing and hit a rock or a tree. The extra rope could even cause you to hit the ground. For this reason, as I get lower, I’ll often double-up my trolley draw. Why not?

According to recent reports, now let’s imagine we’ve lowered all the way down to the first bolt. As mentioned, the farther we end up from the plumb line, the higher the potential swing risk. Sometimes it is safe to unclip and take the swing. Other times, you might hit trees, rocks, or the ground. If both parties decide the swing is safe, the climber must first unclip the trolley draw before taking the swing. If you forget to unclip the trolley draw, you’ll drag the belayer along the ground as you swing. Very unpleasant!

In a recent development, if the belayer is firmly anchored you can opt to keep the trolley draw in place to minimize the swing. However, since most sport crags don’t have convenient ground anchors, this option isn’t always possible. Just remember, don’t expect your belayer alone to stop your swing!

If you’re unsure whether a swing is safe, it’s usually best not to risk it. The horizontal distance of a swing is only a small part of understanding the potential impact. A giant King Swing can be perfectly safe, while a seemingly harmless three-foot swing can be devastating. The greater the starting angle of the swing, the more gravitational potential energy the climber has.

Once past the rope’s vertical plumb line (the lowest point of the swing), the climber begins losing speed. However, impact force depends just as much on how abruptly the climber is stopped as it does on their speed. Finally, account for rope stretch, which can increase the swing’s radius and lower the climber’s trajectory. Always make sure your swing won’t put you into the ground or another obstacle!

Industry observers note that even if the swing is all air, there can still be a risk of sharp rock cutting the rope. For this reason, it’s best to avoid big swings if the rope is rubbing rock. Usually, it’s the swing back toward the wall where rope damage is most likely to occur. Ropes cut most commonly from sideways grinding or sliding. If the rope must press rock, I prefer to place the rope where the rock is perpendicular to the rope’s force.

If a swing looks risky, the safest and easiest thing is to leave a draw or a carabiner. In my 20-plus years of sport climbing, I’ve never left a carabiner, but I do love this method because it’s allowed me to collect hundreds of free carabiners over the years, which I repurpose as lower-offs on anchors.

Besides cost, there are additional downsides to leaving gear. It is annoying to clip a bolt that has a bail carabiner. Numerous reported accidents exist wherein a climber falls after clipping a draw to the hanger over an existing carabiner, causing the draw’s carabiner to break. For this reason, people climbing after you should hopefully know to slide their draw between the carabiner and the wall when clipping.

On coastal routes, solid gate carabiners will eventually corrode shut, requiring a saw to remove. On the coast, only leave wiregates unless the wall is frequently trafficked. Speaking of difficult to remove, quick links should not be left on lead bolts. They require someone else to stop their climbing to use two hands to clean up after you. They are not cheaper than carabiners, unless you use the cheap hardware store ones that rust over and eventually require a saw to remove. If you must leave something, it must be a carabiner. Buy a stick clip and you’ll get an endless supply of free carabiners!

Industry observers note that let’s say we’ve decided to leave a draw. Now just stay connected with your trolley and continue lowering to the ground. The system will experience extra friction with the zigzag in the rope, which is nice. If you want to leave just a carabiner, you’ll go in direct to the draw you wish to clean, slack the rope, and clip the carabiner to the bolt above the draw. Then insert the climber’s end of the rope to the carabiner. Take hard, then remove the draw, and lower.

It has been revealed that with both of these methods, you can still retrieve your draw/carabiner. The fastest, and sketchiest way to do so is to solo up to the first bolt (and back down). If it’s easy climbing and you’re comfortable, it does get the job done promptly. Otherwise, removing the draw with a stick clip is much safer, and won’t take too much longer.

Now let’s dig into a couple specialized scenarios.

Technically, the advice that follows on reclaiming the quickdraw from the first bolt safely is part of cleaning a route on the way down. But it involves some niche skills. So, let’s imagine you don’t want to leave a carabiner or draw behind on the first bolt. And you also don’t want to solo up to the first bolt, nor do you have a stick clip. If it’s a substantial, rounded glue-in, you can do a lower-out off the first bolt. In short, a lower-out is using a length of rope to do a secondary lower that safely equalizes the climber onto the plumb line. The goal here is to cancel out the swing potential, not to lower to the ground, so the belayer should hold tight. Do not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete or you’ll use up more rope on the lower-out than expected.

Sources indicate that there are several ways to set up a lower-out. My favorite method? Give myself a huge tail on a figure-8 on a bight when cleaning the anchor. I make that tail double the length of the distance from the bolt to the object I might hit on a swing. When I arrive at that bolt, I go in direct. Then I unclip the trolley and ask my belayer to relocate under the anchor so they don’t swing. Once they’ve taken hard, I pass the extra long tail through the bolt, tension the extra tail, unclip my attachment to the bolt, lower myself out, then pull the rope through the bolt.

In a recent development, lower-outs can be done with a knot on the end of the lower-out strand or without. Remember, you should always have the knot in the end of the belayer’s strand! Having a knot on the lower-out chord can keep you from lowering off the end and taking a bad swing if the chord comes up short. However, other times, skipping the knot can sometimes be safer (more on that in a minute). This is where stopping and analyzing is key.

Sources indicate that lower-outs can be done with and without a belay device. If it is a pure roof or horizontal traverse, I will use a belay device to lower-out as the forces are significant. This also puts a lot of friction (wear and tear) on the hangers, and should be done sparingly. If the angle is less extreme, I often prefer to lower-out by hand without a belay device. With this method, it is absolutely imperative that the belayer does not lower the climber until the lower-out is complete. Otherwise, the force on your hands will go from very comfortable to dangerous.

According to recent reports, but, why on earth would I ever prefer not using a belay device? If your lower-out chord is a tad short, finishing the lower-out by hand is often necessary to maximize your reach before letting go of the chord. The most dangerous option is to use a belay device and no knot; the glitch being that it is very difficult to lower without your back facing the wall you’re trying to avoid hitting. Additionally, transitioning from lowering with the device to lowering by hand is risky. The safest thing is to knot the end, lower-out with an assisted braking belay device, hang on the device to clear the knot, then finish lowering by hand. If the pendulum angle is mild enough, I’ll skip those first steps and lower the whole way by hand.

Industry observers note that if you use the lower-out method, make sure you have extra rope, as well as a knot in the belayer’s end of the rope. I’d recommend practicing lower-outs in no-risk scenarios first to understand the forces. You may be surprised how easy and safe it can be to two-hand the rope. After the lower-out, simply pull the rope to retrieve. If the belayer avoids lowering during the lower-out, the rope friction on the bolt is minimal and wear and tear on the bolt is non-existent. Still, it’s better to avoid making a habit out of this.

It has been revealed that but what if it’s not a fat rounded glue-in bolt? In that case, I’d highly recommend against a lower-out due to the rubbing of the rope on the sharper hanger. In this case, I would do a rappel-out. You’d rig it the same as a lower-out, but you set up your extra tail as a rappel instead of a lower (find the midpoint of your tail). Similarly, the belayer must avoid the temptation to lower.

Recent findings suggest that while you are rappelling out, negligible rope pressure exists on the hanger, but you won’t create any tensioned rubbing friction like you would when lowering. When equalized onto the plumb line, you can pull the rope through the bolt hanger just like before. To further lessen any friction of the rope on the hanger while pulling, flick the tail and pull when the rope is lightest. This way, there will be no wear and tear.

Sources indicate that let’s say you weren’t planning to do a lower-out or rappel-out. Your belayer can toss you the bottom of the lead line to use just the same. Just make sure that before you untie the stopper knot at the end of the line, that the belayer ties a fresh stopper knot on their break strand (an overhand on a bight is fine). This requires a bit more rope than the first method, so just be careful.

In a recent development, but what if we don’t have enough rope for a lower-out and you don’t have the means to retrieve the draw any other way? If the bolt is solid, you can rappel straight through the bolt hanger. Blasphemy! This is clearly a last resort, but if you’re going to do it, you should at least know the best method. Firstly, never lower through a bolt hanger. That creates much more friction on the rope and bolt than a lower-out or pulling the rope after rappelling.

Sources indicate that I personally do not believe pulling the rope after rappelling would cause any wear and tear, especially if it is a fatty rounded glue-in. What about an expansion bolt’s hanger? Recent tests have shown this scenario to hold around 11kN. There is some mild risk to the rope when pulling it due to the sharper edges. Just like the rappel-out, you can flick the end of the rope and pull the rope when it’s lightest. Additionally, having minimal extra rope to pull through the bolt is important. Rig the rope so its end barely touches the ground.

According to recent reports, lastly, avoid this technique above 15-20 feet off the ground unless it’s an emergency scenario because the rope weight will cause more friction when pulling. And of course, this can all be avoided with a stick clip.

If the bolts are close enough together, it’s often easier to just down-aid the route. The steeper the route, the less I’ll tension the rope. In a full roof with close enough bolts, I won’t tension the rope at all. There’s no need for bulky aiders though. I like to keep a 120cm sling coiled up on a lightweight carabiner permanently on my harness, using draws as a PAS.

If the route involves a full roof, it’s usually best to just down-lead/back-aid the route. This is the standard method with the massive roof cracks in Canyonlands. If you can bump cams then there’s no need to tension the rope.

However, this article is about sport climbing. What do you do in a pure roof with spaced out bolts? After running into this scenario many times, I find it easier to do a mix of toprope to clean and jugging the rope. I leave my Grigri on the rope, while the belayer belays with their Grigri, sometimes taking in slack, and sometimes acting as a meat anchor. A Black Diamond grappling hook on the bolt hanger allows me to easily unhook the bolt and take the swing.

According to recent reports, speaking of getting creative, let’s wrap up with what will likely be one of the more controversial takes in this article. I’ve often found the fastest, safest (if you pay attention), and easiest (overall for the team) method is for the climber and belayer to both clean simultaneously. I can’t outright recommend it, unless you have a great attention to detail and years of experience with all of the previous techniques, as well as a variety of other techniques. But I’m including it for those climbing veterans who want to help their partners clean faster and easier.

I generally jump to this method if cleaning the lower part of the route on the way down would be a nuisance or dangerous, but cleaning the top on lower is no-problem. First, I tie off the brake strand on my Grigri. Then, in order to lower the climber, I will climb up the route. I go up, they go down. In doing so, they cancel out much of my weight. If the climbing is hard, I’ll just jug up to the first bolt, clip in, and lower them to their next bolt. We both clean our respective bolts at our leisure. The only communication needed is for the climber to call the standard, “lower” and “hold.”.

The climber should stop cleaning one bolt before (above) entering any dangerous swing potential. Once they’ve hit that point, they just hang in space as the belayer continues to ascend with a mix of free, aid, and ascending as they clean. Of course, the belayer should tie backup knots when appropriate.

Industry observers note that once the belayer reaches that final draw left on the wall, they should double check that they are in fact above the danger swing potential and take the swing. If the belayer is still in the dangerous swing potential zone, they can use their brake strand to perform a lower-out. Then the belayer can lower themselves, and then the climber, to the ground. This method is fast and very efficient. It’s also nice for the tired climber who doesn’t want to clean the whole route. Just go about it very carefully and thoughtfully.

See? Cleaning steep routes doesn’t have to be a huge nuisance. If these techniques are all too much, just remember your safety comes first. Play it safe and leave a carabiner or a draw anytime. Yes, it’s not ideal, but carabiners are much cheaper than broken legs.

Supermoon Season Is Coming. Here’s Where to Watch in Every Single State.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026.
  • I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania.
  • The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving week will bring the first supermoon since January 2026. It kicks off a series of not one but four oversized full moons in a row, including the closest supermoon of the decade thus far in December. While you can admire the bright sphere throughout the night, a few specific tips and tricks will dramatically improve your view—including strategizing when and where to watch.

I’ve chased at least a dozen supermoons as an astrophotographer and night-sky tourist, from the badlands of South Dakota to Serengeti National Park in Tanzania. In this guide, I’m sharing everything you need to know as we enter supermoon season, including timing logistics and guidance on where to watch the luminous sphere in every state.

The Thanksgiving-week supermoon will hit on Tuesday, November 24 It reaches full illumination that morning, but there’s an even better time to view it: sunset.

In a recent development, the round orb looks especially large and bright as it rises and sets due to an effect known as the moon illusion. A supermoon can appear up to 30 percent brighter and 14 percent bigger than the smallest full moon. Near the horizon, it looks even more gargantuan. If you’re hoping to snag supermoon photos, moonrise and moonset are the times to do it.

According to recent reports, the full moon rises in the east to northeast as the sun sets in the west, and sinks in the west as the morning sun appears out east. The golden hour hues only add to the drama, turning the globe a tangerine tinge.

The last two supermoons of 2026 line up perfectly with holiday-season gatherings. In addition to a Thanksgiving-week event on November 24, we also have a full supermoon right before Christmas on December 23. It’s the closest full moon we’ve witnessed yet this decade, at 221,667 miles away.

After December, we have two more supermoons in early 2027: January 22 and February 20. You can use the following locations to watch these or any future supermoons, since moonrise and moonset locations remain relatively the same all year.

While the supermoon looks stellar during both moonrise and moonset, I’m especially partial to its ascension because it doesn’t come with an early wake-up call. The full moon’s first appearance coincides with sunset. And soon after it rises, I can begin spotting a few constellations.

According to recent reports, with that in mind, here are the best places to watch the rising supermoon in every state. Remember: These locations are just starting points. You can absolutely watch the magic beyond this list. Just scout a viewpoint with relatively unobstructed vistas to the east, where the evening moon first shows.

Industry observers note that pair supermoon watching with thick forest overlooks in Cheaha State Park, set 70 miles east of Birmingham. Out here, you can watch the crater-pocked orb rise from Alabama’s tallest point, Bunker Tower at around 2,400 feet. The simultaneously setting sun will turn the hardwood landscapes into varying shades of peach and pink.

Watch the supermoon ascend over mountain-flanked Kachemak Bay from the east-facing side of the Homer Spit, a thin sliver of land crossing 4.5 miles into the waterway. This glacier-carved landmass provides two-for-one awe; watch the sun set in the west and the moon rise out east. If you’re lucky, the northern lights could follow, too.

In a recent development, catch the eye-popping supermoon rising above one of America’s most famed landmarks, the Grand Canyon. Mather Point’s east-facing view provides the perfect vantage point, although you’ll have numerous other lookouts to scout from, including Yaki Point and Shoshone Point, or further in the canyon along the South Rim trail. (Just read ahead on travel restrictions given recent flooding closures.).

According to recent reports, head slightly west of Little Rock for one of Arkansas’ best supermoon viewpoints: Pinnacle Mountain State Park. The getaway’s visitor center is a popular spot for sunrise, which makes it great for moonrise, too.

Death Valley is about as otherworldly as national parks get, even more so with a supersized moon rising above its surrounding peaks. Watch for the sphere above the badlands from Zabriskie Point, or head to Mesquite Flat Sand Dunes to marvel as it inches above the Grapevine peaks.

According to recent reports, perched above Boulder, the Colorado Chautauqua—a hub for arts, culture, and outdoor adventure—provides the perfect supermoon view. The earliest portion of the Chautauqua Trail, including the trail overlook, provides unobstructed glimpses to the east. For an easier vista, spot it right from Chautauqua Park. Don’t miss the sun setting behind the snowy Flatirons to the west, too.

Recent findings suggest that from Hammonasset Beach State Park’s boardwalk and shoreline, you can peer back and forth from the east’s supermoon to the west’s sunset, with the Long Island Sound in your foreground. Head to the park’s southern end, Meigs Point, for the most panoramic view. The beach is just over 20 miles east of New Haven.

Industry observers note that the Point in Cape Henlopen State Park, where the Delaware Bay meets the Atlantic, offers another 360-degree supermoon and sunset perch. You can watch the moon crawl above the ocean as the sun dips beneath the bay and, if you situate yourself correctly (about one-third of the way up the west-side beach), behind the Delaware Breakwater East End Lighthouse. East-facing Rehoboth Beach just south of here is another stellar supermoon spot.

According to recent reports, barrier island Key Biscayne offers over a mile of east-facing beachfront perfect for catching the supermoon. Head to the Cape Florida Beach at Bill Baggs Cape Florida State Park to enjoy it while watching for dolphins or visiting the Cape Florida Lighthouse; the park is within ten miles of downtown Miami.

In a recent development, for supermoon views with a surreal foreground, head to Jekyll Island’s east coast. Here, you’ll find Driftwood Beach, a waterfront made famous by its graveyard of gnarled oaks and pines. The lunar views continue down the coastline, including public access points like the South Dunes Picnic Area and Great Dunes Park. Or, join a Jekyll Island Dolphin Tour to swoon over the rising moon while scouting for cetaceans.

With miles upon miles of scenic east-facing coastlines, the options for supermoon watching in Hawaii run the gamut. Try Pololū Valley on the Island of Hawaii for the chance to see our neighboring space rock as well as migrating whales, which visit the area from December to April. Catch it from the elevated overlook, or via a hike down to the waterfront.

For a sky-high vista, stroll the pedestrian sidewalks on Perrine Memorial Bridge in Twin Falls, Idaho, just as the sun sets and the supermoon appears. Make sure to walk the east side to catch the lunar marvel above the Snake River, which runs over 1,000 miles from Wyoming to Washington state.

Downtown Chicago’s 18-mile lakefront pedestrian and bike trail is situated perfectly for a supermoon ascent. The route, located on the city’s east side, offers countless vantage points. Peer moonward from North Avenue Beach, the end of Navy Pier, or the viewpoint just behind Adler Planetarium.

It has been revealed that brown County State Park, nicknamed the Little Smokies, is the largest park in Indiana—and one of the best places in the state for seeing the supermoon. Drive up to the Hesitation Point overlook. It’s a local favorite for sunrise, which makes it perfect come supermoon season.

According to recent reports, stare slack-jawed as the supermoon rises above the Wisconsin River and the Mississippi from Pikes Peak State Park, one of Iowa’s best outdoor getaways. Viewpoints like the Pikes Peak Scenic Overlook are reachable by car, although you can get water-view hikes along the park’s 11.5 trail miles. It’s around 100 miles from Cedar Rapids.

Sources indicate that the closer you can spot the supermoon to the horizon, the better, and Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve’s vast and flat fields do the trick. From the preserve’s scenic routes, such as Southwind Nature Trail, you can admire the lunar wonder along with potential bison, deer, and hare. The destination, part of the world’s largest remaining tallgrass prairie landscape, is 75 miles southwest of Topeka.

According to recent reports, see the supermoon soar above the Appalachians from Pine Mountain State Resort Park in eastern Kentucky. The destination’s one-mile Chained Rock Trail leads you to a favorite local sunrise spot, gaining around 250 feet of elevation via stairs and packed dirt. Keep watch for wildlife like bears while you’re out here.

Recent findings suggest that any supermoon view will delight, but watching the orange orb reflect off water is especially enchanting. For that, try Louisiana’s Lake Martin, roughly 50 miles west of Baton Rouge. Fantastical cypress trees dot the water body, with frequent avian sightings from egrets to spoonbills. You can admire the scenery from the five-mile Levee Trail, or via kayak or boat.

Few coastal landmarks are as recognizable as Portland Head Light, a 1790s-era lighthouse perched atop Maine’s craggy coast. From here, sky-watchers can enjoy unobstructed views to the east—excellent for a sunrise or, soon, a supermoon. The lookout is six miles from downtown Portland.

From North Point State Park, you can watch the supermoon ascend above the country’s largest estuary, Chesapeake Bay. Get your legs moving on the park’s four-mile Hiker-Biker Trail, then watch the pockmarked moon appear from Crystal Pier or its adjacent beach.

Hear the crashing waves as you watch the peachy moon travel above the Atlantic. Halibut Point State Park provides a multisensory experience, complete with the scent of sea spray on the 440-million-year-old granite rocks. For the best viewpoint, head to the park’s northern tip, where you can look east to watch the supermoon and west to admire the plummeting sun.

Detroit’s 982-acre Belle Isle provides ample moon-viewing coordinates, all with the Detroit River as your backdrop. Hit the northeast section of the Belle Isle’s Driker Trail for the most unobstructed vista.

It has been revealed that perched atop a 130-foot cliff, Split Rock Lighthouse in northern Minnesota comes with serious supermoon potential—and, if you’re lucky, a chance to see the northern lights. To watch the moonrise down at lake level, make a detour to adjacent Pebble Beach.

Sardis Lake, which is actually an over 98,000-acre reservoir set 60 miles south of Memphis, provides numerous supermoon vantage points. Watch the moon soar above this beloved fishing hole at the end of Pats Bluff or from the John W. Kyle State Park Campground.

See the supermoon’s first appearance from America’s smallest national park, Gateway Arch. This east-facing getaway has the perfect photo-composition recipe: if you’re standing in the right place (west of the arch), you can photograph the moon rising beneath the 630-foot colossus.

Visit the west side of glassy Flathead Lake to watch the lunar globe wow above the Mission Mountains. Stop-offs like West Shore, Major Arm, and Volunteer Park offer stunning vistas that are especially quiet come winter. If time allows, detour up to Glacier National Park just under 60 miles to the north.

Industry observers note that standing Bear Lake, located 20 miles from downtown Omaha, offers a unique urban vantage point on the roughly four-mile paved Standing Bear Lake Loop trail. Alternatively, try Omaha’s Glenn Cunningham Lake, with a variety of overlooks and campgrounds on the water body’s western side.

According to recent reports, head to the crimson crags of otherworldly Valley of Fire State Park. From the 1.5-mile Fire Wave Trail or the route’s scenic turnaround point, you can spot the supermoon above the sandstone. Other good moon-watching routes in this park, set around 50 miles from Las Vegas, include the Balanced Rock Trail and White Domes.

Newly introduced Hampshire’s largest lake delivers a variety of supermoon vantage points. Try the Lincoln Park waterfront or the 1.5-mile route up Mount Major, a challenging ascent that leads to the 1,786-foot summit with granite balds and 360-degree views.

In a recent development, pair the supermoon with the Statue of Liberty or Manhattan skyline for scale at Liberty State Park, one of New Jersey’s most scenic public spaces. Hit the roughly two-mile waterfront walk for the best overlooks in this Jersey City park. It’s near the tail end of the 18-mile Hudson River Waterfront Walkway, which runs from the George Washington Bridge to Bayonne.

In a recent development, sunset is one of White Sands National Park’s most popular moments, and for good reason. Golden hour turns this typically snow-white gypsum sand a mosaic of blush and tangerine hues. The landscape gets even more magical with a supermoon to top it off. You can catch the show throughout the dune system, particularly along the Alkali Flat Trail; just leave ample time to hike in and out, and note that the park closes 30 minutes after sunset.

It has been revealed that few destinations are as perfect for this winter’s two holiday supermoons as Lake Placid, particularly along the western side of Mirror Lake. The quaint mountain town goes all out with festive décor and winter fun, including bobsledding and ice skating. Meanwhile, you can see the supermoon reflect off of Mirror Lake from several overlooks, including Mid’s Park.

With its position along the Atlantic Coast, the Outer Banks boasts supermoon sightings galore. Hatteras Island wows with some of the area’s most impressive scenery, including the black-and-white-striped lighthouse circa 1870 and easily reachable beaches like Cape Point.

Theodore Roosevelt National Park is known for many things: its free-ranging bison, badlands scenery, and potential contiguous U.S. northern lights views. This winter, add a supermoon to the mix, particularly along the park’s scenic stop-offs like Badlands Overlook and Skyline Vista.

Sources indicate that ohio is another great place to pair lunar wonder with lighthouse explorations. Marblehead Lighthouse State Park, located right along Lake Erie, faces east for sunrise and, on lucky nights, a supermoon. This is the Great Lakes’ oldest continually operated lighthouse; it was first lit in 1822.

Visit the 2,500-acre Lake Hefner near Oklahoma City for supermoon wonder in the Sooner State. The Bert Cooper Trail loops you around the lake for roughly nine paved miles; the best lunar sightseeing awaits on the west side, including Lakeshore Park.

In a recent development, the 16,000-square-foot Pittock Mansion brims with history, but that’s not all that’s on offer here. Pittock Mansion comes with one of the best views of Portland out to Mount Hood—all facing east. That means you could see the supermoon rising above the city, with the snowcapped 11,249-foot colossus in the distance. The grounds stay open into the evening, although mansion tours are limited to the daytime.

A hook of land juts out into Lake Erie from northern Pennsylvania, and it’s one of the state’s best spots for supermoon spotting. The getaway, Presque Isle State Park, is just four miles outside of downtown Erie. The National Natural Landmark comes with numerous east-facing vistas, from the sprawling beach to Gull Point Observation Deck (reachable via a 1.5-mile hike).

Many come to Newport for the Cliff Walk’s mansions, but the trail’s east-facing views promise incredible supermoon lookouts, too. Start at The Breakers and stroll north toward Forty Steps or beyond. You’ll have a number of views to choose from en route, not to mention a glimpse of the lives of Rhode Island’s rich and famous.

For a South Carolina supermoon show, visit Folly Island, a roughly seven-mile barrier island that’s located about 10 miles outside of Charleston. The getaway’s public beaches make it easy to admire that scenic space rock. Try Folly Beach County Park for a land-based evening, or join a sunset boat tour from the island for the chance to see cetaceans beneath the shining orb.

Another otherworldly supermoon scene awaits in Badlands National Park. Stop-offs like Bigfoot Pass Overlook and Panorama Point look east across the park’s striated landscapes. Get a unique moon glimpse on the Door Trail, a short boardwalk that leads to a rugged and east-facing badlands hike with yellow posts to mark the way.

The Kuwohi Observation Deck atop Great Smoky Mountains National Park offers a bird’s-eye view that’s spot-on for supermoon season. The only catch: You need to arrive early. This tower gets busy, particularly around golden hour. The road in also closes seasonally from December to March, so be prepared to hike if you’re coming for the later supermoons. Other options include the Newfound Gap parking area or the Gatlinburg Scenic Overlook just outside the park.

Scenic stop-offs abound along the 30-mile Ross Maxwell Scenic Drive in Major Bend National Park. Several offer great positioning for the supermoon to the northeast. Bookmark Blue Creek Trail, Sotol Vista Overlook, and the Goat Mountain Observation Point. For a near-private show, book a dome at stargazing retreat The Summit at Big Bend near Terlingua; guests can access a secluded hilltop complete with picnic tables, hammocks, and Chihuahuan Desert views.

With fewer crowds and flexibility to drive the Zion Canyon Scenic Drive generally between December and February, winter is one of the best seasons in Zion National Park. It’s even better when a supermoon’s on the horizon. Try Checkerboard Mesa pullout for some of the park’s clearest views to the northeast, or the paved Pa’rus for stellar scenery with the moon illuminating the canyon after it’s risen.

Sources indicate that find the supermoon rising above Malletts Bay from the three-mile Colchester Causeway. This serene perch is especially secluded in winter, as it’s not maintained for bikes. Instead, you can stroll it on foot from its starting point, Causeway Park, to soak up the scenery before driving back to Burlington, just nine miles away.

Sources indicate that admire the lunar sphere from Virginia Beach’s miles of sandy shoreline as it ascends over the Atlantic. Overlooks include Fort Story, home to the 157-foot-tall Cape Henry Lighthouse; Little Island Park from the Sandbridge Fishing Pier; or the Virginia Beach Oceanfront Boardwalk.

Rattlesnake Ledge in Washington’s Snoqualmie region is a favorite for sunrises, and the four-mile jaunt is just as impressive during supermoon season. From the peak, you can see Mount Washington, Mount Si, and the surrounding lakes. Expect fewer crowds than peak summer, but winter does bring the chance for ice and snow, so dress appropriately, especially when descending in the dark.

West Virginia’s only national park brims with supermoon viewpoints. Chief among them is the Grandview Overlook, which peers across the Newly introduced River’s horseshoe bend. Or get your heart pumping while chasing lunar wonder with a hike on the 2.4-mile Endless Wall Trail; make sure you reach Diamond Point Overlook by moonrise.

Spy the supermoon over Lake Michigan from many public waterfront lookouts in Sheboygan, nicknamed a freshwater surf capital of the world according to Livability.com. There’s North Point Park, kiteboarding haven Sheboygan Kite Beach, and the South Pier, which overlooks the Sheboygan Breakwater Lighthouse.

The prairies stretch to the horizon in Thunder Basin National Grassland, an 875-square-mile ecosystem in northeast Wyoming. These endless views create the perfect recipe for supermoon views. Set trails are few and far between here—most visitors explore cross-country—but some hiking options include the East Upton Trailhead and Kellogg Trailhead in the grassland’s northeast corner.
